News.title: From 'dirt poor' to philanthropic superstar - the life of Dolly Parton
News.content:
Iconic country musician Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80, her family announced on her social media.

"Sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Parton's nephew Brian Seaver said in a video announcement.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her show business career that spanned more than 60 years.

Follow for live updates and read more about Dolly's life.

News.title: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October
News.content:
Energy prices for millions of households will rise to the highest level for three years, under regulator Ofgem's price cap.

Ofgem said the price cap will increase by 4% on 1 October, driven by higher wholesale gas prices due to the Iran war.

A household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay Â£60 a year more, but more than a third of households are on fixed tariffs so their prices will not change.

The government said its cut to VAT on electricity bills will save households Â£45 and it was doing more to address cost of living pressures, but opposition parties said Labour was not doing enough.

The new cap will hit household bills as the colder weather arrives in October.

Suppliers say energy debt has rocketed and, with high bills likely to persist, have called for more support for those struggling to pay.

News.title: Cosmic radiation link in flight attendant's breast cancer, French court finds
News.content:
A French court has for the first time recognised cosmic radiation as a factor in the breast cancer of a long-serving flight attendant.

Sophie Lainault, a 59 year-old former stewardess on Air France, sought to have her cancer recognised as an occupational disease, brought on by conditions at work.

This has now been confirmed in a landmark court ruling in the southwestern town of Bayonne, which said that cosmic radiation was one of three carcinogenic hazards arising from her profession. The other two were passive smoking and prolonged night work.

Smoking was authorised on Air France flights until 2000.

The decision means that Lainault, who is in remission from her cancer, can take early retirement with any further treatment fully reimbursed by the French health system.

And by establishing breast cancer as an officially-recognised risk for flight crews, the court has also cleared the way for many other similar claims, lawyers say.

"My dearest wish is that the decision encourages other women who up until now have not had the courage to take this step," Lainault said.

As stewardess and later purser on Air France airliners, Lainault clocked up 12,600 flight hours between 1989 and 2019. More than half of these were at night.

Many long-distance high-altitude flights from Paris would have taken her near the North Pole, where exposure to radiation from space â strictly speaking particles from the sun and other stars â is the most intense.

News.title: Why Pride is facing a backlash - from inside and outside the LGBT community
News.content:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcomingâ¦ has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

News.title: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
News.content:
The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".

On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

"Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do."

"And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."

During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.

A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

"Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.

Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.

The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.

News.title: Yellow warnings remain in force as rain and thunderstorms hit parts of UK
News.content:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid until 22:00 BST, and was amended on Wednesday morning to cover northern and eastern Wales, as well as north-west England, the Midlands and parts of eastern and southern England.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

Another Met Office yellow warning is in place for Thursday, when more thunderstorms are expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

News.title: Ex-England footballer Sterling charged with dangerous driving after crashing Lamborghini
News.content:
Raheem Sterling will appear in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation after crashing his car into motorway barriers in May.

The former England winger, who most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, crashed his Lamborghini into barriers on the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of Thursday, 28 May.

The 31-year-old was arrested and then released on bail pending further enquiries.

A Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary spokesman said: "A driver will appear in court next month to face charges following a collision on the M3.

"Raheem Sterling, 31, from Berkshire, has been charged for the following offences: dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, failing to provide a specimen.

"The charges come following a single vehicle collision, involving a Lamborghini, on the M3 southbound, close to the Minley Interchange [Hampshire], on 28 May, 2026.

"No other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported. Mr Sterling is due to appear at Basingstoke magistrates court on 15 September."

Police suspected Sterling of "driving a vehicle whilst unfit through drugs," but that has not been included in the charges.

In May a source close to Sterling told BBC Sport there was "no proof" of drugs in his system.

The source added the player had faced "an extremely tough couple of years" and had been made to "feel worthless" and "forgotten about".

Sterling has been without a club since leaving Dutch side Feyenoord at the end of last season.

He joined Feyenoord in February on a short-term contract after leaving Chelsea by mutual consent.

Chelsea paid Â£47.5m to sign Sterling from Manchester City in 2022, where he had won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and one FA Cup in seven years.

In 2024 the former Liverpool winger joined Arsenal on loan, but upon returning to Chelsea in 2025 was exiled from the first-team squad and made to train separately.

Sterling earned 82 England caps between 2012 and 2022, and appeared at three World Cups and two European Championships.

News.title: Major Scottish gangland figure Steven Daniel arrested in organised crime raid
News.content:
One of Scotland's most high-profile gangland figures has been arrested during an early morning police raid.

Steven 'Bonzo' Daniel, 46 was taken into custody at around 06:00 from his home in Robroyston in the north of Glasgow.

Daniel is understood to be the head of the notorious Daniel crime family which has been engaged in a violent feud with the rival Lyons family for 25 years.

He was arrested in connection with serious and organised crime, firearms and drugs offences as part of Operation Ventetic, a major UK-wide operation which has dismantled several gangs.

News.title: NHS failing child sexual abuse victims in adulthood, say psychiatrists
News.content:
People sexually abused as children who seek help in later life for mental health problems are being failed by the NHS, senior doctors have told the BBC.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists is issuing a public apology for what it says is decades of mismanagement and misdiagnosis in the UK.

For some, it has worsened their traumas, it said.

The college said mental health staff have been too focussed on treating symptoms rather than exploring how past traumatic experiences can still affect patients.

Support is improving, it said, but there must be better training and more investment - something NHS bosses have said is being introduced.

The apology has been included in a report, external by the college and given to the BBC.

Immediate past president of the college, Dr Lade Smith, said she was "sorry" that, too often, victims have suffered "avoidable harm when seeking help".

The report details how treatment has sometimes been inappropriate, while people have been re-traumatised by the experience of repeated assessments and history-taking and not always being believed.

Dr Smith told the BBC it was clear people were not getting the support they needed, and that this was not just a failing of psychiatrists, but the whole mental health system.

"Services are so fragmented. The system is set up to provide short, discrete episodes of care. Psychiatrists do not get the time to build up a relationship with patients so they can be properly supported.

"They are lucky if they get eight sessions of therapy, when it could take eight sessions for a person just to disclose the abuse.

"And these are just the people who get support â many don't even get seen by mental health services because services are so stretched," she said.

News.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
News.content:
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.

The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.

They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.

And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.

News.title: 'Ironing board' seats to be replaced on Thameslink
News.content:
"Ironing board" seats on some commuter trains will get extra cushioning, the transport secretary has said, more than a decade after the government spent Â£1.6bn of public money building the fleet.

Heidi Alexander announced that more than 60,000 seats on all 115 Thameslink trains would get new cushions and backrests, replacing much-criticised thin and hard seats.

She said the work, set to begin in 2027 and last two years, was "public ownership of our railways in action" as part of the new Great British Railways programme.

However, some have criticised how the Department for Transport (DfT) awarded a Â£1.6bn contract for the trains despite being warned of the seat discomfort at the time.

The seat upgrades are part of wider improvements planned for the Thameslink network after Greater Thameslink Railway came into public ownership in May 2026.

Other measures included an increase in Gatwick Express services from December and a programme to refurbish train toilets and remove graffiti across the fleet.

Alexander said: "We'll start getting rid of the dreaded 'ironing board seats' so passengers can enjoy comfier, more pleasant journeys on some of Britain's busiest commuter routes."

She said wider rail reforms would continue under the planned Great British Railways organisation, which is intended to oversee rail services across England.

The class-700 Thameslink trains were heralded by the DfT as "state-of-the-art" and "a fantastic deal" for taxpayers when they were rolled out between 2016 and 2019.

That followed the DfT spending Â£1.6bn of taxpayers' money for German manufacturer Siemens to build the trains in 2013, following a bidding process which began in 2008.

DfT's own procurement guidance document for the fleet, seen by the BBC, stressed that they should be "high capacity" and "reduced weight".

It said the new electric fleet would have a design that "must cater for [about] 1,000 people to board or alight at one time" and a "2+2 seat layout to ease flow and provide standing space".

Some have claimed that this aim to maximise capacity and standing space for commuters led to the seats being so thinly cushioned.

Responding to Alexander's post on X praising the new re-cushioning project, Graeme Pickering, senior correspondent at Railway Magazine, wrote: "Might have been wise not to frame this as 'public ownership fixes private sector mess' when it was the DfT which procured said trains."

Two years before the Thameslink trains were rolled out to the public, a prototype was unveiled at London's Excel centre in 2014.

News.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: 'I'm still paying a mortgage for a home destroyed by a fire'
News.content:
Sarah Williams vividly remembers watching her home burn down on the news. On 26 August 2024, she was on holiday when a neighbour texted her to say the Spectrum Building in east London was on fire.

But two years on from the blaze in Dagenham, which left more than 80 people homeless, residents including Williams say they are still "in limbo".

The leaseholder said: "We're still just stuck waiting for other people to make decisions about our future."

She added that in a year's time, the money they were given through insurance to pay for alternative accommodation will run out, and she is still paying her mortgage for a home that does not exist.

At the time of the blaze, from which at least 20 people were rescued, work was under way to remove dangerous cladding. An investigation found the scaffolding around the building at the time had caused the fire to spread, although the exact cause of the blaze is unknown.

The government had provided almost Â£6m through its Building Safety fund to remediate the building - administered by the Greater London Authority (GLA) â with a clause stating that if the work was not completed, the money would have to be repaid.

The Spectrum Building was demolished in December 2024 after surveyor reports deemed it unsafe.

The building's freeholder, Arinium Ltd, has since gone into administration, leaving the administrators, FRP, in control of the company's assets, including the insurance proceeds.

The government says, external the GLA has told the building's administrators that the GLA may be owed money as part of the insolvency process.

The government says this is a standard procedural step and would not affect the money residents are owed, as the GLA would only receive any funds left after residents had been fully compensated.

The GLA said that, as is standard practice in insolvency law, it had informed the administrators of the government's interest as a potential creditor.

News.title: Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder
News.content:
The campaign has been started by Lynne Mackenzie, herself a domestic abuse survivor, who lives a few miles from the isolated cottage where Stacy was killed in July.

Stacy's husband Jim Mair, 43, whose body was found beside her, had been charged with assaulting her but had reportedly been granted bail, external on condition that he did not approach her.

While Mackenzie did not know Stacy personally, she said she was shocked at her murder which happened just six days after the death of another domestic abuse victim, Vikki Soloman, in Edinburgh.

She told BBC Scotland News the killings led her to question whether enough was being done to protect women in Stacy's situation.

"Every time driving in and out of the village I was aware of the police at the end of the road," she said.

"And it really got me thinking what could we have done? What could have been put in place beforehand? What else do we need?"

She has been in contact with Stacy's family who have agreed for her name to be associated with the campaign.

News.title: 'We just want to get home' - dozens stranded in Tunisia after cancelled Belfast flight
News.content:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent Â£4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said she and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay Â£4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

News.title: Father's house rammed before son died in A66 crash
News.content:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

Volvo’s latest over-the-air software update could help its drivers avoid everything from a crash or a set of roadworks to a pedestrian, cyclist or even a large animal wandering into the road.

The Swedish brand is adding four new Connected Safety alerts to its EX60, EX90 and ES90 electric cars, giving drivers more warning about what might be waiting for them around the next corner.

The most eye-catching of the new alerts is the new Large Animal Alert, which can warn drivers if a large animal is detected on or near the road ahead. Hundreds of thousands of wild animals are reportedly killed on UK roads each year.

open image in gallery Volvo's Vulnerable Road User Alert also highlights danger to pedestrians and cyclists ( Volvo )

In addition to the Animal Alert, Volvo has also updated its cars with a new Vulnerable Road User Alert which highlights danger to pedestrians and cyclists who might be detected on or close to highways, plus warnings for roadworks and accidents further along the route.

The idea is pretty simple: compatible Volvos can share information about hazards they come across, allowing other connected cars approaching the same spot to give their drivers an early heads-up. It could be particularly useful when visibility isn’t great, whether that’s because of bad weather or simply because the road twists and turns.

Volvo has been offering connected safety technology since 2016 and says more than one million of its cars now have it activated. The new alerts join existing features including Slippery Road Alert and Hazard Light Alert.

In true Volvo fashion, the tech doesn’t all stay within the Volvo family, either (remember, Volvo invented the seat belt then shared its patented tech with other car makers). Information can also be passed through the European Data for Road Safety system, allowing relevant alerts to reach cars from other manufacturers and national traffic management centres. Volkswagen Group, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Ford and Geely are all signed up to the European Data for Road Safety partnership.

“Built on decades of our real-world safety insight, these innovations represent another step towards our vision of zero collisions,” says Åsa Haglund, head of Volvo Cars Safety Centre. “Every time a Volvo car shares safety intelligence, it helps other drivers prepare earlier to avoid accidents and feel safer.”

The latest update isn’t just about avoiding trouble on the road. Volvo is also giving EX90 and ES90 owners with the Bowers & Wilkins premium audio system Spatial Audio support through Apple CarPlay.

open image in gallery Volvo's EX90 and ES90 models are also getting a software update to bring Dolby Atmos and Spatial Audio to Apple CarPlay ( Volvo )

The 25-speaker system already supports Dolby Atmos and the addition of Spatial Audio is designed to make music, podcasts and live recordings sound more three-dimensional, with vocals and instruments appearing to come from different positions around the cabin rather than simply from the speakers nearest to you.

It’s another example of car makers increasingly using software updates to add new functions after a car has left the showroom. Volvo says it was recently recognised by S&P Global Mobility as the only traditional car maker to achieve Level 5 capability for software-defined vehicles, with cars designed to gain extra features during their lifetime rather than remaining much as they were when they were delivered.

Women who begin hormone replacement therapy (HRT) during a specific timeframe in midlife may lower their risk of developing dementia in later years, according to major new research.

A team led by the University of East Anglia and the University of Exeter examined medical data from more than 183,000 post-menopausal participants enrolled in the UK Biobank project.

Over an average follow-up period of 13 years, nearly 4,000 of these women received a dementia diagnosis.

Researchers discovered that taking hormone therapy was linked to a 10 per cent lower risk of overall dementia and a 16 per cent reduction in Alzheimer’s disease specifically.

Commencing treatment between the ages of 46 and 56 offered the greatest benefit.

They found that those who started HRT aged 46 to 50 had a 13 per cent reduced risk of dementia, while those who started taking HRT when they were aged 51 to 56 saw a 23 per cent reduced risk.

open image in gallery A large new study of post-menopausal UK women found that taking the common treatment for menopausal symptoms can significantly reduce a women’s risk of dementia ( Getty Images )

Meanwhile those who carry the gene variant APOE4 – a risk factor for Alzheimer’s – who also took HRT, had a 13 per cent reduced risk of dementia.

And stronger links were found with women who took HRT after surgical menopause; these women had a 26 per cent lower risk of being diagnosed with dementia.

The study also found that women who naturally had lower exposure to oestrogen over their lifetime, due to starting their periods late or early menopause, seemed to have a 16 per cent reduced odds of dementia after taking HRT.

“HRT use was associated with lower dementia risk, and these findings may help inform more tailored approached to HRT prescribing in relation to women’s lifetime dementia risk, the authors wrote in the journal Alzheimer’s and Dementia.

Study lead, Professor Anne-Marie Minihane, director of the Norwich Institute for Healthy Aging at UEA, said: “We found that women who had used HRT were about 10 per cent less likely to develop dementia, and 16 per cent less likely to develop the Alzheimer’s disease form of dementia, than women who had never used it.

“But the protective association between HRT and dementia was not the same for all women.”

She added: “While HRT has long been prescribed primarily to relieve menopausal symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats, this work suggests it may also play a role in long term cognitive health for some women.”

open image in gallery After examining information on dementia diagnoses and HRT use, the research team found that taking hormone therapy was associated to a 10 per cent reduced risk of all dementia and a 16 per cent reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease specifically ( PA Wire )

Prof David Llewellyn, from the University of Exeter Medical School, added: “These findings represent a significant step forward.

“Rather than asking simply whether HRT affects dementia risk, we’ve been able to identify which women are most likely to benefit, and when.

“That’s the foundation on which genuinely personalised approaches to women’s brain health can be built.”

Dr Amanda Collis, executive director for Research Strategy and Programmes at the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council, which funded the study, said: “This study provides valuable new insights into how menopause and the timing of hormone replacement therapy may influence dementia risk in women.

“The findings suggest that HRT could have greater protective benefits for some groups, highlighting the potential for more personalised approaches to prevention.”

Commenting on the study, Aimee Spector, professor of clinical psychology of ageing and the director of the Menopause Mind Lab at University College London (UCL), said: “The results are promising in that they analysed data from the UK Biobank using large samples.

“The novelty of their findings was timing of HRT initiation, with those who started HRT between the ages of 46-56 conferring the greatest benefit.

“This supports the ‘window of opportunity’ hypothesis, suggesting that HRT use during the menopause transition phase, where symptoms are typically more problematic; is important.”

A murder investigation has been launched after two people died in a house fire in Grangetown near Middlesbrough, Cleveland Police said.

Officers were called to a house on Birchington Avenue at 5.23am on Wednesday, where sadly two people have been confirmed dead. The scene has yet to be fully examined.

The draw for the Carabao Cup third round takes place this week as more teams from the Premier League, including current cup winners Manchester City, enter the competition and learn who they will face.

Most top-flight clubs, such as Chelsea and Tottenham, entered the tournament in the second round with those who are competing in European competitions this season now involved as well.

Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United are among those to enter at this stage.

Their participation also means that the third round will be played across two midweeks in order for the teams involved in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League to juggle their match schedules.

Here’s everything you need to know about the draw:

When is the Carabao Cup third round draw?

The draw for the Carabao Cup third round will take place today, Wednesday 26 August. It will follow the conclusion of the second round tie between Preston and Everton which kicks off at 8pm BST, meaning the draw could start at around 10.15pm BST.

How will the draw work?

Pre-draw

Before the main draw, there is a pre-draw to decide if the eight Champions League and Europa League clubs will be at home or away. This part is before Preston North End’s Round Two tie against Everton on Sky Sports.

Main draw

The main draw will take place following the conclusion of Round Two tie, the first eight ties will involve those Champions League and Europa League clubs. Their home or away position will have already having been decided. They will then be drawn against a team in a separate bowl with the remaining teams in the competition – so cannot meet one another at this stage.

Following the conclusion of those eight ties being drawn, the final eight ties will be drawn as normal.

From Round Three onwards, there is no longer a divide between the Northern and Southern sections.

How can I watch the Carabao Cup draw?

The Carabao Cup third-round draw will be shown live on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports Football following the conclusion of Preston v Everton.

Sky Sports subscribers will also be able to watch the draw live online via the Sky Go app.

Which teams are involved?

32 teams are involved in the draw including 23 winners of second round ties and nine additional Premier League clubs who are also competing in European competitions this season.

Those teams in Europe and entering the competition for the first time this season are: Arsenal, Aston Villa, Bournemouth, Brighton & Hove Albion, Crystal Palace, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Sunderland.

Of those, Brighton can be in Europe through the Conference League, but that competition does not begin until October, so it does not affect the Round Three schedule.

Tesco have urgently recalled a popular meal deal item over concerns of food poisoning.

The supermarket has issued a warning for their Finest Mozzarella Pearls and Pesto Orzo salad, over the risk it may have been contaminated with E.coli.

The side effects include severe diarrhoea with or without blood in the stool, abdominal pain, vomiting, dehydration and sometimes haemolytic uremic syndrome, (HUS), a serious condition that can lead to kidney failure and can be fatal.

Tesco have warned that if anyone presents any of these symptoms, they should isolate away from work, school or nurseries for two days.

The 215g packet has the use by dates of 25, 26 and 27 August.

open image in gallery Tesco has recalled their Mozzarella Pearls and Pesto Orzo salad product ( Tesco )

Anyone who has purchased the product should return to the store for a refund, with no receipt required.

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) said: "If you have bought the above product, do not eat it. Instead, return it to any Tesco store for a full refund. For further information, please visit Tesco's customer services at: tesco.com/help/contact."

Tesco has issued its own alert, which will also be displayed in its stores. It said: "We’re recalling three date codes of Tesco Finest Mozzarella Pearls & Pesto Orzo Salad 215g. This is due to the possible presence of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), which can cause illness if eaten.

"No other products sold at Tesco are affected by this recall."

In April, Tesco issued a recall for its Tesco Finest summer edition chocolate affogato dessert due to the possible presence of plastic, rendering it unsafe to eat.

They confirmed that no other products had been affected by this specific recall, though it recently recalled cured meat over listeria contamination.

On Tuesday, the chilled and frozen food specialist Summit Foods recalled various filled wraps over potential Shiga toxin-producing E.coli contamination.

This included individual packs of Snacksters Chicken Fajita Wraps, Snacksters Hoi Sin Wrap, East Street Deli Sweet Chilli Chicken Wrap and Target a Snack Chicken Fajita Wrap with dates up to and including the 5 September 2026.

Manchester City have signed Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille for £85m in a record deal for a teenager in Premier League history.

Bouaddi has signed a five-year contract at the Etihad Stadium, becomes their second midfield signing of the summer after Elliot Anderson.

City’s midfield revamp has now cost over £200m – with Anderson a club record purchase at £85m – with the potential of a third arrival there and interest in Enzo Fernandez of Chelsea.

Bouaddi excelled in the World Cup for Morocco as a teenager and City see him as a talent with the ability to get better still.

Director of football Enzo Maresca said: “Ayyoub’s potential is extremely high - a player equipped with everything a top midfielder needs.

“At just 18, he already has outstanding football intelligence and that will only improve under the guidance of Enzo [Maresca, the manager].

“We have watched him very, very closely and throughout that process we have become increasingly convinced he is a huge talent who will thrive at City.”

Bouaddi, who was the youngest player in Lille’s history, will be charged with replacing Rodri and Bernardo Silva, who have joined Barcelona and Real Madrid respectively.

City could lose four midfielders this summer, with Tijjani Reijnders moving to Al Qadsiah for £51m and Newcastle agreeing a £52m fee for Nico Gonzalez.

open image in gallery Ayyoub Bouaddi. Manchester City have signed Morocco midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille ( PA )

Bouaddi, who will take the No 32 shirt at City, said: “I am really, really happy – really proud to be here at one of the greatest clubs in the world.

“This is a very special day for me and my family. Manchester City are, for me, the best Club in the world. It’s a dream to be here and be able to call myself a City player. I have spent most of my life working hard to become the best player I can be and reach the top of the game.

“I’ve watched City for many years, and I love their style of play. City always try and play quality football. And they have shown they are winners – this Club feels like it’s built to win.

“The squad is world-class and Enzo is a top manager. And I’m really looking forward to playing at the Etihad Stadium, in front of all the fans.

“I think it was the right time because I was good in Lille, I felt very good, but I felt it was the right moment to step over and coming to City.”

Fresh from claiming the PFA Young Player of the Year award following a standout breakthrough campaign, Nico O’Reilly has set his sights on "bigger and better things".

The 21-year-old collected the honour on Tuesday after a stellar 2025-26 season, during which he helped City to a domestic cup double and featured in England's run to third place at the World Cup.

Looking ahead to his future ambitions, O’Reilly said: "Hopefully bigger and better things. I want to go to the next step in my game, I want to go to the next level.

"That’s all I’m trying to do, work every day to try and improve and get better. That’s my goal, that’s my aim.

open image in gallery Nico O’Reilly won a domestic cup double with Man City last season ( PA Wire )

"I want goals, I want assists, I want to keep playing for my country, and I want to win trophies."

Though he progressed through City’s youth ranks as an attacking midfielder, O’Reilly earned his initial run in the senior side playing at left-back.

"It all just happened so quick. The chances came, (I had) a bit of luck and I took those chances. It was an amazing season, one I’m very proud of," he admitted.

Having established himself under Pep Guardiola, O’Reilly is now adapting to life at City under new boss Enzo Maresca, and spoke positively about the transition.

O’Reilly said: "Obviously Pep was at the club for 10 years. He did such a good job and he was an amazing manager. It was so good to learn stuff from him.

open image in gallery O’Reilly is now adapting to life under Enzo Maresca ( PA Wire )

"Enzo’s come in and he’s been very positive since he came in. The sessions have been very intense. He’s very demanding, very passionate and he’s a very, very good manager."

O’Reilly started City’s opening game of the season on Sunday as Maresca’s men came from behind to claim a dramatic 2-1 victory at the Etihad Stadium.

City will be back in action on Friday night when they travel to Selhurst Park to face Crystal Palace before facing newly promoted Coventry City the following weekend.

Attention will then turn to the first Manchester derby of the season, which is due to take place at Old Trafford on 13 September.

The Premier League is back but clubs remain eager to add players and move them on with the pressure of early results tipping the balance.

The Premier League has spent over £2.5bn this summer, with Morgan Rogers at £117m the biggest signing of the summer.

Other big signings that topped the £100m mark include Elliott Anderson (£116m) to Man City and Sandro Tonali (£100m) to Tottenham.

But more big-money deals could go through before the window closes, with Liverpool eager to spend big on a winger, and linked with Bradley Barcola, while Arsenal have also been linked with the PSG star.

Here’s everything we know about the summer transfer window deadline coming up:

When is the Premier League summer 2026 transfer window?

The transfer window opened for business on Monday 15 June and the deadline is on Tuesday 1 September in England, the window shuts at 11pm BST.

There is also a two-hour grace period after the window shuts, which will allow paperwork to be submitted.

When is the 2026 summer transfer window in Scotland?

Like the English transfer window, the window officially opened on 15 June, but the window north of the border shuts on 3 September at 5pm BST, two days after the Premier League deadline.

When is the 2026 WSL summer transfer window?

The Women's Super League transfer window opened on Tuesday 16 June and will close on Thursday 3 September, with a later deadline of 11pm BST.

When does the transfer window close in Europe?

The transfer window for LaLiga shuts at 10.59pm on 1 September, while Bundesliga clubs must buy and sell players before a 31 August deadline at 7pm.

Serie A clubs have until 1 September, with an 8pm deadline.

When is the winter transfer window?

Mid-season additions will be available when the transfer window re-opens in England on 1 January, 2027 and ti closes on 1 February once again at the later time of 11pm GMT.

In Scotland, the window will open four days after the Premier League on 5 January and then shuts on 4 February at 5pm GMT.

In the WSL, the window opens on 4 January and will close on 4 February, the same day as in Scotland.

News.title: China clamped down on exotic wildlife farms – now they’ve moved to Southeast Asia
News.content:
We hear the bamboo rats before we see them. At the bottom of almost 200 concrete containers are hundreds of chunky rodents – some squealing as they scurry in circles, others loudly gnawing corn, sugar cane and bamboo with their sharp protruding teeth.

“They’re very easy to keep,” says Suriyan Wanpakwaen, as he peers into one of the pits at the DIY breeding facility beside his home in Nakhon Ratchasima, a province roughly 150 miles northeast of Bangkok. “My favourite thing is how clean they are, there are no bad smells.”

For almost seven years, Mr Suriyan has been farming bamboo rats – and now, the business is booming. A single rodent can sell for as much as 4,000 baht (roughly £90), and there’s so much demand that Mr Suriyan and his wife can’t keep up.

They’re not the only ones cashing in. Since the coronavirus pandemic, backyard wildlife farms like this have proliferated across Southeast Asia.

While this industry long existed in the region, the mounting new additions are filling a vacuum created when, in the wake of Covid-19, China closed thousands of similar farms over bio-security concerns.

“There was obviously a void and therefore an opportunity,” said Dr Ross McEwing, a project officer focused on the illegal wildlife trade and emerging zoonotic diseases at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in Bangkok.

“There was a coordinated effort to set up these wildlife farms, led by people who could consolidate stock and move that stock illegally across multiple international borders,” he added.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

In August 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a bill – first floated in 2015 – to compensate the families of children born with microcephaly and other disabilities caused by Zika.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

But despite the national law, Ms Sena receives very little support.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Almost everybody born after 2016 has not been exposed to Zika at all... they are naive, and that piles up with the older people who did not get infected,” he told The Telegraph.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

For Erika Silva Costa and her ten-year-old daughter Stephany, the child with severe scoliosis, the struggle to secure that necessary care has reached a standstill.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.
