Sports.title: What makes Norris say “I don't have a car to fight for the championship”?
Sports.content:
The 2026 Formula 1 championship finds itself at a curious intersection where nobody is willing to entertain the idea that they have the best car.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli said after finishing second to Lando Norris in the Dutch Grand Prix that Mercedes no longer has the best car – indeed, that it may only be the third best.

But Norris, now fourth in the standings with 159 points to Antonelli’s 242, was determined to play down talk of him staging a comeback in the final half of the season, despite winning two consecutive grands prix. "I don't have the car I need to fight for a championship," he said after his Dutch GP victory.

Many readers would be tempted to cite the so-called Mandy Rice-Davies principle – "Well they would say that, wouldn’t they?"

What’s clear, though, is that under the latest technical regulations there is still a difference in relative strengths between cars which complicates the competitive picture. In broad-brush terms the McLaren MCL40 thrives in fast corners, Ferrari’s SF-26 is strong in terms of carrying good speed into slow corners, while the Mercedes W17 is somewhere between the two. That makes the competitive balance heavily dependent on circuit layout.

Norris’s contention is that his car is insufficiently rounded to be dominant across the remaining rounds in the way last year’s McLaren was the car to beat at most tracks.

Norris played down the significance of his Dutch GP victory Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"We have a strong car in certain areas," he said. "It's not like last year where we were pretty good everywhere. We're very, very strong in high speed. The place we've improved the car the most is high-speed performance.

"No one matches us in high speed. And that's a good thing. My pace advantage to Mercedes in Turn 7, Turn 8 was crazy.

"But their advantage that they have to us in slow speed is also crazy. And therefore I don't have the confidence to say, yeah, I can easily fight for a championship for the rest of the season. I know I've just won two races in a row and two poles in a row, but at the minute I don't have the car I need to fight for a championship.

"And I know that's quite a big comment, but I think last year I understood what is needed from a car and what was needed from me. And I know the level that I am now and what I can perform at. And I know just what I need from the car – and what tracks we have coming up where we're going to certainly struggle more."

The issue is more complex than simply saying a particular car is fast around a certain type of corner. This year’s cars are shorter, narrower and slightly lighter – and the chassis characteristics are more interconnected with power unit performance than ever before, given the influence of corner-entry speeds on energy harvesting.

McLaren's decision to run a short wheelbase, helping it save weight at the start of the season, has baked in certain shortcomings in terms of how much aerodynamic load the team can squeeze from the floor.

Performance is often hugely variable between tyre compounds. In Saturday’s sprint race, running mediums, Norris struggled with rear degradation and was overtaken by Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc in the closing stages. In the grand prix he took the restart on used softs, was passed by Antonelli at the start, and didn’t really get into the race until the hard-compound tyres went on.

Norris was able to pressure championship leader Antonelli later in the Zandvoort race Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"We put on the hard tyres," he said. "We were a bit more aggressive with how we wanted to approach the stint. And we turned things around. I had that feeling in the car that I wanted. I went from just not feeling like I was going to win a race to at least we can force him [Antonelli] to make mistakes.

"When I get what I need from a car, when I have the front I want, when I get the confidence with the rear on entries – just when I get what I need to be able to know and predict every single corner, I'm going to win a race."

Norris has a driving style slightly more aligned to Max Verstappen than the likes of George Russell or even his own team-mate, Oscar Piastri. Rather than separating the throttle off/brake on and turning phases, he likes to blend the throttle and brakes and take a shallower approach angle. Essentially he is feeling for the point in the overlap where the front tyres begin to exert more lateral grip, which helps rotate the car and carry more speed into the corner, towards the apex.

This requires the car not only to have a 'strong' front end, but also to communicate what the front tyres are doing, which represents a tough engineering challenge. Modern F1 cars require a consistent ride height for the aerodynamics to function optimally, so the suspension geometry is designed to minimise dive and squat. A side of this is that it saps driver 'feel'.

Some can live with that, some can’t, which is why McLaren designed an alternate front suspension geometry with a revised kingpin angle for Norris when he was floundering at the beginning of last season. Once he has that feel he can be very adaptable in terms of his lines and the degree of overlap between throttle and brake, which is why he thrives in low-grip conditions.

But although he has a huge amount of adaptability within this range, he still needs that strong front end, good transmission of feel, and confidence that the rear axle will rotate predictably on cue.

"It's clear where our weaknesses are," Norris concluded. "Therefore we need to attack those things. And until we do that, it's still going to be a very tough end of the season."

Sports.title: FIA explains safety car formation lap after F1 driver criticism at Dutch GP
Sports.content:
The opening stages of the Formula 1 Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort descended into chaos after rain had started to fall during the grid procedure.

Max Verstappen crashed heavily on the exit of the final corner on the opening lap of the race. The Red Bull driver admitted that it was entirely his own mistake. The Dutchman thought he could get back on the throttle, but that part of the track was clearly still too wet.

Behind Verstappen, Gabriel Bortoleto also came close to crashing, although he miraculously managed to keep his Audi out of the wall, while it was even more remarkable that team-mate Nico Hulkenberg managed to avoid him.

The German immediately said over the radio that he feared he was going to T-bone Bortoleto.

"It was just that corner, if I'm very honest with you. It was full wets, that place. I think that's why Max lost it and it was the same for me," Bortoleto said in the media pen post-race.

"I was on the downside of the banking. I did a little reaction move to the left, I think, when I saw big smoke coming up ahead. And when I did that, I just went as well."

According to Gasly, F1 drivers would have been able to get their tyres up to temperature more effectively if the formation lap had been completed without the safety car Photo by: Clive Rose / Getty Images

Would a normal formation lap have been better?

According to the drivers, the rest of the track had already dried by that point, meaning it was simply a matter of surviving the final two corners. Starting on slicks therefore made sense, as did the FIA’s decision to opt for a standing start.

That said, several drivers were critical of how the start procedure was carried out at Zandvoort.

"If we would go the way we did with one lap behind the safety car and a standing start, then I would have preferred to just do a normal out-lap, so we would have pushed a bit faster,” Pierre Gasly said when asked by Motorsport.com.

"I thought the point was to go at least once through the last corner and the banking with the safety car before doing the normal race start. And yeah, it was damp."

According to the Alpine driver, the FIA would have been better off choosing between two conventional options: a rolling start behind the safety car or a standing start with a normal formation lap.

"I'm sure we'll review at the next race what the drivers' feedback was," Gasly continued. "But I think it was either no safety car and only one formation lap or with the safety car at least giving us one extra lap."

Red Bull stand-in Liam Lawson shared that view and added that he already knew before the start that the procedure would lead to chaos.

Lawson emphasises that he deliberately left more margin than his team-mate Verstappen in the final corner Photo by: Anni Graf - Formula 1 via Getty Images

"I don't know why we had the safety car. To do a standing start and also do a lap behind the safety car makes no sense," Lawson said when asked by Motorsport.com.

"I'm not sure what the reasoning of that was, but I feel like we could all see that coming. We were all probably saying the same thing before when we got the news, but we didn't have control over that."

FIA explains reasoning behind safety car formation lap

When asked by Motorsport.com, the FIA clarified that it acted on the information available at the time.

The race director first sent the medical car out for a reconnaissance lap, something an FIA spokesperson said does not normally happen.

The feedback from the medical car was that there was still standing water at Turns 2 and 3, with Turn 3 – the Hugenholtz corner – also being the first banked corner on the circuit. Based on that information, the FIA considered it safer to complete the formation lap behind the safety car.

The intention at that point was to have a standing start, but by completing the formation lap behind the safety car, race control kept both options open. If the standing water had been deemed too dangerous, it could still have opted for a rolling start.

Williams driver Carlos Sainz, however, felt the latter would not have been a solution and would not have prevented the chaos in the final corner.

Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I think, given it was towards the end of the lap, a non-standing start, a rolling start, would have ended up in the same result, because by that time we were all one by one," Sainz said. "So I don't think it would have changed much. It's an unfortunate situation with a lot of water in only one corner."

It therefore came down to the drivers’ own judgement, with Lawson stressing that he deliberately left more margin – considerably more than Verstappen, who was running ahead of him.

"It was just impossible. The whole first half of the lap was dry and then the last few corners were completely soaked. So, it was really easy to do that [what Max has done] when you have this much power on a slick tyre," he said.

"I really lifted out of it because honestly I had no confidence in how much grip we were going to have there and I think Max was probably trying to get closer and make an overtake, and just lost it."

Verstappen himself, however, did not want to blame any external factors and stressed that he had simply made a mistake.

Sports.title: Domenicali hopeful Verstappen’s new deal will end talk of F1 exit | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Stefano Domenicali hopes Max Verstappen’s new Red Bull contract will put an end to claims he could leave Formula 1.

The Red Bull driver, who is one of the strongest critics of F1’s current regulations, said his uncertainty over agreeing a new deal with his team had been “mainly about actually continuing in Formula 1.”

Speaking ahead of Sunday’s Dutch Grand Prix, Domenicali said “the news of Max staying in Red Bull for the next couple of years is a cherry on the cake for this weekend.”

“It’s great news, [I’m] very proud and happy because Max is a world champion, world class person that has a great personality in the sport and I cannot see [imagine] Formula 1 without him.”

In May, Verstappen said it was “mentally not doable for me to stay” if F1 did not alter the power balance between the combustion and electrical parts of its engines next year. It subsequently announced changes will be introduced over the next two years.

“The rules are slowly getting a bit better and, let’s say, I’m willing to live with it,” said Verstappen. “Hopefully by 2030 it opens up another opportunity, potentially with V8 engines coming in, to look again.”

Domenicali hopes Verstappen’s new deal will quieten speculation the popular four-times champion will leave F1. “[I’m] very happy that this news now is official and all these talks that have been happening so far will be out of place,” he said. “Now I’m sure that the focus [will be] for the team to be as good as possible to give Max the best car that he can.”

Doubt continues to hang over the status of F1’s final two rounds this season, which will be held in the Middle East. The conflict in the region has already led F1 to abandon its plans to race in Saudi Arabia in Bahrain this year and arranged for the latter event to take place in Malaysia instead.

Domenicali indicated no decision has yet been taken to cancel the final two rounds in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. “The calendar, as I said, is confirmed, so there are still a few tickets to be sold in Abu Dhabi,” he said. “Everything is progressing well, and we stay focused on delivering the calendar we promised at the beginning of the year.”

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Lenient response to drivers passing red light sets bad precedent | Brief
Sports.content:
Formula 1’s stewarding guidelines state drivers should receive 10-second stop-and-go penalties if they pass a red light at the pit lane exit during the grand prix.

However the stewards opted for much more lenient penalties when Oliver Bearman and Gabriel Bortoleto broke the rule at Zandvoort last weekend. Reader @Alianora-La-Canta says this sets a bad precedent:

The drivers had no way to know that no dangerous situations would be created by ignoring the red light. Therefore a penalty should have been issued that involved a sporting disadvantage. Even mitigating the penalty would be risky, if understandable (due to the point of the procedure, I recognise the risk should have been much lower than usual). Now people are going to ignore the red light if they think it’s under a red flag and they think there’s an advantage in doing so, which is dangerous because the drivers do not have the information the FIA does.

Sports.title: Verstappen to race 100 drivers at once in karts at Silverstone | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen will take on 100 drivers in a special go-kart race at Silverstone, Red Bull has announced.

The four-times world champion will start at the back of the grid with 100 rivals ahead of him.

“In go-karts you learn all the basics: starts, defending, overtaking,” said Verstappen. “Of course, I spent a long period of my life go-karting, so it’s always nice to return.

“It’s about understanding the grip of the go-kart. I’ve done so many years in go-karting that you quite naturally get back into things. I will be looking forward to just seeing the carnage unfold in front of me.”

Red Bull say Verstappen’s rivals will be drawn “from every corner of sport and culture: from Red Bull athletes and celebrities to content creators, personalities and everyday fans invited from around the world.”

The event will take place on September 16th, three days after the Spanish Grand Prix, at a specially designed track at the home of the British Grand Prix.

“Creating a track for 100 drivers at the same time has never been done, never been seen,” said circuit designer and race director David Terrien. “So it’s very exciting.

“When you have Max Verstappen chasing everyone, I think that’s going to be the experience of a lifetime for all the drivers. You’re going to have Max showcasing all these skills of looking through the traffic, trying to prepare and plan where he can overtake people, and going through the traffic at the fastest speed he can because he doesn’t want to let the drivers at the front pull away.”

The event will be broadcast in some territories on Disney Plus and the ESPN app.

Sports.title: Social Media: FIA defends stewards after Colapinto fans’ abuse | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA has condemned abuse targeted at its stewards following the Dutch Grand Prix.

Although the governing body did not specify what the abuse related to, it received several hateful and abusive comments in relation to penalties issued to Franco Colapinto for failing to respond correctly to yellow flags. Two other drivers, Arvid Lindblad, and Liam Lawson, received the same penalties.

“Following the Dutch Grand Prix, FIA stewards were targeted with online abuse after applying sporting penalties in line with FIA regulations,” said the FIA in a statement.

“The United Against Online Abuse coalition condemns all forms of abuse and harassment. disagreement with decisions is part of sport, but it must never justify threats or personal attacks.

“In 2023, the FIA launched the United Against Online Abuse coalition after a steward faced targeted abuse following the United States Grand Prix.

“We urge everyone engaging with our sport to do so with respect and responsibility, online and offline.”

In addition to his penalty at the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, Colapinto has been penalised three times this year for failing to respond correctly to yellow flags.

Sports.title: On This Day: Schumacher’s stunning debut ends early at Spa | Brief
Sports.content:
One of the most famous and consequential debuts in grand prix history came to a disappointingly early end 35 years ago today.

Michael Schumacher had already electrified the Formula 1 paddock at Spa-Francorchamps by putting Bertrand Gachot’s Jordan seventh on the grid. Unfortunately his clutch died as he pulled away from the grid, ending his race on the first lap.

The Jordans were quick at Spa – Schumacher’s team mate Andrea de Cesaris was closing on race leader Ayrton Senna until his Ford-Cosworth engine let him down. That left championship leader Senna to collect a valuable 10 points after title rival Nigel Mansell retired.

Sports.title: McLaren’s car is still “horrible to drive” despite consecutive wins, says Norris | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris may have won the last two grands prix in a row but he says McLaren’s car is still a handful to drive.

The world champion believes this is partly a consequence of the 2026 regulations.

“It’s tough to say, but I do think it’s a trickier car to drive this year in some ways,” said Norris. “I think you can see that because the gaps between team mates are often bigger this year, I would say, than it was last year.”

However Norris says he is doing better at communicating his needs to his team.

“I do believe I’m able to understand situations better, to understand the car in a better way,” he explained. “It’s still just horrible to drive, but I’m doing a better job at just understanding this, relaying this to my team, figuring stuff out.

“So, it’s not just that I’m driving better on track. I’m certainly eliminating my weaknesses on track, and I don’t have so many, but it’s also how I work off the track.”

He said the changes he made on his car between the sprint race and qualifying session in the Netherlands “is a perfect example of [how] the work we put in overnight transformed our race and gave me the opportunity to win.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Norris’s team mate Oscar Piastri also appeared to struggle with his car at times during Sunday’s race, where he finished sixth. At one stage he asked his race engineer Tom Stallard: “Please give me some help on how to drive this thing.”

Despite his wins in the last two rounds, Norris says McLaren must make significant improvements in their car’s low-speed cornering.

“We have a strong car in certain areas,” he said. “It’s not like last year where we were pretty good everywhere.

“We’re very, very strong in high speed, and that’s the place we’ve improved the car the most, is high-speed performance. No one matches us in high-speed, and that’s a good thing. My pace advantage to Mercedes in turn seven and eight was crazy, but the advantage that they have to us in slow speed is also crazy.

“Therefore, I don’t have the confidence to say, ‘Yeah, I can easily fight for a championship for the rest of the season.’ I know I’ve just won two races in a row and had two poles in a row, but at the minute I don’t have the car I need to fight for a championship.

“I know that’s quite a big comment, but I think last year I understood what is needed from a car and what was needed for myself. And I know the level that I am now and what I know I can perform at, and I know just what I need from the car and I know what tracks we have coming up where we’re going to certainly struggle more, and I don’t want to struggle more.

“So I’m just doing my part to make sure, as a team, we don’t relax, we don’t get complacent in any way, and we work more than we’ve ever done before, even more than the last two years when we’ve won championships. I need the guys and girls to work and focus better than ever before to improve on these areas. If we can improve on these slow speeds, I’m confident that I can win every race this season. If we don’t, then it’s much more difficult to believe so.”

Sports.title: Leclerc failed to obey two orders to pit while he held Hamilton up | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc was in no doubt Ferrari wanted him to pit when he was holding his team mate up during the Dutch Grand Prix.

The team originally hoped to bring Leclerc in on lap 41 but did not want him to follow George Russell’s Mercedes into the pit lane. Ferrari told their driver to pit “opposite” Russell, so when the Mercedes came in Leclerc followed his team’s order and did not pit as well.

Meanwhile Hamilton was gaining on Leclerc and becoming concerned his team mate would hold him up. Early on lap 42 Ferrari told Leclerc to come in.

However Leclerc disputed the order, telling Ferrari it would put him at a disadvantage to Russell, who had pitted earlier. After a period of silence, which was long enough for Leclerc to prompt his race engineer Bryan Bozzi for a reply, Ferrari gave the driver a second instruction to pit. But Leclerc did not come in.

Hamilton was becoming increasingly infuriated, telling the team “we’re just losing time.” After Leclerc finally pitted on the next lap, following another instruction from Ferrari, Hamilton sarcastically commented: “Big waste of time guys, good job.”

The Ferrari drivers finished the race behind Russell, with Hamilton fourth ahead of Leclerc.

Sports.title: Oba Carr Had the Tools to Beat Spence
Sports.content:
Speed was not Carr’s only weapon in this hypothetical matchup. In the second round of his December 1994 title fight with Trinidad, he timed a quick right hand that dropped the dangerous champion. Trinidad recovered and stopped Carr in the eighth, but the knockdown showed Carr’s ability to identify an opening and punish an elite puncher ahead of the return fire.

That straight right would be especially important against the southpaw Spence. Carr had the hand speed to fire between Spence’s deliberate advances, then follow with combinations that prevented Spence from establishing his body attack. Crawford used different footwork and possessed a far broader offensive arsenal, but Carr owned enough of the necessary tools to exploit the same declining reactions.

Further evidence came during Carr’s 12 rounds with Quartey, whose stiff jab was faster and more punishing than Spence’s. Two judges had Quartey well ahead, so the majority decision was not as close as the official result suggests. Carr still handled that jab for the full distance and continued returning fire against a powerful natural welterweight.

The 2019 car crash, retinal injury and years of forcing his body down to 147 gradually removed Spence’s best qualities. He defeated Yordenis Ugas, but no longer possessed the reactions or physical condition of his earlier years. By the Crawford fight, he looked depleted and was taken apart in nine rounds.

Prime Spence would make it a much closer contest. His size, body punching and physical pressure would test Carr, who was dropped twice by former lightweight champion Livingstone Bramble before escaping with a disputed split decision in 1991. The damaged Spence seen later in his career would struggle to impose those advantages early enough to stop Carr’s speed from taking control.

The depth of the 1990s placed Trinidad, Quartey, De La Hoya and Pernell Whitaker at the top of the division. Missing out on a belt against those champions did not place Carr below championship level. In Spence’s fragmented era, he would have found several opportunities to collect one.

An empty championship column hides Carr’s quality. He had the speed, power and experience to beat the diminished Spence, even if Crawford remained a level beyond him.

Sports.title: Teofimo Lopez Begins His Path To Undisputed Welterweight Champion
Sports.content:
Lopez told the media at the post-fight press conference of the younger version of himself who would get mad at not being able to land against his opponent and would invite his opponent to hit him; that’s the fighter in him that welcomes a war.

https://x.com/ShakurStevenson/status/2091592063011946634?s=20

Teo outlanded Rolly 124 to 73 in total punches, outlanding him in 10 of 12 rounds. He was almost more effective offensively, having a better connection rate in both jabs (17.7%) and power punches (34.6). Romero was extremely economical with his punches, with a very low output, landing a single-digit number of punches in 11 of 12 rounds (Compubox). Former opponent Shakur Stevenson spoke of Lopez’s ability on X and what makes him special: “Teo has some sort of ability to make other fighters not throw a lot of punches and move a lot more than their usual style. I seen it with Loma, Ortiz, Sandor Martin, and now Rolly. Nonetheless, Teo did what he could with the style that was presented and got the job done!”

Teo stated at the post-fight presser he felt Rolly was not active enough and did not do enough to win the fight and thus is not deserving of a rematch. Romero expressed after that fight that he felt he won and did enough to merit a rematch. However, with no rematch clause in the contract, it is unlikely one will be given.

Teo stated at the post-fight presser his ultimate goal is to become undisputed champion, saying the following, “I got four fights, well now three fights with DAZN and all are road to undisputed. We’re going right to every world title. We’re not taking no defense, no nothing, so whoever is next we’re going for them.” The other current champions in the division are (WBC) Ryan Garcia, (IBF) Liam Paro, and (WBO) Devin Haney. Only Ryan has a fight scheduled, and Garcia did express interest in fighting the winner of Romero-Lopez; however, he must first get by Conor Benn. After the fight, Paro congratulated Teo on X, saying, “Teofimo Lopez congrats, let’s unify.”

As to who he fights next remains to be seen, but Lopez did express to the media that the current champions he would like to face are Haney last and earn his undisputed designation against him due to the controversy that occurred at lightweight when Teo was not recognized as the undisputed champion at lightweight. Lopez has demonstrated throughout his career that he does not fear fighting the best and continues his search for greatness as he continues his path to becoming undisputed welterweight champion.

Sports.title: Boxing’s Biggest Stars Were Never Universally Loved
Sports.content:
Joe Louis reached an even broader audience. His 25 consecutive heavyweight title defenses remain a division record, but his importance extended beyond the ring. Louis conducted exhibitions during World War II and served in the Army, becoming a national figure at a time when Black athletes faced severe racial barriers.

Sugar Ray Robinson followed as one of boxing’s most admired performers. His speed, combination punching and long career helped establish the standard by which later pound-for-pound greats were judged. Henry Armstrong defeated 16 world champions and once held the featherweight, lightweight and welterweight titles at the same time. His nonstop attacking style made him a fan favorite.

Rocky Marciano finished his career at 49-0 with 43 stoppages. His knockout victory over an aging Joe Louis was one of the best-known wins on his record.. Manny Pacquiao later became an international attraction, winning titles across eight divisions and carrying the expectations of the Philippines whenever he fought.

Not every major attraction was universally liked. Jack Johnson became heavyweight champion during an era of open racial hostility. Much of the opposition to him came from white Americans who resented seeing a Black champion defeat white challengers. The search for a “Great White Hope” revealed more about the country than it did about Johnson’s popularity. He was a hero to many Black fans while being vilified elsewhere.

Pernell Whitaker never generated the same commercial following as several less-accomplished fighters. His defensive style required viewers to appreciate positioning, timing, and subtle movement rather than constant exchanges. When I once asked him to name his toughest opponent, he replied, “All of them!”

Larry Holmes also struggled to receive the appreciation his ability deserved. He followed Muhammad Ali, defeated an aging version of him, and later angered Marciano supporters by saying, “Rocky couldn’t carry my jockstrap” after losing to Michael Spinks. That bitterness overshadowed a heavyweight reign that included 20 successful title defenses.

Ali demonstrated how hostility itself could be turned into business. His boasting encouraged some spectators to adore him and others to pay in hopes of watching him lose. I met him at his Cherry Hill, New Jersey, home in 1973 and again at his Deer Lake, Pennsylvania, training camp in 1977. Away from the cameras, he was far different from the confrontational character used to sell fights.

Ricky Hatton, Mike Tyson, Marvin Hagler, Sugar Ray Leonard, Willie Pep and Alexis Arguello also built devoted followings through different combinations of personality, nationality and fighting style. I met all except Hatton and found each of them to be a gentleman.

The history shows why ranking boxers only as “popular” or “unpopular” is too simple. Some were loved, some were resented, and a select few became enormous attractions by giving audiences reasons to feel both.

Sports.title: Ade Oladipo Misreads George Foreman’s Place in History
Sports.content:
“That’s horrendous,” Ade said. “What? Because he can sell grills, all of a sudden he can fight?”

He then assigned almost all the Rumble in the Jungle’s importance to Muhammad Ali, arguing that Ali could have faced someone else and produced the same event.

“I’d never heard anything about Foreman,” Oladipo said. “That is all Muhammad Ali.”

During his interview with Helwani, Oladipo first claimed the clip had been taken out of context. He described the original exchange as a light argument over the most famous boxer ever, with Gough bringing up the Foreman grill while Oladipo defended Ali. That account softened the substance of his own remarks.

“It wasn’t necessarily anti-George Foreman. I think it was so pro-Ali that I was like, ‘No, no, my guy,’” Oladipo told Ariel Helwani. “I was just saying my guy is numero uno, and by defending my guy kind of shot down others… I certainly didn’t mean to be disrespectful to the late, great George Foreman… I was just trying to back my guy, and I think maybe I batted a bit too hard.”

That is closer to an admission than a defense. Oladipo knew while recording the segment that his remarks might generate criticism. He now accepts that Foreman was one of the greatest heavyweights ever and that he unfairly diminished him while arguing for Ali.

Before making that concession, Oladipo spent several minutes attacking his critics. He called them jealous, dismissed some as “minions” and suggested members of the boxing media were using the clip to pursue his broadcasting position. He also complained that boxing expects commentators to possess the equivalent of a university doctorate in the sport’s history.

Born in 1981, Oladipo was not around for Foreman’s rise. He never experienced the sequence of an Olympic gold medalist developing into boxing’s most destructive heavyweight, wiping out established champions and arriving in Zaire with the aura of an unbeatable force.

Foreman’s 1973 destruction of Joe Frazier remains among boxing’s most memorable title changes. Howard Cosell’s repeated cry of “Down goes Frazier” entered American sports culture as Foreman dropped the champion six times in two rounds.

Frazier had defeated Ali two years earlier. Ken Norton had broken Ali’s jaw and beaten him in 1973. Foreman needed only two rounds to destroy Norton, then later stopped Frazier for a second time.

He was the Mike Tyson of an earlier generation. Spectators watched because Foreman’s knockouts carried a frightening inevitability. Ali supplied unmatched personality and global celebrity in Zaire, while the champion across from him represented terrifying physical danger.

Claiming that Ali could have fought anyone in Kinshasa and created the same spectacle also reduces Ali’s accomplishment. The Rumble in the Jungle achieved immortality because Ali conquered the undefeated destroyer whom many believed might seriously hurt him. Replace Foreman with a routine contender and the event becomes another Ali title fight rather than a defining moment in sports history. Foreman’s reputation was not incidental to the legend. It was the obstacle that made Ali’s victory extraordinary.

The grill argument reverses the cause and effect. Foreman’s fame did not originate with kitchen appliances. Their enormous commercial success relied on a recognizable former heavyweight champion with an extraordinary personal story. Modern casual fans may associate the older, smiling Foreman with television commercials, but audiences in the 1970s knew him as an intimidating knockout artist.

His second career further weakens Oladipo’s dismissal. Foreman returned after a decade away, rebuilt himself in public and knocked out Michael Moorer in 1994 to regain the heavyweight championship at age 45. That accomplishment introduced him to another generation and completed a remarkable reinvention. His popularity rested on the combination of his terrifying first reign, historic comeback, and transformed personality. The grill capitalized on that story; it did not create it.

A broadcaster does not need personal memories of every boxing era. Curiosity is supposed to fill that absence. Foreman’s rise is not obscure material from 1922, as Oladipo’s comparison suggested. The heavyweight era containing Ali, Foreman, Frazier and Norton is foundational knowledge for anyone paid to discuss boxing professionally.

Calling critics jealous avoids that distinction. They were not demanding expertise in forgotten bare-knuckle champions. The criticism followed because a prominent broadcaster showed limited preparation on one of the sport’s central figures, then treated the reaction as an attempt to take his job.

The mistake was not choosing Ali as the more famous man. It was mistaking the older George Foreman Oladipo knew for the young fighter the world feared. Blaming the reaction on missing context and professional jealousy does not correct that historical blind spot.

Sports.title: Richardson Hitchins Blames “Higher Ups” for Avoiding Norman
Sports.content:
“You not it the higher ups don’t care to see me whoop you #Facts,” Hitchins posted on X. “It would be bullying lil ni**a only thing that’s gone beat you up is ya ballz I’ll spank you from 1 to 12 bum.”

The contradiction could not be more obvious. If Norman truly offers zero resistance, Hitchins should jump at the chance to fight him. Dominating a recognizable name would solidify his status at welterweight, generate valuable highlight reels, plus give instant credibility to his claim that he belongs among the elite.

Instead, Hitchins dismisses Norman as unworthy while refusing to back up the insult. That is an ancient boxing trick, giving a fighter an easy exit from a dangerous matchup without having to confess to the hesitation underneath.

Nothing on his record justifies that kind of arrogance. His crowning moments came against Liam Paro and an undersized George Kambosos Jr. Hitchins edged Paro by a narrow split decision in late 2024 before stopping Kambosos in the eighth round half a year later. Kambosos was a lightweight moving up to junior welterweight who had already dropped three of his last five ring appearances. Bragging about bullying legitimate welterweights sounds absurd when your biggest triumph came against a faded, outsized opponent.

Norman brings power, real physical size, plus elite speed. He is entering his prime at his natural weight class, representing a completely different tier of danger. Gustavo Lemos brought relentless pressure. Jose Zepeda brought veteran craft. Neither man carried the firepower to punish mistakes the way Norman can.

Shutting out Ricardo Salas in July proved nothing about competing with the elite. Salas provided a gentle introduction to 147 pounds. That easy win offered zero evidence that Hitchins can handle a destructive puncher who will force real exchanges.

The tough talk collapses under any honest examination of his ring identity. Hitchins postures like a vicious finisher online, yet inside the ropes he operates strictly as a cautious technician who controls distance, avoids messy trades, and collects decision wins. He possesses real boxing skill, but his safety-first style looks nothing like the beatdown he advertised.

Belittling Norman looks especially weak after Hitchins pulled out of the Oscar Duarte bout on the day of the event in February. Instead of rebooking a dangerous assignment, he sat idle for months before returning against a harmless opponent in Salas. Choosing the soft path in matchmaking makes his loud talk impossible to take seriously.

Elite fighters who actually want an opponent take control of the situation. They order their teams to send contracts, call out rivals directly on camera, and force the other side to say no publicly.

Hitchins has done none of that. He mentions no specific promoters, points to zero failed talks, and produces not a single rejected contract. His vague talk about unnamed suits is simply a convenient hiding spot, letting him posture online without ever having to back up his words in the ring.

Until Hitchins tells his team to put real paper in front of Norman, dismissing the matchup as bullying remains pure theater. It is the cheap talk of a fighter whose matchmaking stays safe while his mouth makes promises his ring choices refuse to keep.

Sports.title: Mannix: Teofimo Lopez Knows Ryan Garcia Is Next
Sports.content:
Losing to Benn would remove that justification. Garcia would no longer bring the WBC belt, leaving Lopez to choose a commercially valuable voluntary defense over a mandated consolidation. Allowing it would amount to the WBA discarding its order because Lopez found a more profitable opponent.

Catterall is not merely a contender waiting after winning an eliminator. He captured the WBA Regular welterweight title by defeating Shakhram Giyasov and was promised a fight against the primary champion within 180 days. Lopez inherited that obligation when he took the WBA title from Rolando Romero.

The sanctioning body must now decide how much its own order is worth. A Garcia unification would produce greater attention and a larger sanctioning fee, but another postponement would further reduce the value of holding its Regular title. Fighters are asked to compete for that belt, pay sanctioning fees and trust that victory will lead to the primary champion.

Lopez’s apparent freedom to plan around Catterall shows that commercial appeal may defeat enforcement. If the WBA permits Garcia to go first, especially after a loss to Benn, it will make itself look second-rate by showing that its orders apply only when champions have nothing richer available.

Matchroom Presses WBA To Force Teofimo Lopez vs. Jack Catterall

Jack Catterall confirmed Tuesday that Eddie Hearn and Matchroom sent a letter to the WBA in an attempt to get his title fight with Teofimo Lopez enforced.

“Letter was sent to them yesterday by Eddie and Matchroom,” Catterall posted on X in response to a supporter asking his team to act.

Catterall also revealed that WBA president Gilberto Mendoza personally promised him that the 180-day commitment would remain in place regardless of who held the Super title.

“When I met Gilberto Mendoza in Egypt, I shook his hand and he gave me his word if I beat Giyasov, someone who was avoided and waited for his shot for two years, I will get my shot within 180 days regardless who has the belt. So I believe the WBA will do the correct thing,” Catterall posted.

That account removes much of the uncertainty about what the WBA intended. Its published resolution named Rolando Romero, but its president allegedly told Catterall that the commitment followed the title. Lopez still has a technical argument based on the written wording, yet the WBA would have to break Mendoza’s personal promise to let him move on.

The dispute began after Lopez openly denied that Catterall was his mandatory during Monday’s Inside the Ring show. Lopez plans to pursue the three additional titles he needs to become the undisputed welterweight champion, beginning with the winner of Ryan Garcia versus Conor Benn on September 12.

That pursuit leaves no place for Catterall, but the secondary WBA champion has rejected the easiest negotiated solution.

“There’s not $1 that can persuade me to step aside to allow a unification bout to happen. I’m here to fight,” Catterall said.

His refusal means Matchroom cannot be paid to wait while Lopez pursues the Garcia vs. Benn winner. The WBA must enforce the consolidation fight, permit a unification first, or allow its two welterweight champions to remain separated.

The 180-day period expires on November 19, based on Catterall’s May 23 victory over Shakhram Giyasov. That leaves less than three months to settle the dispute. The cut Lopez suffered over his right eyebrow against Rolando Romero places more strain on the schedule, although there has been no indication that it will keep him out for an extended period.

Teofimo may believe the WBA will permit a unification to take priority over its internal consolidation fight. Sanctioning bodies regularly move mandatory obligations aside when champions pursue another belt, giving his team a stronger argument than the wording omission alone.

Catterall brings tactical risk with little financial reward. His awkward southpaw style and sharp counterpunching deny opponents clean offensive opportunities. Ryan Garcia, Conor Benn and Devin Haney generate massive paydays. Catterall brings no comparable commercial appeal, only a genuine threat to expose Lopez inside the ring.

WBA Loophole Gives Teofimo Lopez Easy Out On Jack Catterall

A review of the WBA’s published rulings supports part of Teofimo Lopez’s argument. No public order currently names Jack Catterall as the mandatory challenger for Lopez’s newly acquired Super welterweight title.

The May 21 ruling required Rolando Romero to face the Catterall-Shakhram Giyasov winner within 180 days. Its language named Romero specifically. It did not say the obligation would transfer to Romero’s successor if the title changed hands.

That omission gives Lopez a technical basis for denying that Catterall has been formally assigned to him. The WBA would need to issue another ruling, clarify that the original order followed the championship, or designate Catterall as Lopez’s challenger.

Teofimo still goes too far by claiming Catterall was lied to. The WBA sanctioned the Giyasov bout and publicly stated that its winner would receive Romero within 180 days. Catterall’s expectation came directly from the organization, not from an invented promise by his team.

The real issue is poor wording from the WBA. It created two champions and ordered them to meet, yet attached the obligation to Romero by name rather than clearly attaching it to the Super title. Lopez is now using that opening to pursue the Garcia-Benn winner while Catterall waits for the WBA to explain what its own ruling means.

Teofimo Lopez Denies Jack Catterall Mandatory Status

Teofimo Lopez claims Jack Catterall is not his WBA mandatory and says the British contender was lied to about his right to challenge for the welterweight title.

During today’s Inside the Ring show, Catterall confronted the new WBA champion after Lopez discussed facing the Ryan Garcia vs. Conor Benn winner and eventually meeting Devin Haney for the undisputed championship.

“He’s not. He’s not my mandatory,” Lopez said when Catterall was identified as next in line. “By the sanctioning rules, he’s not my mandatory, and I think they lied. I think they lied to him.”

“It’s in the contract,” Catterall answered.

Teofimo’s denial conflicts with the WBA’s own published ruling. When the organization elevated Rolando Romero to Super champion in May, it sanctioned Catterall’s bout with Shakhram Giyasov for the vacant secondary title and stated that Romero had to face the winner within 180 days.

Catterall defeated Giyasov and now holds that belt. Lopez may argue that the ruling named Romero rather than whoever defeated him, or that no separate order has been issued since Saturday. Neither explanation supports his claim that Catterall was lied to. The WBA publicly connected the two titles and imposed a deadline for bringing them together.

The exchange became entertaining because Lopez tried to rewrite the situation while Catterall was on the screen looking directly at him. Rather than explain the supposed sanctioning rule, Teofimo declared that the obligation did not exist and blamed unnamed people for misleading Catterall.

After making that denial, the new champion returned to the familiar claim that he will face anyone.

“I’m always willing to fight anybody and everybody,” Lopez said.

“I’m glad you won on the weekend because I know you don’t duck nobody,” Catterall replied. “It would have been more difficult to get Rolly into the ring. I’m happy for you, but we’ve got to get it on.”

Catterall played the interaction perfectly. He congratulated Lopez, reminded him that Romero would have been harder to bring into the ring and declined to turn the conversation into a shouting match. That left Teofimo arguing against a contract he had not seen while Catterall calmly insisted the terms were already written down.

There was also some clever pressure inside Catterall’s praise. Telling Lopez, “I know you don’t duck nobody,” gave the champion little room to reject the fight without contradicting the reputation Catterall had just assigned to him.

The WBA now needs to explain the status of its own ruling. It can grant Lopez permission to pursue a unification, arrange a step-aside payment or order the title consolidation. What it cannot credibly do is remain silent while its new champion claims the other titleholder was fooled.

Lopez is clearly trying to look past the mandatory to chase the massive paydays against the Ryan Garcia vs. Conor Benn winner or a unification with Devin Haney. Catterall holds the regular belt after beating Shakhram Giyasov, which, in standard WBA procedure, makes him the direct mandatory to unify the titles.

Sports.title: Frank Warren Expects Fury-Joshua Fight in America
Sports.content:
“I genuinely think it will happen. His Excellency, Turki Alalshikh, he will announce that fairly soon. I know there’s been some issues with contracts with Matchroom and AJ; I believe they will iron all those out. In the meantime, Tyson has flown off to the States. He’s in Miami, and he’s preparing for the fight,” said Warren to Sky Sports News.

Fury recently placed the fight in “serious doubt” and accused Joshua of wanting more money after plans moved away from a British stadium. Eddie Hearn has argued that Joshua signed for a UK event and that staging it in America would reduce his earnings after taxes while adding obligations to the contract.

That account undercuts the suggestion that Joshua alone wants to keep the event in Britain. Warren said Fury also prefers Wembley, but the broadcaster and financial backers have chosen America.

“They could refuse to fight. We don’t get the fight we want to see,” Warren said. “I think because of the amount of money involved, I hope I’m wrong, but I think it will go on in America.”

Much depends on how determined Joshua and Hearn are to increase his purse or force a return to the original terms. Hearn has openly rejected the venue change without amendments to Joshua’s contract, added payment and other demands from Alalshikh’s side.

Those public complaints may also have irritated Alalshikh, Sela and TKO Boxing. Joshua has lost the ability to negotiate the way he did during his prime. He has no world title, lost twice to Oleksandr Usyk and was knocked out by Daniel Dubois.

His last fight further weakened his position. Kristian Prenga was brought in for a showcase tune-up, but the second-tier heavyweight dropped Joshua twice in the opening round. Joshua was saved by the bell before returning to stop Prenga in the second.

Hearn can demand more money for moving the event, but the organizers have far less reason to agree to it than they would have had six years ago. The Prenga scare gave them another reason not to treat Joshua like one of the best heavyweights in the division.

This matchup is roughly six years past the point when it carried its greatest sporting value. Fury and Joshua once held every major heavyweight title between them, but repeated negotiations never brought them into the same ring. Usyk eventually beat both men and took away the argument over which one was the best heavyweight of their generation.

Fury has declined as well. He lost twice to Usyk before retiring and returning when another enormous payday became available. Training in Miami does not change what has happened to him or Joshua.

No longer a contest to determine Britain’s best heavyweight or the leading fighter in the division, it is now a nostalgia event for supporters who followed both men during their primes. The fight still makes money because of who Fury and Joshua used to be, not because of what either man has left.

Joshua may have the contractual right to reject America, but using it risks losing a payday that may never return. Hearn can continue pressing for revised terms, although his case weakens if the financial backers decide the price is too high for a fight between two heavyweights who are shot to pieces.

Eddie Hearn: Nobody Can Stop Fury-Joshua Fight

Eddie Hearn insists Anthony Joshua’s fight with Tyson Fury remains legally binding and can only collapse if Sela breaches the signed agreement.

Fury claimed Friday that the fight no longer looked likely, blaming Joshua and Hearn for seeking more money. Hearn has now rejected that account, maintaining that both fighters are signed and Joshua’s side is only waiting for Sela to provide a date.

“The update is quite simple. We’ve signed the contract. We’re waiting for a date. You saw Tyson Fury on the elliptical trainer, shouting and screaming. There’s nothing to shout about. The fight’s done, the fight’s signed,” Hearn told DAZN Boxing. “No one can pull out of the fight. You can’t just pull out of a contract. So, we’re waiting on the date.”

The dispute remains tied to the location. Joshua’s agreement calls for the fight to take place in the UK, while Sela, Netflix and the other parties involved favor New York. Hearn has submitted separate terms that would allow Joshua to accept Madison Square Garden, but he made clear that his preference remains a British stadium.

If Sela rejects those changes, Hearn expects the company to follow the existing contract and deliver the event in the UK.

“If they deliver on the contract, which they have to legally, the fight’s happening in the UK, and we’ll be very, very happy,” Hearn said. “The only way it can stop from happening is if they actually breach the contract.”

That line leaves Sela with two direct options: honor the UK agreement or meet Joshua’s terms for America. Sela can still abandon the event in practice, but doing so may expose the company to a costly legal claim. The possible damages cannot be calculated without seeing the cancellation and breach provisions.

Hearn’s claim is legally forceful but practically overstated. Sela cannot withdraw without risking financial penalties, but it can still refuse to finance the event. A contract creates legal consequences for breaking an agreement; it does not guarantee that a boxing match reaches the ring.

The greater issue may come after the lawyers finish. Joshua has received some of his largest purses through Turki Alalshikh and Sela. Hearn can use the UK clause to secure better terms for New York, but pushing too far risks damaging the relationship that makes paydays of this size possible. Few other backers can offer Joshua comparable money at this stage of his career.

Sports.title: How Boxing Turned Sonny Liston Into Its Monster
Sports.content:
There were legitimate reasons to scrutinize him. Liston’s history included prison time for armed robbery, further arrests and ties to men with organized crime interests in boxing. Frankie Carbo and Frank “Blinky” Palermo held financial interests in his career. Reporters were justified in questioning those relationships.

The coverage frequently went beyond examining his history. It allowed that history to obscure every other part of him. Boxing offered Liston no rehabilitation story, even though prison was where he learned to box and found the skill that gave him a legal profession. His past was not presented as something he had survived. It became proof that he remained permanently dangerous. Race also influenced how America saw him. Patterson was considered respectable, articulate, and safe for the heavyweight title. Liston became the large, scowling Black man coming to take it away. His size, stare, and criminal record were packaged together until the fighter disappeared behind the character.

Liston did little to soften that image because he never looked comfortable performing for the press. He rarely smiled, gave short answers, and looked ill at ease during interviews. Reporters often interpreted his discomfort as hostility. He lacked the education, confidence, and media training to present another version of himself.

Other Black heavyweight champions had qualities that helped reassure or captivate the public. Joe Louis projected quiet dignity. Patterson displayed sensitivity and vulnerability. Muhammad Ali later controlled every room through humor, intelligence, and language. Liston possessed none of those qualities. His silence allowed promoters and reporters to define him.

Destroying Patterson strengthened the monster boxing had created. Liston knocked him out in 2:06 at Comiskey Park, then required only four additional seconds to repeat the result in their July 1963 rematch. Those victories should have confirmed his place as an exceptional heavyweight. Instead, they made him look cruel.

The performances were also reduced to physical intimidation. Liston possessed enormous strength and punching power, but he was not an unskilled bully. His long jab controlled distance, his body punches weakened opponents, and his ability to cut off the ring prevented smaller heavyweights from escaping. Cleveland Williams and Zora Folley were beaten by a technically developed fighter, not merely a frightening man with heavy hands.

Cassius Clay understood Liston’s public identity and used it against him. He mocked Liston’s appearance, age and intelligence before taking the championship in February 1964. When Liston remained on his stool after the sixth round, the supposedly indestructible champion was recast as a coward. The disputed first-round finish in their 1965 rematch added another permanent stain. Questions about those fights have followed Liston for decades, but they now overshadow almost everything he accomplished. His mob associations, two losses to Ali and mysterious death dominate his story. His jab, strength and destruction of the leading heavyweights of his era receive far less attention.

Liston contributed to his reputation through his criminal activity and the people surrounding his career. Those facts ultimately swallowed every other part of him. Boxing built a monster, profited from the fear, and discarded the man once Ali supplied the sport with a more charismatic champion.

Ghana News.title: World Bank warns Ghana’s recovery remains structurally incomplete
Ghana News.content:
Robert R. Taliercio

Ghana’s economic recovery has been strong but remains structurally incomplete, with persistent poverty, weak job creation and infrastructure gaps threatening the sustainability of recent gains, the World Bank Division Director for Ghana, Liberia and Sierra Leone, Robert R. Taliercio, has said.

Speaking at the launch of the World Bank’s *Tenth Ghana Economic Update* in Accra on Wednesday, August 26, 2026, Mr Taliercio said the economy grew by 6% in 2025, the fastest pace since 2019, before accelerating further to 6.4% in the first quarter of 2026.

According to him, the country had also made significant progress in macroeconomic stability, with headline inflation falling from 23.2% in February 2025 to 3.2% in March 2026, although it had since increased to 4.6%*.

He stated that Ghana’s successful completion of its International Monetary Fund Extended Credit Facility programme was a major milestone that demonstrated restored economic credibility.

He added that the country recorded a primary fiscal surplus of 2.5% of GDP in 2025, exceeding the 1.5% target, while public debt declined from 70.3% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 2024 to 49% at the end of 2025.

“Government deserves full credit for the difficult decisions that made these results possible,” Mr Taliercio said.

However, he cautioned that the gains should not obscure the structural weaknesses still confronting the economy.

“The recovery remains structurally incomplete,” he said, noting that the fiscal surplus had been achieved largely through expenditure compression”.

He said capital spending was *38% below budget*, warning that such an approach was not sustainable for long-term growth and development.

Mr Taliercio said Ghana must strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation to support sustained fiscal consolidation, while also addressing poverty and inequality.

He noted that *56.4% of Ghanaians remain in poverty*, with spatial disparities widening, creating a disconnect between headline economic growth and improvements in living standards.

He also raised concerns about the ability of the economy to create enough jobs for Ghana’s growing youthful population, saying growth was being led by sectors with limited employment absorption.

Risks to the recovery

Mr Taliercio projected economic growth at *4.8% in 2026*, converging to around 5% over the medium term, provided fiscal discipline is maintained and external debt restructuring is completed.

He, however, warned that the outlook remains vulnerable to both domestic and external risks.

He said a prolonged conflict in the Middle East could disrupt global trade, increase energy and production costs and create renewed inflationary pressures.

Ghana’s heavy dependence on gold and cocoa exports also leaves the economy exposed to adverse movements in commodity prices, which could put pressure on the exchange rate, inflation and public finances.

Domestically, he identified financial pressures in the energy and agricultural sectors as major concerns.

“Delays in energy sector recovery programmes cost the country approximately $1 billion annually,” he said.

He also called for reforms to the operations of the Ghana Cocoa Board (COCOBOD), arguing that its financial and operational inefficiencies were putting pressure on farmers and public finances.

Mr Taliercio said the World Bank welcomed continued discussion on reforms to the COCOBOD Act and advocated far-reaching changes to promote market-based principles and minimise quasi-fiscal risks.

Transport sector remains major constraint

The World Bank official said Ghana’s transport infrastructure was another major obstacle to economic transformation, making it the special focus of this year’s Ghana Economic Update.

“This is not just an infrastructure story. It’s a growth story, competitiveness story and a job story,” he said.

According to him, only 27% of Ghana’s 94,200-kilometre road network is paved**, while more than half of the network is in fair-to-poor condition, with feeder roads particularly affected.

He said Ghana’s rail network had also suffered a significant decline, falling from 947 kilometres of operational rail in 1960 to just 160 kilometres in 2020.

The World Bank estimates that road safety incidents alone cost Ghana about *2.1% of GDP annually, equivalent to approximately *$4.55 billion**.

Mr Taliercio said the situation was compounded by fragmented institutional responsibility within the transport sector, which undermines effective coordination, planning and execution.

He outlined six priority areas for transforming the sector: operationalising the *Road Maintenance Trust Fund*, developing a unified national transport strategy, revitalising freight-led rail services along the western and eastern corridors, treating road safety as a fiscal and public health emergency, adopting climate-resilient design standards and extending Ghana’s Digital Single Window to Takoradi and inland terminals.

$500m Investment in Feeder Roads

Mr Taliercio said the World Bank was supporting the government’s efforts through the Ghana Market Access and Connectivity Project, which was ratified by Parliament in July.

Under the project, the World Bank is investing $500 million to rehabilitate approximately *1,050 kilometres of feeder roads under performance-based maintenance contracts.

He said the investment would target areas where poor connectivity was constraining agricultural productivity and rural livelihoods, while also supporting the operationalisation of the Road Maintenance Trust Fund.

Mr Taliercio stressed that capital investment alone would not resolve Ghana’s infrastructure challenges.

“Building roads without maintaining them simply accelerates the cycle of degradation that we are all trying to break,” he said.

He said the World Bank remained committed to supporting Ghana’s macroeconomic stabilisation and structural reforms to make the recovery more inclusive, job-intensive and resilient.

Ghana News.title: Ayitey Powers remanded for one week over alleged threat against NSA boss
Ghana News.content:
Former Ghanaian boxer Michael Ayitey Okai, popularly known as Ayitey Powers, has been remanded into police custody for one week by the Dansoman Circuit Court over an alleged death threat against National Sports Authority (NSA) Director-General Yaw Ampofo Ankrah.

Ayitey Powers appeared before the court on Tuesday, August 25, a day after he was arrested by the Accra Regional Police Command.

He is expected to reappear on September 2, 2026, as police investigations into the alleged threat continue.

The former boxer reportedly reported himself to the police after receiving an invitation from the Accra Regional Police Headquarters over a video circulating on social media in which he was allegedly seen threatening Mr Ampofo Ankrah.

He was subsequently arrested, detained and processed for court following a call by the Ghana Boxing Interim Management Committee (GBIMC) for his arrest and prosecution.

The GBIMC described the alleged conduct as unacceptable and called on the Ghana Police Service to investigate the matter and take appropriate action.

The committee has also initiated disciplinary proceedings against Ayitey Powers, which could have further implications for his standing within the boxing fraternity.

The police have meanwhile urged the public to refrain from circulating unverified information as investigations into the alleged threat continue.

Ghana News.title: Black Stars midfielder Kwasi Sibo joins Libyan side Al-Swehly
Ghana News.content:
Ghana international Kwasi Sibo has completed a move to Libyan top-flight side Al-Swehly in a permanent deal.

Sibo joins the club on a three-year deal with the option to extend for another year, signing as a free agent following the expiration of his contract at Real Oviedo.

The Black Stars midfielder played in the Spanish La Liga last season before his deal expired at the end of the 2025/26 campaign, with the club choosing not to extend his contract.

The move to Libya comes after a proposed move to the Turkish top flight did not materialise, while he also turned down clubs from France and Major League Soccer.

According to reports, the deal could be worth $10 million, with the financial package also linked to a broader government-backed effort to bring in more African talent to the Libyan league.

The midfielder returned to Ghana on Tuesday after flying out to Cairo to sign his deal with the Libyan side ahead of the start of the 2026/27 season.

The 28-year-old was part of the Black Stars squad for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, which was staged in Mexico, Canada and the United States of America, starting in all of Ghana's games.

Ghana News.title: Repeat traffic violations captured under TraffiTech could lead to licence revocation – ACP Obeng
Ghana News.content:
Director of Education, Research and Training of the Police Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD), Alexander Kweku Obeng, has said the introduction of the automated traffic enforcement system known as TrafficTech would enable the Police to track motorists who repeatedly commit offences within a specified period.

Motorists who repeatedly violate road traffic regulations could face arrest, prosecution, revocation of their driving licences and a one-year ban from driving, the Ghana Police Service has warned.

Speaking on JoyFM Super Morning Show on Wednesday, August 26, ACP Obeng explained that traffic offences captured by cameras would first be transmitted to a Police back office, where designated personnel would review and validate the incidents before enforcement action is taken.

He said the system would allow authorities to monitor repeat offences and apply progressively tougher sanctions in accordance with the Road Traffic Regulations, 2020 (L.I. 2590).

According to ACP Obeng, motorists who commit repeated offences within a 24-month period could eventually lose the option of paying an ordinary police-issued fine.

“On the fifth offence, Police cannot issue you with a fine. The law says that we should look for you, arrest you physically, and then process you for Motor Court,” he said.

He explained that the matter would then be taken before the appropriate court, where the offender could face further sanctions if found guilty.

“If you are found guilty, your licence will be revoked, and then you will be banned for one year from driving,” ACP Obeng stated.

READ ALSO: Interior Ministry introduces TraffiTech to track and penalise road traffic offenders

The Police official said the escalating penalties were intended to discourage motorists from repeatedly breaching traffic regulations and to promote greater discipline on the roads.

He noted that the automated system would not simply impose penalties without human oversight, stressing that officers at the back office would validate captured incidents before fines or other enforcement measures were applied.

ACP Obeng said the deployment of cameras, sensors and other technological devices formed part of the Ghana Police Service’s broader efforts to modernise traffic enforcement and reduce preventable road crashes.

He urged motorists to comply with prescribed speed limits and other road traffic regulations, warning that persistent violations could have serious legal consequences.

Ghana News.title: TraffiTech system will not replace police visibility, ACP Obeng says
Ghana News.content:
Director of Education, Research and Training at the Police Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD), ACP Alexander Kwaku Obeng, has clarified that the introduction of a technology-driven traffic enforcement system, TraffiTech-GH, does not mean the police will disappear from the roads.

According to him, police officers will continue to be physically present on the roads to manage traffic, respond to road crashes and deal with situations that require direct human intervention.

Speaking on the Joy FM Super Morning Show on Wednesday, August 26, ACP Obeng said the use of cameras was intended to complement, rather than replace, conventional police work.

Responding to a question about whether the introduction of automated traffic enforcement would affect police visibility on the roads, he said, “It doesn't necessarily mean that police physical presence will not be there."

ACP Obeng explained that police visibility would remain necessary because there were several situations that could not be effectively handled by cameras or other digital tools.

“Visibility will be there, first of all, even in the case that there are certain instances that we need police to be controlling the traffic,” he said.

He added that officers would still be required to respond quickly to road crashes, manage traffic around accident scenes and ensure that injured people received assistance.

“Even in the case that when accidents occur, police officers have to be quickly deployed to ensure that roads will be managed,” he said.

“Persons who are injured are being attended to. Those who have suffered brutality are being referred, among others,” ACP Obeng added.

He said that certain provisions under the road traffic laws would also continue to require the physical presence of police officers.

According to him, police officers would also remain available to assist members of the public and deal with situations where roads are deliberately obstructed or used inappropriately.

“Is it not the case that people may obstruct the road and do all manner of things? So, policing will be sustained,” he said.

ACP Obeng, however, said digital enforcement would reduce the need for police officers to physically stop motorists for certain traffic offences.

He explained that technology could allow the police to gather evidence of traffic violations and engage vehicle owners or drivers without necessarily stopping them on the road.

“But issues regarding gathering evidence that normally will require arrest, impound, let's go to a police station, and the convenience and all that, it is easy for us now to use digital tools, simple technologies, and software applications that will run on it for us to interface with the person who owns or who is driving without necessarily stopping or taking them to the police station,” he added.

ACP Obeng said the digital system was being introduced as part of a broader effort to create a safer and more resilient road environment.

“We are bringing it alongside, in the hope that in the future, we will have a more resilient road environment where digital tools will assist police,” he said.

He said the system could also encourage motorists to become more conscious of their behaviour, particularly when they know that traffic violations can be detected even when an officer is not physically present.

ACP Obeng said the ultimate objective was to prevent avoidable traffic offences and the crashes, deaths and injuries associated with them.

“I think police are there, day and night. So that people will be safe from committing certain preventable infractions that are exposing many of our compatriots and citizens to danger that are leading to preventable crashes, associated deaths, and injuries,” he said.

He said Parliament had permitted about 49 offences to be dealt with under the relevant framework, with additional motor-related infractions bringing the number to about 79 under Regulation 174.

“So I'm not surprised Parliament permitted about 49. And if you add the motor infractions, about 79 under Regulation 174,” he said.

According to him, the expanded enforcement framework would help protect road users, including motorists and users of two, three- and four-wheeled vehicles.

“So that we'll be able to protect many of our citizens who are permitted to come onto the road space to drive either two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers, and many of the vehicles that are running on multiple axles,” he said.

“So that as the roads are being opened up, drivers will be conscious that they are driving for life,” he added.

The TraffiTech-GH has been introduced to identify, track and penalise motorists who violate road traffic regulations.

TraffiTech-GH is an automated traffic enforcement system developed by the Ghana Police Service to monitor road use and improve road safety.

The system uses fixed intersection cameras, mobile vehicle-mounted cameras, handheld and tripod devices, as well as other digital monitoring tools to capture traffic offences.

Ghana News.title: Excessive speeding linked to about 60% of road fatalities – ACP Obeng
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Police Service has identified excessive speeding as a major cause of preventable road crashes, attributing about 60 per cent of road fatalities to the offence.

Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Alexander Kwaku Obeng, who is Director of Education, Research and Training at the Police Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD), said motorists who exceed prescribed speed limits expose passengers, pedestrians and other road users to considerable danger.

Speaking in an interview on the planned deployment of the TrafficTech system on Joy FM's Super Morning Show on Wednesday, August 26, ACP Obeng said the technology would allow the police to use cameras and other devices to detect and document traffic violations.

He cited motorists driving above 50 kilometres per hour in school zones and densely populated areas, as well as those exceeding 100 kilometres per hour on motorways, among the dangerous practices the system would target.

According to him, the required hardware and software have been procured and are undergoing testing, while a back-office system has also been developed to support enforcement.

He said the Ministry of Transport, with support from agencies within the road safety management sub-sector, was expected to undertake the necessary certification process.

“We hope to issue court notices to those who may be violating speed limits in their vehicles,” ACP Obeng said.

He explained that the TrafficTech initiative was backed by Regulation 242 of the Road Traffic Regulations, 2020 (L.I. 2519), which provides for automated road traffic offences and fines.

The police are also developing a mobile application that will enable officers to use handheld devices and smartphones to gather evidence of traffic offences on the roads.

ACP Obeng said the digital enforcement approach would reduce the practice of stopping suspected offenders and taking them to police stations, as evidence captured by the devices could be used to pursue the vehicle owners or drivers involved.

Ghana News.title: Bosomtwe DCE denies galamsey allegations, threatens defamation suit against Assembly Member
Ghana News.content:
The District Chief Executive (DCE) for Bosomtwe in the Ashanti Region, Ing. Hamidu Abdallah, has denied allegations that he is involved in illegal mining, describing the claims as false and a deliberate attempt to damage his reputation.

The DCE’s denial follows allegations by a group of Assembly Members in the district that he was allegedly colluding with illegal miners whose activities have degraded farmlands and water bodies in some communities.

Nana Akwasi Asare Nyansapor, Assembly Member for Akokofe and leader of the group, alleged that illegal mining was ongoing in communities including Beposo, Yaase, Adwafo, Amakom and Konkoma.

“The DCE, Hamidu, is colluding with illegal miners to degrade our environment. Right now, illegal mining is ongoing in some communities,” he alleged.

The Assembly Members further claimed that the DCE had denied the existence of illegal mining in the district until a recent operation by a regional task force led to the seizure of five excavators.

They have threatened to petition President John Dramani Mahama and pursue a vote of no confidence against the DCE.

DCE denies allegations

Ing. Abdallah, however, strongly rejected the allegations, insisting that he has never been involved in mining, whether legal or illegal.

“I have never been involved in any form of mining, be it legal or illegal, in my entire life, let alone illegal mining. I have no concession, no excavator, and no hand in galamsey anywhere in Bosomtwe,” he said.

He also denied claims that he had sought to conceal the existence of illegal mining in the district, saying his administration had instead been actively involved in efforts to curb the practice.

According to him, the Assembly has been particularly focused on protecting areas around Lake Bosomtwe, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve.

Ing. Abdallah said a recent operation that resulted in the seizure of five excavators and the dismantling of pumping machines was carried out under his leadership in collaboration with the Ashanti Regional Security Council (REGSEC) and the District Security Council (DISEC).

“How can I be the one leading the operation to seize excavators and at the same time be accused of owning those same excavators? The logic does not hold,” he said.

He explained that after receiving reports of illegal mining activities near Lake Bosomtwe, he personally led a team to inspect the affected areas.

He subsequently wrote to the Ashanti Regional Minister and the Minerals Commission requesting that mining licences within the enclave be reviewed and that a task force be deployed to the area.

“The Assembly was duly informed. The Presiding Member and key stakeholders were part of engagements after the operation. So to say the Assembly was kept in the dark is factually incorrect,” he added.

DCE threatens legal action

Ing. Abdallah said he had instructed his lawyers to take legal action against Nana Asare Akwasi Nyansapor over the allegations.

“As for the allegations of illegal mining levelled against me, I will never forgive them. I have instructed my lawyer to file a lawsuit against the accuser to compel him to provide evidence of my involvement in such activities before the court,” he said.

The DCE attributed the allegations to what he described as internal political disagreements, alleging that some Assembly Members were frustrated after their attempts to secure mining-related favours in the district were blocked.

He, however, reaffirmed his commitment to supporting the government's efforts to combat illegal mining and protect the environment, water bodies and farmlands in the Bosomtwe District.
