World.title: Target faces renewed backlash for Halloween costume with 'minstrel show features'
World.content:
Target faces renewed backlash for Halloween costume with 'minstrel show features'

toggle caption Charles Krupa/AP

Retailer Target pulled a children's Halloween costume from its shelves Monday after widespread social media backlash, apologizing for selling a garment critics said evoked racist minstrel caricatures.

Critics say the costume, along with its promotional image of a Black child modeling the get-up, is reminiscent of caricatures from Jim Crow-era minstrel shows that embedded stereotypes into popular culture and helped justify discrimination, segregation and racial violence.

"As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry. The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment. It is no longer available for sale," Target said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

"We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners. Removing the costume is an important first step, and the company is looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won't happen again."

The costume misstep happened as Target's sales have started rebounding from earlier company moves that alienated some customers and from a perception the quality of its stores and merchandise had declined.

It is the latest controversy for the retailer, which joined companies like Meta, Walmart, and McDonald's in rolling back their diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts after President Donald Trump won the 2024 election.

The "Kids' Glows Under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween costume," an orange-and-black circus clown costume, now deleted from the Target website, featured gloves, a top hat and a grinning mask with large teeth.

'Not simply getting it wrong'

"A Jim Crow-era minstrel costume is not simply getting it wrong. It is a profoundly harmful symbol of racism that should never have been designed, approved, or sold by Target," said the Rev. Jamal Bryant, a Georgia pastor who led a 40-day "Target Fast" boycott last year. "It shows that Target still lacks corporate diversity among decision-makers and needs concrete internal change."

Sponsor Message

In January 2025, the Minneapolis-based corporation ended its three-year DEI program, stopping reports to external groups like the Human Rights Campaign and ended a program focused on carrying more products from Black- or minority-owned businesses, replacing it with a new "Belonging" strategy. The company previously stated that the murder of George Floyd was a catalyst for its DEI initiatives.

Activist-organizers called for a boycott of Target, which lost roughly $12.4 billion in market value by the end of February from January.

Minnesota civil rights activists, separate from Bryant, organized a national Target boycott, resulting in a 33% fall in the corporation's stock prices and wiped out over $20 billion in market value.

Target's recent recovery

Target has managed a recovery in recent months. The stock closed at $165.44 on Aug.21, a fresh 52-week high, after a strong second quarter. On Aug. 24, Target's shares closed at $169.89.

Target's stock is up roughly 63% this year, a sharp rebound from the depths of the boycott. The company's turnaround strategy, launched by new CEO Michael Fiddelke after former CEO Brian Cornell stepped down, includes store refreshes, increased staffing, and more aggressive pricing. Target announced a plan in March to invest $2 billion in 2026, including $1 billion in additional operating investments, with plans to open more than 30 new stores this year as part of its path to 300 new stores by 2035, while investing in over 130 planned full-store remodels.

Bruce Winder, a retail analyst and former retail buyer, says that inventory errors, such as the recent Prada and Gucci controversies, "can happen to the best of them."

"These things happen over time. I think the most important thing for Target, and they did it, was to quickly take accountability, quickly say sorry, acknowledge that this was a big mistake, and pull the product from the shelves," Winder said.

Boycott organizers undeterred

Target boycott organizers in Minneapolis, including Nekima Levy Armstrong and community leaders Monique Cullars-Doty and Jaylani Hussein, remain steadfast in their divestment calls.

Sponsor Message

They have continued to press the company to reinstate its DEI programs and continue its commitments to Black communities, and they say the costume controversy is a refresher on their mission.

"It's important for people to understand that the Target boycott never ended; that it was indefinite from the beginning, unless and until Target reversed course on its decision to roll back diversity, equity, and inclusion," said Armstrong, an organizer of the national Target boycott.

"What we've seen is Target engaging in PR campaigns: recruiting high-visibility Black ministers to meet with them, partnering with (rapper and businessman) Jay-Z, all types of different shenanigans to deflect from the fact that they abandon their commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion, and capitulation to the Trump administration."

Hussein, another boycott organizer, said the costume incident was "not surprising."

"It was almost predictable because of the behavior of Target, and I think this is going to build on the momentum of the boycott. More people are going to be upset," he said.

"It's not just an incident with a costume. There are a lot of people right now in this country across many parts who've changed their culture of shopping, who have found other places to put their money behind."

Target Corporation's stock closed at $163.47 on Aug. 25, dropping 3.78% from its previous close the day prior.

World.title: More than 50 kidnapped as violent gang attack in Haiti leaves 47 dead
World.content:
More than 50 kidnapped as violent gang attack in Haiti leaves 47 dead

toggle caption Odelyn Joseph/AP

PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti — At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped when armed men attacked a once-peaceful community near Haiti's capital earlier this week, the United Nations said Tuesday.

It is believed to be one of the largest mass kidnappings in Haiti in recent years, and one gang leader is threatening to kill the hostages if authorities kill any gang members as they try to secure the community nestled in the hills above Port-au-Prince.

Sunday's attack on Kenscoff pierced the belief that security in the troubled Caribbean country was improving.

"This is a major political and security test, for the government, for the police and for the international mission," said Romain Le Cour, head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.

Sponsor Message

He said the threat of executing hostages is a trap: If forces don't act, they've failed to protect them; if they do and hostages die, the gangs will blame the state.

Kenscoff resident Marc Paul, 42, said gangs kidnapped his brother, stepmother, stepfather and two cousins. He said his 16-year-old niece also was kidnapped and raped but was able to escape and has reunited with him.

"I had to run over bodies," he said as he recalled how he fled the attack. "I can't sleep knowing all these people died."

Paul and his family had already lost their home to a previous gang attack in January 2025, but he said it was not as violent as Sunday's attack. Paul was upset about the video the gangs posted: "My brother is probably going to die."

A threat posted on social media

In a video posted on social media, the gang leader threatened Vladimir Paraison, director of Haiti's National Police.

"Paraison, if any of our soldiers are hurt, I will kill all of them," he said, referring to the hostages.

The gang member identified himself as Izo 2, a reference to Izo, or Johnson André, one of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders.

Le Cour said Izo 2 is also known as "Didi" and leads the armed group in Kenscoff on behalf of and in coordination with Izo and other gang leaders.

Sponsor Message

Kenson Paul, the 17-year-old nephew of Marc Paul, said he managed to escape the attackers.

"They have not called us to let us know what they want," he said of the gang. "I worry for my family's life."

Le Cour said the aim of Sunday's attack could be to force Haiti's police and the U.N.-backed gang suppression force to disperse even more of their limited resources.

"They don't have enough personnel," Le Cour said in a phone interview. "If you force them to deploy more troops, it would inevitably be at the expense of other areas."

The attack might also just be a show of force and a message to Haiti's government and police as the country prepares to hold general elections on Dec. 13 for the first time in more than a decade.

"This is a message to the government and the police that their claims of protection do not match reality," Le Cour said. "The gangs are saying: when we choose to attack, we can, and we will succeed."

Attacks on Kenscoff have escalated

The first major attack on Kenscoff occurred in January 2025, and since then, there have been sporadic attacks in the mountains surrounding the city center.

But Sunday's attack was the largest yet. At least five of the 47 people killed were children, according to the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti, known as BINUH.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack on Tuesday, noting that 22 of the victims were reportedly executed in a church compound where they had sought shelter: "The relentless gang attacks on communities and the loss of lives underscore the alarming security conditions in Haiti," he said.

Kenscoff Mayor Jean Massillon told The Associated Press on Tuesday that gangs set fire to 25 homes and killed two government employees including his cousin, who served as his security detail.

Sponsor Message

"The atrocity of this crime reminds us that we have to continue working stronger every day to bring peace to the community," Massillon said. "I'm optimistic that the state will continue working to eradicate the gangs in Kenscoff."

Gangs are coveting Kenscoff because it allows them to surround and control the upscale community of Pétion-Ville and alternate routes connecting Haiti's capital to its southern region, said María Fernanda Arocha, a researcher with the nonprofit Armed Conflict Location & Event Data.

Between January and August this year, security operations had managed to reduce violence in Kenscoff by 66% prior to the attack, she said in a statement.

"While security forces have concentrated their efforts on operations aimed at regaining control in the central areas of Port-au-Prince, criminal groups have instead sought to expand into rural communities that are vulnerable due to the limited response capacity of the police, but which remain strategic hubs," she added.

Haitians demand police protection

Some survivors accused the government of not providing enough protection prior to the attack, with Haiti's National Police rejecting those accusations.

Le Cour said that if police and armored vehicles were indeed stationed in Kenscoff prior to the attack, then the assertion is concerning: "You let the gangs come in even if you had everything in place?"

Haiti's National Police issued a statement Tuesday saying Paraison ordered an investigation to establish the truth about the attack "whether due to complicity or negligence." He also ordered additional specialized units to the area, saying "It is an obligation to protect the civilian population."

Armed men control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince and swaths of land in Haiti's central region and beyond.

Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,050 people were reported killed from January to June, according to U.N. statistics released Tuesday.

Sponsor Message

The U.N. noted that nearly 800 rapes were reported from April to June, with 87% of those cases representing collective rapes.

At least 81 people also were reported kidnapped during that time period, according to a new U.N. report.

"These figures represent only a portion of the total number of people kidnapped," it stated. "In many cases, victims' relatives do not report kidnappings to the police or service providers and choose to negotiate directly with the kidnappers, believing that this approach allows for a quicker release and avoids possible reprisals."

The number of kidnappings reported from April to June represents a more than 40% increase compared with the previous quarter.

World.title: Instagram head Adam Mosseri testifies in defense of Meta in child safety trial
World.content:
Instagram head Adam Mosseri testifies in defense of Meta in child safety trial

toggle caption KARL MONDON/AFP via Getty Images



OAKLAND, Calif. – The head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said in court on Tuesday that a feature introduced in 2021 to try to help teens regulate their time on the app had lower uptake than he had hoped for and he wished it had been fixed sooner.

Attorneys representing California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey are suing Instagram's parent company Meta , accusing it of designing Instagram and its other flagship platform, Facebook, to hook kids and harvest their data and of hiding the truth about dangers the platforms posed to young people. In an Oakland, California courtroom, attorneys for Meta have denied the accusations and sought to show that the company was sensitive to the risks of overuse, and tried to address them .

Sponsor Message

Under questioning from a lawyer for the states, Mosseri spoke about the feature, called Take a Break, which has a pop-up message suggesting to young users that they pause their use of the app once they have been on it for a fixed period of time. In court, an internal document admitted as evidence by the prosecution showed that at one point only 1.8% of teens actually used the feature.

The pop-up notifications "helped, but not nearly as much as we hoped," Mosseri said.

In late 2024 the company made the feature the default on all teen accounts, which were also introduced that year. By then, Mosseri said, the point about initial low uptake was "entirely moot."

But Jason Slothouber, with the Colorado Attorney General's office, pushed back, noting that the change was made after the states had already sued Meta in 2023.

The states argue that Meta withheld relevant information from users and parents, who might have benefited from knowing the ineffectiveness of the feature and others like it, constituting a violation of consumer protection laws. And to press that point, Slothouber noted a blog post from Mosseri around the time the feature was introduced that stated that "more than 90%" of users of the feature kept it on. But, he noted, Mosseri did not indicate that a very low number of people actually used the feature in the first place.

Sponsor Message

Asked to confirm that there was no way at the time for parents to know that only 1-2% of teens would use the feature, Mosseri replied: "Correct." Asked to confirm that Meta has never disclosed the figure, Mosseri again said: "Correct."

Mosseri noted that Take a Break and Quiet Mode, another feature that silences Instagram alerts, were a small number of the many features Meta has introduced to try to address problematic use by teens, a remark that appeared to jibe with Meta's broader argument in court that it was aware of issues involving teens and took many steps to address them.

"In general, there are no silver bullets to problems like this. We have to do many things that add up," Mosseri said.

The trial is part of a surge of cases brought against tech companies in the wake of various studies and public health advisories saying that social media can cause harm to the mental health of young users.

Mosseri is a longtime Meta employee who started as a product designer just three years out of college in 2008, when the company was called Facebook, and worked his way up to helm of one of the world's most popular social media apps. He has been the head of Instagram since 2018.

Meta reported in July that Instagram has 2 billion daily active users — nearly a quarter of the Earth's population. The app is particularly popular among young people; according to a 2024 Pew Research Center survey, roughly six in 10 U.S. teens say they use Instagram. Roughly half of teens say they use it every day.

Slothouber also asked Mosseri about communications among Instagram employees about a presentation that they were preparing to give Mosseri that dealt with the kinds of problematic content teens are exposed to on Instagram. The communications refer to the product designers having been advised by Meta's lawyers to limit what data Mosseri would see in the presentation to check his "litigation exposure."

Sponsor Message

Mosseri said he was not aware of this exchange, but added that it "makes sense" that the document's creators would want to be sure the information was accurate and truthful.

In what seemed to be an effort to show that Meta prioritized avoiding legal liability over sharing important data with Mosseri, Slothouber asked Mosseri if it would be fair to say that a product designer or person who deals with data in their job would have a better understanding of what data is important to present to him than a lawyer.

"Yes, I think a lawyer would be a less qualified designer than a product designer," Mosseri said.

Mosseri defended Meta's efforts to protect teens, and voiced opposition to what he considered the use of certain bits of information out of context.

"I think parents want to have good information about services, risks, etc. That's different than reporters or lawyers taking small bits from much larger documents and focusing on them in things like articles and trials," he said.

The stakes in this case are high for Meta, a market leader and one of the most profitable social media companies in the world. An initial estimate of potential penalties runs as high as $1.4 trillion — roughly the entire value of Meta's equity on the Nasdaq.

Some legal experts compare this moment to landmark litigation against tobacco companies in the 1990s that forced them into big settlements and changed their behavior — and the public discussion about the risks of cigarettes.

Mosseri is expected to continue on the stand again on Wednesday. The trial is expected to last about five more weeks.

World.title: Retaliatory tariffs could raise costs for Canadian businesses already weathering the trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Derek Friesen says the Canada-U.S. trade war had mostly bypassed his agricultural equipment manufacturing business, save for some of his products that were hit by an earlier round of 10 per cent duties.

That is, until retaliatory Canadian tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. goods were announced today.

His Manitoba company, PhiBer Manufacturing Inc. makes agriculture equipment, including dash trailers that are used by large-scale farmers to tend to crops. They've long imported the frames for these machines from Iowa, but starting Sept. 8, those frames will be subject to new retaliatory tariffs.

Friesen says taxing an important and expensive part like that will inevitably drive the sticker price way up.

"Farms can't absorb another big increase like that," Friesen said.

PhiBer Manufacturing Inc.'s Dash trailers, used by large-scale farmers to tend to crops are made with frames imported from Iowa. Starting on Sept. 8, those frames will be subject to new retaliatory tariffs. (Jaison Empson/CBC)

He expects these trailers, which make up about 70 per cent of his sales, might no longer be economically feasible to buy or sell in a few weeks time.

For some business owners, retaliatory tariffs will bring higher costs, making it harder for some to weather the worsening trade war — even if others are hopeful these new countermeasures could boost their sales within Canada.

Targeted list of newly tariffed items

Canada will impose tariffs of 15, 25 or 50 per cent on a number of products from the U.S. starting on Sept. 8.

The new levies will impact a variety of goods including seafood, certain paper products, furniture, apparel, tools and motorcycles. Some of the categories facing the largest tariffs are products made of iron or steel or the raw metals, paper products and machinery and parts.

Bradley Saunders, an economist with Capital Economics, says that based on the list, it seems like the federal government took a targeted approach when deciding what to tariff.

"The majority of these goods have been picked as they have readily available domestic alternatives, in an effort to hurt American businesses while minimising the hit to Canadian consumers and industry," Saunders wrote in a note on Tuesday.

He said the countermeasures would be relatively insignificant in the big picture, only giving a slight boost to inflation, while government support measures for businesses could offset about half of the possible drag on business growth.

According to another read of the numbers by University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe, nearly three quarters of the counter-tariffed items are industrial supplies or things used to manufacture other goods — costs that would be felt more by businesses rather than consumers.

But for some businesses like Danby Appliances based in Guelph, Ont., the new tariffs could even help a little.

Danby owner Jim Estill says some of the parts his company uses will now face higher prices because of the retaliatory tariffs — for example, some of the cables used in their snowplows will now be subject to a 15 per cent tax under the new rules.

Jim Estill, the owner of Guelph, Ont.,-based Danby Appliances, says retaliatory tariffs won't increase costs at his business by much, and could help keep U.S. competitors out of the Canadian market for some products like refrigerators. (Zachary Proulx/CBC)

Estill says those added costs are manageable for him. And retaliatory 25 per cent tariffs on things like refrigerators could actually make his Canadian-made products a more competitive option for consumers in this country compared to those brought in from the U.S.

"So we may gain a little bit of market share," he said. "It's a double-edged sword."

But the counter-tariffs will still likely hurt more than they help, Estill says — especially if the trade war causes customers to hold off on making big purchases, like a new fridge.

Supports for businesses still not enough: CFIB

Simon Gaudreault, chief economist at the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB), agrees that the retaliatory tariffs are mostly bad news for Canadian business owners.

CFIB data shows that there are about two businesses that import components from the U.S. for every one that exports finished products south of the border, which means retaliatory tariffs can pose a larger threat to Canadian businesses.

"Our economy is based on two-way trade. So now, on top of those export tariffs that the U.S. is putting on our shoulders, we are also putting counter-tariffs on our own shoulders," Gaudreault said.

While many of those measures were later suspended, Gaudreault worries fresh ones will have a similar effect and says he's concerned that business owners won't have the capacity to withstand another shock like this.

WATCH | Feds announce 'dollar-for-dollar' counter-tariffs on billions in U.S. imports: Feds announce 'dollar-for-dollar' counter-tariffs on billions in U.S. imports | Duration 1:15 Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says Canada will match the latest round of U.S. tariffs in a 'proportionate, targeted and strategic' way. Champagne says the tariffs, which will impact more than $27 billion in U.S. goods, are 'all about fairness.'

He's also not optimistic that new support measures will do much to help.

Along with announcing the retaliatory tariffs, the federal government said it would create a $7.5-billion support package for businesses and workers affected by the trade war.

Some of that will go toward enhanced employment insurance measures, while $1.5 billion will be set aside for medium-sized businesses to access through regional development agencies, and millions more will go toward grants and interest-free loan programs.

Gaudreault says those programs are "unfortunately similar" to past programs the government has used to try to stimulate businesses earlier in the trade dispute.

He says only one per cent of the CFIB's membership used them, largely because they had certain requirements — like requiring $2 million in revenue in order to access supports — that prevented small business owners from applying.

And while that particular threshold was lowered to $1 million in Tuesday's announcement for a certain program, Gaudreault still worries the measures will miss lots of businesses.

Friesen says the only thing that will really help is an end to the trade war.

"We just need this to be resolved," he said.

World.title: Food and shelter have driven Canada's affordability crisis. Health care isn't far behind
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Rising food and shelter costs have been in the spotlight as drivers of the affordability crisis. But consumer price index (CPI) data shows that what Canadians pay to stay healthy has soared almost as much since overall inflation hit a peak in June 2022.

The jump in health-care costs may go under the radar for many Canadians, experts say — in part because many costs are covered by the public health-care system (which also means they aren't included in CPI data) and in part because typical out-of-pocket health expenses may be sporadic.

"You pay your rent every month and you pay your grocery bill every week," Jimmy Jean, vice-president and chief economist at Desjardins Group in Montreal, said in an interview with CBC News. "So it's very much in consumers' faces in a way that you couldn't say for a dental appointment that you have twice a year."

But health-care prices have nonetheless followed a "sharper curve" in recent years, said Andrew Longhurst, a senior researcher at the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives (CCPA) — one that may get steeper still.

"I think that growth is only going to increase as we see greater aging and we see provincial governments — especially among the larger provinces — really pulling back and choosing fiscal restraint and austerity," Longhurst said.

The overall measure of inflation — called all-items CPI — has risen a bit over 11 per cent since June 2022. The broad category called health and personal care has gone up much more — just over 15 per cent in that time, behind shelter costs (more than 16 per cent) and food prices (up almost 19 per cent).

But the subset of health-care services, which include things like eye exams, physiotherapy appointments and basic dental care, is up 18.5 per cent — nearly as much as food.

Dental care services and eye care goods have both seen prices rise 20 per cent since June 2022, and both are emblematic of a public-private split within the health-care industry, Longhurst said, with costs controlled on only one side.

"Prescription eyeglasses and contact lenses — most of that industry is all private for-profit, increasingly investor-driven, private equity is involved. And it's similar with dental care," he said. "These are areas where there is virtually no public provision, very limited not-for-profit provision, and there are no public constraints on what those costs are."

A long-running trend

Statistics Canada data shows that the prices of health-care services have generally tracked well above overall inflation since well before the COVID-19 pandemic. In the previous 20 years, year-over-year inflation in health-care services has exceeded overall inflation 85 per cent of the time.

During that period, health-care services inflation was significantly lower than overall inflation only during the pandemic-era inflation spike — reflecting a period when other prices spiked, rather than a slowdown in health-care costs.

Part of the long-term trend is due to the economic realities of health and dental services, where a big expense is skilled labour costs, said the Desjardins Group's Jean.

"It's a function ... of sectors where it's very difficult to extract efficiency gains or productivity gains that would reduce costs a bit more," he said.

"Those sectors tend to respond a lot to wage costs — and again, you've seen labour shortages and we've also had more population. So demand has been there for those services at a time where in some categories of health-care services, it's been harder to find qualified, trained, skilled workers."

Another issue, as Longhurst of the CCPA pointed out, is that nothing is stopping those costs from going up, unlike for services covered by provincial health insurance, such as visits to a doctor.

"Public health-care rates are subject to agreements between governments and providers," he explained. "So in the case of physicians, those fee amounts are negotiated, and so there's some control in terms of containing those costs."

In 2024, after the 2022 inflation peak, Canada rolled out the Canadian Dental Care Plan, but dental care CPI numbers have continued to climb. The dental plan may have added to demand, Jean said, in a sector constrained by skilled labour needs.

The plan is also administered by a private insurer, Longhurst said, so "the onus was placed upon the patient to ensure that they were going to a dental office where the public portion would cover what they needed." Many people pay an additional out-of-pocket amount, he said.

The program also continues to create challenges for patients and dentists.

WATCH | Patients want more clarity over why national dental claims are being denied: Patients, dentists call for more clarity of dental coverage under national plan | Duration 3:51 The Canadian Dental Care Plan provides care to uninsured Canadians with a household income of less than $90,000. More expensive procedures like crowns or dentures require pre-authorization. Patients and providers say those pre-approvals are frequently denied by Sun Life, which administers and processes claims.

Out of sight, out of wallet

Still, many Canadians may only be dimly aware of health-care price inflation. The public system covers a substantial portion of people's costs, making the out-of-pocket remainder less consequential than some other expenses. In 2025, food and shelter made up almost 50 per cent of the total CPI basket, while health and personal care was about a 10th of that.

As Jean noted, many health-care expenses are significantly less top of mind because they aren't featured in monthly or weekly budgets. And while dental and eye care are essential and don't amount to discretionary purchases, patients have some short-term flexibility.

"What we're seeing with the affordability squeeze is in things like life insurance — those are the things that people will try to save on or delay because they're less urgent," Jean said.

"It could be the same thing for a dental appointment or eye care: Facing a squeeze, people will tend to focus on paying their mortgages and putting gas in their cars."

The growing private burden

Private spending on health care may not be in the range of spending on food and shelter, but Canadians are increasingly shouldering more of the load with private spending. A recent CCPA analysis of data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information found that from 2021 to 2023, private health-care spending per person grew by 8.1 per cent — almost twice as fast as public spending.

"We see that spending growth is increasing fairly rapidly as the population ages and also as provinces pull back on investment in those areas," Longhurst said. "So people need those services — they're not going to go without them. And that's why we see health-care inflation continuing to run quite hot, because unlike a traditional good where maybe people can postpone the purchase of a car, they need those services and they're going to continue to pay for them."

The risk is that the burden of additional costs will affect people less financially equipped to handle them, Longhurst warned, saying there are already "significant gaps in who has access to care based on their income and their ability to purchase out-of-pocket the services they need."

Those variations are likely to grow, he said, "if provincial governments and the federal government don't step in to fill those gaps. That is certainly pronounced going forward as we see access challenges across the country, whether it's emergency departments or family doctors."

World.title: Unity or bust: How U.S. tariffs get spun into Alberta's separatism debate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A foreign trade threat that has prompted a rally-’round-the-flag moment for Canadians may also have provided a boost for a pro-unity group whose emblem is a modified Canadian flag.

Thomas Lukaszuk said he pulled in more than 11,000 viewers for an online town hall Sunday to update his Forever Canadian group’s fight to counter Alberta separatism. That’s far more than he garnered at virtual gatherings this spring, or at the height of Forever Canadian’s massive petition drive last year, and he credits the higher traffic to the concerns around the newly escalated U.S. tariff war against Canada.

It was perhaps inevitable that interest would rise in his group’s patriotic lawn signs as the calendar ticked toward the Oct. 19 referendum on Alberta’s future in Canada. But this weekend’s acrimonious collapse in bilateral trade talks could heighten the movement’s urgency, Lukaszuk said.

“I'm finding that the outpour of support for Forever Canadian is rising every time we see these existential threats to our sovereignty, particularly from [the] United States,” he told CBC News.

“We have to be particularly united at this point in time.”

Thomas Lukaszuk of the Forever Canadian campaign next to his Unity Bus during a tour stop in Fort McMurray, Alta., on Aug. 13, 2026. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)

The rising friction has prompted Quebec’s separatist Parti Québécois to pledge that if elected this fall, it won’t hold a secession referendum until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said this weekend she won’t follow suit, not with this referendum process well under way.

According to an Angus Reid Institute poll taken this weekend, more than three-quarters of respondents support Canada refusing the Trump administration's trade deal terms, and responding with dollar-for-dollar tariffs. Support for those positions among Albertans is not as strong, but is still well into majority territory.

That much solidarity risks not leaving much rhetorical room for separatists to make their own case to break away the province from Canada amid Trump’s punitive measures and continued threats.

But the independence advocates are determined and they see an opportunity.

They are leaning into their side’s existing distrust of the federal Liberal government, and paint the latest developments as a national disaster that Albertans should walk away from.

To deride the crowd that favours an “elbows up” response to the tariff threat, some separatists on social media like to call them “elbozos.” That includes Alberta Prosperity Project’s Jeffrey Rath , who conveys this all as Prime Minister Mark Carney’s crass play to gin up patriotism.

Jeffrey Rath of Alberta Prosperity Project is one of the vocal separatists who says supporters of an 'elbows up' trade posture are 'elbozos.' (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

Another user of the “elbozo” swipe is Derek Smith, host of the popular pro-independence Unacceptable Fringe show on YouTube.

He has said the failure in trade talks is an economic disaster for Canada against a more powerful neighbour, and a sign of Carney’s “Trump derangement syndrome.”

In one of his videos Monday, he said any Canadian leader like Carney will focus their policies and attention on the more populous parts of Quebec and Ontario, which he highlighted in a graphic.

“This is why Alberta wants to leave,” Derek Smith said. “This red portion of the map decides who’s in charge of the country.”

In a livestreamed Unacceptable Fringe episode later Monday — with more than 31,000 views — Derek Smith and his guests claimed Carney is an inadvertently great salesman for Alberta secession.

“I for one tend to be optimistic about this because at the end of the day, what's bad for Canada is good for Alberta independence, baby,” one of Derek Smith’s guests told the show.

In this broad, decentralized independence movement, not all voices take part in the “elbozo” name-calling or overtly root for the country to suffer. Jason Lavigne, a fellow daily YouTuber who touts independence, said he hadn’t heard that term until CBC News asked about it.

But like the others, he puts a positive spin on the deterioration of the Canada-U.S. trade relationship and argues this could sway undecided Albertans to vote for a binding referendum to leave the country.

“What they're paying close attention to is whether or not Canada can work, and this will be a strong indication that quite possibly it can't work,” Lavigne told CBC News.

Pro-independence YouTube streamer Jason Lavigne has been a key voice for his side, and launched his own third-party advertising group with lawn signs. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)

To this point, Alberta has largely escaped the damaging effects of tariffs, with oil, gas and agricultural products exempted by Trump. But Lavigne now sees high downside risk for his province from this trade war escalation, either in higher costs from retaliatory tariffs to the lingering prospect that oil and gas export taxes are imposed as leverage tactics.

“There's a lot of people here in Alberta that really strongly believe that if there was a negotiation where Alberta could have the [lead], it would have come out much differently,” he said of an independent Alberta. “It likely would have led to no tariffs, possibly some free trade.”

Thus far, separatists appear to have struggled to win broad support for their movement, repeated polls suggest.

And opposing them is an ever-growing movement that spans much of Alberta’s political spectrum, including former NDP and UCP premiers Rachel Notley and Jason Kenney on a newly launched joint campaign with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

“Most Albertans are proud Canadians at heart, and we’re reminded of that with the attacks that our country is facing from abroad,” Kenney told CBC Radio’s Calgary Eyeopener on Tuesday.

LISTEN | Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley join forces against Alberta independence: Calgary Eyeopener 12:24 Former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney on national unity, and the Canada-U.S. trade relationship Should the province leverage energy exports in the ongoing trade fight with the United States? Jason Kenney joined us to weigh-in.

But it’s hard not to notice some envy of the American system among Alberta separatists. Alberta Prosperity Project’s recent discussion paper on an independent Alberta floats elected judges and senators, open-carry gun laws, and a president with veto power — all the trappings of U.S. constitutional framework.

While supporters of Carney and his government’s position may express frustration with Trump, some separatists are more likely to side with the U.S. president.

Derek Smith, the Unacceptable Fringe host, said this week that if Trump offered citizenship to Albertans, “I’d happily pack up and go to the United States at this point. At least they have real leadership there.”

Part of that may be strategic, Lavigne suggests, because the U.S. president’s support and recognition of an independent Alberta would be pivotal to a would-be country.

Trade talks have broken off between the Trump and Carney governments, and it's unclear when they'll resume. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

The host of The Lavigne Show said Trump’s more overheated “51st state” rhetoric doesn’t help the independence cause, but he also echoed the president’s new threat to rebrand Lake Ontario.

“To the people of Ontario, you deserve better leaders,” Lavigne wrote Tuesday on social media. “Carney and [Ontario Premier Doug] Ford are sinking you. Soon, you'll find yourself at the bottom of Lake America.”

As Trump’s attention stays on Canada during this trade sniping, it may well turn to the Canadian disunity that Alberta independence has helped stoke.

If his higher tariffs are altering the campaign now, it’s hard to know what a more direct Trump foray into the debate would do to those who want to safeguard Canadian unity and those who’d rather abandon it.

World.title: Insurance covered the rebuild of her house after a fire. Why didn’t the bank release the money on time?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Property owner Antonina Gladkova is warning others to pay attention to their mortgage agreements after her lender didn't dole out insurance payments on pace with her contractor's invoices, leaving her on the hook to cover costly shortfalls to rebuild her property after a fire.

The fire that destroyed Antonina Gladkova's property at the beginning of 2024 was just the beginning of years of frustration and financial stress that's cost her tens of thousands of dollars and left her wanting to warn other homeowners about what's in their mortgage agreements when it comes to insurance claims.

But the fire "was just the first nightmare," she said. "It became worse."

At first, Gladkova says she was relieved with the smooth process of dealing with her insurance company, which covered the full cost to rebuild her half of the semi-detached house in Georgetown, Ont.

But, her mortgage provider didn't dole out the insurance payments on pace with her contractor's invoices, and now she says she and her boyfriend are out tens of thousands of dollars and on the hook for a private mortgage they had to get to cover the shortfalls and keep construction going amid costly delays.

"We were absolutely outraged," she said.

While it's routine for insurance payments to be released in installments through a homeowner's mortgage lender, legal experts say situations like Gladkova's are becoming more common. That's why she's warning others about her experience in hopes of preventing it from happening again.

"The whole system doesn't work. And that's why I want people to know … be prepared," she said.

'A chicken and egg situation'

In February 2024, a fire broke out in the neighbouring half of Gladkova's semi-detached property. Her neighbour tragically died in the fire, which spread to her half, completely destroying it. Gladkova, who originally lived in the home, had been renting it out for several years after she moved in with her boyfriend.

Just over a year after the fire, the insurance payment to rebuild the home was approved at just over $508,000. Because they had a mortgage, the lender, Simplii Financial, was responsible for releasing the funds.

The couple's contractor required the first payment of $101,600, but Simplii only released $25,000, according to bank statements reviewed by CBC News.

After the couple brought up the issue, Simplii, which is part of CIBC, released another $25,000 as part of what they called a "one-time exception." But the couple was still 50 per cent short.

A fire broke out on the other side of Antonina Gladkova's semi-detached house in Georgetown, Ont., in February 2024. It spread to Gladkova's half of the property, completely destroying both homes. (Mehrdad Nazarahari/CBC)

Gladkova says the inital process was for the bank to release funds based on invoices from the builder and confirmation of completed work. But that would require the contractor, who she says was chosen by the insurance company, to finance the work upfront.

"You cannot build without the money. So it's like a chicken and egg situation," Gladkova said.

The couple filed a formal complaint with Simplii, requesting that the bank release an additional $51,600 so they could pay the invoice in full and keep construction going. The bank declined.

Gladkova says they didn't have enough money to pay the difference, so they got a private mortgage with a 10 per cent interest rate.

After the formal complaint, documents show Simplii changed its process to provide funds based on progress reports of the work that was completed. For example, if 20 per cent of the work was completed, Simplii would have provided 20 per cent of the total insurance payment.

But, emails between Gladkova and Simplii show the bank began making the calculation on the first insurance cheque rather than the total insurance payout, which Gladkova says resulted in the couple consistently being about 35 per cent short on paying the contractor.

Antonina Gladkova's property was completely destroyed in the fire and her insurance company paid to rebuild the house. (Submitted by Antonina Gladkova)

Simplii did eventually release all of the money, including through another additional exception payment this past April to cover a shortfall for the third construction invoice.

The rebuild was completed this past June, about six months behind schedule, according to the construction contract.

Gladkova says the couple has paid around $15,000 in interest on the private mortgage and counting, plus thousands to set up the private mortgage and legal costs.

There's still an outstanding balance of about $19,000 owed to the contractor as a result of delays because the couple didn't have funds to pay him on time, Gladkova says.

She says that because of the private mortgage and the insurance payouts not keeping pace, the amount they owed "accumulated and skyrocketed in no time."

Simplii's response

In a statement, Simplii spokesperson Kira Smylie says the company empathizes with clients managing property damage and that "wherever possible, we work with our clients to provide flexibility, and we did so in this case."

Smylie also said Simplii's mortgage terms allow the bank to determine how insurance proceeds are applied.

"Before finalizing the payment terms with a contractor, clients should confirm the payment schedule with us so they can make informed decisions," she said.

Gladkova says she wants to warn others about how vague some mortgage agreements are written. She says that had the bank told them they would be responsible for any shortfalls, the couple would have made other arrangements.

How to protect yourself

Standard mortgage provisions require insurance money be paid to the lender, which will then release the money on a schedule, because the lender has an interest in the property and wants to ensure the funds are used to rebuild it, according to real estate and home insurance lawyers.

Fy Virani, the founder of Virani Law, which specializes in home insurance claims, says situations like Gladkova's that result in payment schedules not alligning are occurring more often. He says that's because lenders are exerting tighter control over insurance payouts since there are now more total loss claims from fires and floods.

Fy Virani, a home insurance claim lawyer and the the founder of Virani Law, says he's seeing the issue of insurance payment schedules not aligning with contractor invoices more frequently. (Submitted by Fy Virani)

"We're running into more and more total losses as a result of fires and floods," he said. "So the result becomes this communication gap between these entities that aren't used to being on the same page."

Virani says in order to prevent this, property owners should establish clear and open communication with lenders, contractors and insurance companies to ensure all parties are on the same page and that payment schedules align before construction begins.

"It's very hard to fix once money is already moving," he said.

Filing complaints

At the end of 2025, Gladkova filed a complaint with the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments (OBSI), which is an independent and impartial Canadian organization that helps resolve disputes between banks, investment firms and customers.

Gladkova wanted Simplii to compensate them for the interest on the private mortgage and $4,000 in fees that came along with it.

She says the OBSI completed its investigation last June and found that while Simplii is not responsible for the extra costs incurred, and was not bound by the agreement the couple reached with the contractor, the bank did cause extraordinary distress and inconvenience by not explaining to the couple that they may need additional financing to complete the project.

The OBSI recommended that Simplii give the couple $500 in compensation, which the couple did not accept.

"It was a slap in the face," Gladkova said.

In a statement, the OBSI said its complaint resolution process is confidential and cannot comment on an individual complaint.

Gladkova has since filed a complaint with the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, which supervises federal external complaint bodies, including banks and the OBSI. She hopes to see changes to mortgage agreements so banks will release insurance payments directly to contractors.

"Hopefully, this can be fixed," she said. "No one should experience this as it was life changing."

World.title: Unearthed letters show how N.L. bishop handled allegations in Baie Verte
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The first letter is dated March 31, 1970.

Father Leonard Joseph Kelly was told to leave his parish in a hurry. The bishop could see no other option.

“It seems that you have been committing these acts over a long period,” reads the letter from John Michael O’Neill, then the bishop of Grand Falls. “You should make immediate preparations to leave Baie Verte permanently. To avoid scandal, you can say that you have not been feeling well and need medical care.”

The wording is ambiguous. The bishop never spells out exactly what the priest has done. He refers to it only as a “problem” far more “deep-seated” than was previously known.

O’Neill asks Kelly for frankness and honesty — and underscores his desire for secrecy.

“I thought of calling a meeting of the consultors but decided against it for fear that something might [get] out,” O’Neill wrote.

Rather than alert authorities, newly unearthed letters show the bishop referred the priest to the Southdown Institute — a controversial therapy centre near Toronto, where priests have been treated for a range of issues from alcoholism and depression to pedophilia for decades.

These letters, discovered in Kelly’s personnel file at the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Grand Falls, are now at the centre of an uncommon legal action in central Newfoundland.

The church's own insurance provider is seeking a Norwich order — an exceptional move compelling a third party to hand over vital documents that could lead to a lawsuit against another entity.

In this case, Guardian Insurance is asking a judge to compel the Southdown Institute to turn over its files on Kelly to find out exactly why he was admitted there in 1970.

Guardian believes the records could show the church knew Kelly was a risk to children before entering into an insurance policy in the 1980s. Those records could lead to another court action, in which Guardian would seek to avoid covering the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Grand Falls for Kelly’s abuses during its policy period due to material non-disclosure or misrepresentation.

I cannot be expected to condone the seriousness of his betrayal of confidence and the terrible scandal which, but for the discretion of the family involved, could have blighted the whole life of the church in this small province. - Bishop John Michael O'Neill

The church is currently facing a lawsuit, filed in 2022, accusing Kelly of sexual abuse in Gander.

The plaintiff alleged he was “subjected to regular and frequent forced oral sex and occasionally other invasive sexual touching by Kelly” between 1977 and 1983, when he was between the ages of six and 12.

Kelly was also convicted of sexually assaulting a pair of 12-year-old boys in the mid-1980s. A provincial court judge sentenced him to two years of probation, contingent on him returning to the Southdown Institute for treatment.

The province’s court of appeal found that to be inappropriate, and instead sent Kelly to jail on a four-month sentence in 1988.

Bishop credited family’s ‘discretion’ in avoiding scandal

The Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Grand Falls is the church’s corporate body overseeing larger centres such as Grand Falls-Windsor and Gander, while also serving dozens of smaller churches dotting rural outports throughout the island.

Father Kelly — who hailed from Windsor — was ordained in 1955. He was welcomed to the priesthood by Bishop O’Neill at a ceremony in his hometown in front of 500 people “eager to honour the young cleric,” according to an article published by the Advertiser on June 9, 1955.

It’s not clear when he moved to Baie Verte.

Three months after being told to leave the parish, Bishop O’Neill began exchanging letters with the Southdown Institute about Kelly’s progress. The first letter quotes from a psychiatric evaluation conducted after his admission, referring to his actions as “rather pathetic homosexual adventures” fuelled by alcoholism.

“I do not feel the sexual episodes will cause any future difficulties if this priest is successful in his attempt to separate himself from alcohol,” it reads.

The person evaluating Kelly recommended he return to the priesthood in the Diocese of Grand Falls.

“It is felt that when returned to the ministry, Father Kelly should not be removed from the diocese since sexual problems play only a small role in his total inability to adjust. Rather than being removed from the home diocese, he should be given considerable support in his attempt to attack his central alcoholic difficulties.”

Bishop O’Neill responded two weeks later, pushing back on the idea.

“It must be obvious to him, as it is to me, that he was lucky to get out of Baie Verte with his name unsullied,” O’Neill wrote. “There could well have been a court case with all its ugly implications. Even he should realize that it is not merely a case of taking up where he left off.”

The bishop suggested Kelly should be moved to Halifax on a temporary basis.

“While my sympathy goes out to Father Kelly, as it would to any poor priest in trouble, I cannot be expected to condone the seriousness of his betrayal of confidence and the terrible scandal which, but for the discretion of the family involved, could have blighted the whole life of the church in this small province.”

The response — authored by Southdown’s executive director, John Kelly — came close to spelling out the nature of the complaint against the priest, without explicitly stating it.

“I am keenly aware that his conduct could have created wide-spread scandal and I am grateful that this was avoided,” the director wrote. “The more we see of Father Kelly, the more we become convinced that he can make a good recovery. His motivation is good and it becomes increasingly apparent that prolonged drinking had removed, as it frequently does, the restraints which normally he would have exercised in his relationships with the boys in question.”

He goes on to suggest they find Father Kelly an assignment close to the Southdown Institute in Ontario, so they can keep an eye on him before returning to Newfoundland.

O’Neill obliged, and conveyed the message to Father Kelly on July 30, 1970. They’d start him in Ontario, he said, before moving him to Halifax with the goal of working his way back to Newfoundland.

“It is apparent you were a very sick and mixed up priest,” O’Neill wrote. “As it is, we are all fortunate that the situation did not become public with irreparable damage to the Church and the priesthood. Now, fortunately, all that is past and I am happy to forget the whole thing and look forward to your future work in the holy Priesthood.”

Kelly’s personnel file shows he took up a pastoral assignment in Gander in 1977, before moving home to Grand Falls-Windsor in 1983.

O’Neill died in 1974. He didn’t live to see the consequences of his decision to “forget the whole thing.”

Court filing seeks to uncover Winter Commission mystery

Kelly was part of the first wave of Catholic clergy and Christian Brothers to face criminal charges in the late 1980s. What began as a trickle turned into a flood of allegations, prompting the Archbishop of St. John’s, Alphonsus Penney, to call for a commission of inquiry.

"It's a great mystery to me how such a thing could go on for so long without somebody blowing the whistle,” Penney told CBC News in 1989.

The Winter Commission report was released in 1990, and found allegations of sexual misconduct spanned back as far as at least 1975 — when Penney himself sent a priest from the Diocese of Grand Falls to the Southdown Institute over allegations of pedophilia. Penney did not report the priest to authorities, and the Winter Commission did not uncover the priest’s name.

Guardian Insurance is now asking the court to compel Southdown to turn over its records on the unnamed priest, as well as Father Leonard Joseph Kelly.

“Guardian has a reasonable basis to believe that the offending priest was Kelly, or alternatively another Grand Falls priest whose attendance at Southdown was precipitated by inappropriate interactions with a child, thus the priests’ identification in the Southdown records would be material to Guardian’s coverage investigation,” the company’s application reads.

The Southdown Institute employs a team of psychologists and psychiatrists who mostly deal with clergy suffering from any range of mental health issues such as alcoholism and depression. It has also treated priests accused of abusing children. (Southdown Institute website)

The Winter Commission found church officials in Newfoundland and Labrador relied on Southdown for a range of reasons, starting with the unnamed priest in 1975.

The letters unearthed by Guardian Insurance show that reliance existed at least five years earlier than previously known.

In total, the Winter Commission report referenced five Newfoundland priests who were sent to Southdown, including four who were accused of inappropriate relationships with minors.

“The Southdown facility seems to have been seen as a quick fix for nearly any kind of behavioural problem,” the report reads.

The Southdown Institute still operates today, offering psychotherapy, counselling and spiritual direction to clergy, lay pastoral ministers and “all adults who consider faith and spirituality to be integral to their lives.”

Lawyers for Guardian Insurance, Southdown and the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Grand Falls were in court earlier this month for a brief appearance. A hearing on the application will be held on Jan. 26, 2027.

World.title: Peach trees in Ontario's Niagara region under threat due to recent historic flooding
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Recent torrential rains in Ontario's Niagara region that flooded thousands of homes and overwhelmed sewage systems had another significant impact: Threatening the region’s peach industry.

Peach and other tender fruit trees, including ones bearing nectarines and cherries, don’t tolerate excess water and can die when their roots are waterlogged for too long.

That means the multiple storms that flooded the region between July 21 and Aug. 2 are likely to take their toll on peach trees.

“That's a given,” said Jay Subramanian, a professor of tree fruit breeding and biotechnology at the University of Guelph.

He said it could take weeks or months for affected trees to die, so it'll be some time before the full loss is known.

“It could be anywhere between, you know, 20 per cent … even upwards of 40 per cent.”

Peaches, wine may cost more

An organizer of the Winona Peach Festival, which is this Friday to Sunday in the east Hamilton community of Winona, told CBC Hamilton its peaches haven't been affected. Vendors come mostly from the immediate area, including Winona and Beamsville in Niagara. The festival will have its usual amount of pies and peach sundaes, said Terry Gudgeon.

Subramanian said several peach trees on his Vineland research farm in the Niagara region already show signs of being impacted and are dying.

If the damage is heavy, he said, consumers will feel it next summer. “That will obviously drive prices up."

The same may hold true for wine costs.

Most of Ontario’s grapes are grown in the region, and like peaches and nectarines, grape vines also cope poorly with water.

Jamie Slingerland, director of viticulture at Pillitteri Estates Winery, said two hectares of grapevines were flooded.

WATCH | The toll of Niagara floods on region's vineyards: How grape growers from Niagara-on-the-Lake are dealing with back-to-back rainstorms | Duration 1:44 Grape growers in Niagara are scrambling to save their crops after two extreme rainstorms flooded thousands of homes and businesses in the region in just a few days.

“All this humid weather, every disease that you can imagine starts to grow. You start to have downy mildew, powder mildew, black rot, botrytis … and the list goes on and on.”

Slingerland said the flooded vines could cost the winery $250,000 in lost revenue.

Other impacts of changing climate

Flooding isn’t the only climate-change related threat to Niagara’s fruit.

Subramanian said the warming climate comes with a variety of challenges.

As an example, he pointed to the Harrow Diamond — an iconic Ontario, cold-weather peach bred in Harrow in Essex County.

“This variety used to ripen around July 28, 29 in Vineland,” he said. “Now I'm harvesting the same variety between July 12 to 15. So that's a two-week to 2.5-week advancement, within 25 years.”

Subramanian explained this earlier ripening means the peaches don’t have as much time to develop, which can lead to smaller, less flavourful peaches. Warmer weather also presents new pressures from pests.

Subramanian is working on breeding varieties of peaches that are resistant to such changes.

He said Canada needs to treat this issue with more urgency.

The country is an outlier because few places produce that much fruit in the cold.

Comparatively, we are really in a tough spot. We have to breed varieties for our needs. - Jay Subramanian, University of Guelph professor

While growers in warmer locales — like southern Europe, Australia or the U.S. — can try out new varieties from any number of other warm-weather countries, Canada is forced to be more reliant on varieties developed at home.

“Comparatively, we are really in a tough spot. We have to breed varieties for our needs,” he said, adding that such efforts have plummeted in recent years.

Subramanian said he’s among only about five people in Canada who are working to breed climate change-resistant fruit.

He said government support has dropped in recent years, and the industry has stepped up to help fill gaps in funding, but there needs to be more to continue to do meaningful research.

Without it, Subramanian said, homegrown, quality fruit will be harder to find.

In an email statement to CBC, the ministry of agriculture, food and agribusiness said in 2023, the provincial government "invested over $343 million to support research and innovation across Ontario's agri-food sector, including research that helps address real-world challenges facing tender fruit growers."

The government has also invested $41 million "in research infrastructure to expand Ontario's capacity to deliver cutting-edge agricultural research and practical solutions for farmers," Miriam Leardi, senior communications advisor, wrote.

Ministry representatives have visited the flood-affected areas, the statement also said, and will "continue working with farmers across the region, including through supports available from AgriCorp," referring to the Ontario agency that offers crop insurance.

World.title: California governor 'absolutely' believes Trump will restart trade talks with Canada in 'a matter of days'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom says pressure from within the Republican Party will bring U.S. President Donald Trump back to the negotiating table with Canada.

"He's getting crushed. He's getting hammered by his own party right now," Newsom told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton in an interview.

The comments come just a few months before the U.S. midterm elections that will test Trump's presidency. Republicans currently hold majority control of both the Senate and House of Representatives but are at risk of losing both in November.

Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down late last week, with Prime Minister Mark Carney halting negotiations. Trump's new tariffs on some $28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect hours later.

But Newsom said he believes Trump can't afford to stretch out the hiatus.

"I absolutely believe within a matter of days, I can't imagine more than two, three weeks, he'll be back at the table," the governor said.

Newsom made California's position clear: "We do not in any way, shape or form condone the behaviour of this president as it relates to how he's treated you."

WATCH | CBC's Rosemary Barton speaks with Gavin Newsom: California governor says Carney is ‘playing this well’ in Trump trade fight | Duration 10:23 California Gov. Gavin Newsom responds to the collapse of U.S.-Canada trade talks, telling CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that Prime Minister Mark Carney is ‘playing this well’ because Donald Trump doesn’t respect weakness.

The vocal Trump critic told Barton he's "disgusted by the invasive species in the White House, Donald Trump. I am. And I'm embarrassed as an American."

California is being hit hard by the trade war, including wines produced in the state being off of most provinces' shelves for over a year.

Canada was the largest foreign market for California wine. But according to the U.S. Census Bureau, wine exports from the U.S. to Canada dropped by $343 million US between 2024 and 2025.

When asked by Barton if there's animosity for Canada from California wine makers, Newsom responded, "Yeah, I think there is."

He described their situation as "painful" and said the blame should be put on Trump.

"It's not California," he said. "I'm the most un-Trump state in America."

Despite this, Newsom says he understands why wine won't return to shelves any time soon, after a deal that would have ended the booze ban was scrapped.

He praised Carney's approach to Trump: "His strength, clarity, conviction: Trump respects strength, he does not respect weakness."

"T. Rex Trump," Newsom said, "devours you" if you're not strong.

Newsom is not seeking re-election as California's governor. He is widely believed to be a Democratic contender for the 2028 presidential bid.

When asked by Barton if his push against Trump's tariffs is posturing for a potential run, he said that "it has nothing to do with why I'm doing this."

But Newsom did not rule out running.

"That's fate ... but I'm not naive about where fate goes," he said.

World.title: Fire in Pakistan hospital kills 14 newborns, officials order immediate inquiry
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A fire erupted early Wednesday in a nursery for newborns at a major government hospital in Pakistan's capital, killing 14 babies, according to hospital officials and the government.

The Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad housed at least 15 newborns in the nursery from the fire that began about 6:45 a.m. local time after an air-conditioning unit compressor exploded inside the nursery on the third floor, hospital and rescue officials said.

The fire was confined to the nursery in the gynecology ward, while the rest of the hospital remained unaffected and there were no other injuries reported, according to hospital officials and witnesses. Television footage showed rescue workers using ladders to reach the area through broken windows.

Federal Health Minister Mustafa Kamal confirmed at least 14 children had died.

"One baby was rescued by a doctor," said Dr. Aneeza Jalil, a hospital spokesperson. She said the bodies of six babies had been handed over to their families, while the remaining bodies would be released soon.

Javeria, the mother of a newborn victim, is consoled following the deadly fire. At least one baby was rescued, officials said. (Akhtar Soomro/Reuters)

The deaths of the children sent a wave of shock and grief across the country. Police were deployed at the hospital as grieving parents and relatives gathered, some weeping while others called for accountability and demanded answers about how the fire began and whether the nursery had adequate firefighting equipment.

Mohammad Sami said she gave birth three days earlier and her baby was receiving intensive care in the nursery when the fire erupted.

"I don't know what to say or whom to blame," she said through tears. "I have lost my child."

'Irreparable loss'

Firefighters quickly responded and extinguished the blaze and rescue teams began cooling operations at the site, local media reported. Islamabad Chief Commissioner Suhail Ashraf later said the fire had been extinguished and authorities were co-ordinating with the families.

Within hours, the Islamabad district magistrate appointed a multiagency fact-finding committee with directions to submit a report within 24 hours. The panel will investigate the cause of the fire and its spread, determine whether adequate fire-safety measures were in place and evaluate the emergency response, a government notification said.

A multiagency fact-finding committee has been directed to submit a report within 24 hours. The panel will investigate the cause of the fire and its spread. (Akhtar Soomro/Reuters)

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the fire.

"A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss," said Sharif, who ordered an immediate investigation.President Asif Ali Zardari also offered condolences to the families, describing the deaths as "heartbreaking and an irreparable loss."

Zardari called for those responsible to be identified and dealt with under the law and urged hospitals to ensure effective fire-safety measures and emergency procedures, particularly in wards caring for newborns.

PIMS, one of Islamabad's largest public hospitals, which recently was the site of a medical examination of imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan.

World.title: Could Trump really rename Lake Ontario? Yes, but here’s why he shouldn’t
World.content:
Article content

Indeed there are. At the United Nations (headquartered in New York City, the settlement originally known as New Amsterdam), the Group of Experts on Geographical Names (UNGEGN) “supports the national and international standardization of geographical names… (by) promoting the use of standardized geographical names.” So right off the bat, unilaterally changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America would not only put state authorities of New York in a quandary over whether to follow the federal lead, it would also raise a standardization problem between Canada and the U.S. In a conference report from 1972, this United Nations group contemplates the problem of competing names arising when countries do not share a language, and that if they “do not succeed in agreeing on a common name form, it should be a general rule of international cartography that the name forms of each of the languages in question should be accepted.” It says nothing, however, about deliberate renaming of shared lakes as an act of economic belligerence.

World.title: Robot dogs are here and they’re cheap, Canada, but their software still needs a human and their security has flaws
World.content:
Article content

Makris and his colleagues found another way in. Setting these robots up on Wi-Fi is done over Bluetooth, and that step accepts whatever text it is given without checking, so commands can be smuggled in through the password field. The encryption protecting the exchange uses a single key, hardcoded and identical on every machine Unitree ships. Anyone who knows it and stands within Bluetooth range gets full control. The flaw covers the company’s humanoids and its robot dogs, including the model sold in Canada.

World.title: Carney’s retaliatory tariffs ‘are very much a tax on ourself’: Trevor Tombe
World.content:
Article content

Just when it seemed like a trade deal was close at hand, the Canada-U.S. trade relationship has taken a sharp turn for the worse. The new, higher U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods have come into effect, and Canada has officially confirmed the retaliatory tariffs that will come into effect on Sept. 8. So what will all of this mean for the Canadian economy? And is our retaliation worth the cost that it will impose on our economy? The National Post’s Rob Breakenridge speaks with Trevor Tombe, professor of economics at the University of Calgary and director of fiscal and economic policy at the School of Public Policy, about the economic consequences of this escalating trade war. As Tombe outlines, tariffs are essentially a tax, meaning Canadian consumers and businesses will bear much of the cost of Ottawa’s retaliation. The same, though, is true of the aggressive American tariffs. We’ll take a closer look at what the fallout from this trade war could look like, as well as the sort of tax reform the Carney government could deploy to mitigate the damage, while still boosting Canada’s competitiveness and productivity.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.

World.title: Colombia expands disaster region in 2nd emergency decree
World.content:
Colombia’s government drastically expanded the region affected by the August 10 earthquake in a second decree declaring an economic emergency.

According to the decree, President Abelardo de la Espriella declared the emergency in 15 of the country’s 32 provinces “for a period of thirty (30) calendar days, in order to conjure the crisis and prevent the spread of the disaster’s effects.”

“The territorial scope includes all municipalities listed in UNGRD Situational Report No. 36 and any additional municipalities where direct damage from the August 10, 2026 earthquake is specifically demonstrated,” said the decree.
