World.title: Comment “le mur de fer” promis contre l’immigration clandestine à Mayotte s’est enlisé
World.content:
Un plan opérationnel “avant fin 2029, voire 2030”

Un appel d’offres, publié par le ministère de l’Intérieur le 12 août et repéré par POLITICO, dévoile l’ampleur du retard pris par le programme “mur de fer”. Celui-ci vise à recruter un prestataire extérieur, dont le rôle sera justement d’accompagner l’administration dans la mise en place globale du dispositif. Selon le phasage détaillé dans le règlement de consultation de l’appel d’offres, le plan “Uhura wa shaba”, dans toutes ses composantes, pourrait ne pas être pleinement opérationnel avant fin 2029, voire 2030.

En effet, une fois le prestataire sélectionné — fin 2026, au plus tôt, d’après les délais fixés dans ce document — celui-ci devra s’engager dans la préparation, puis l’organisation d’un “dialogue compétitif” pour choisir les industriels susceptibles de fournir les équipements et technologies nécessaires, pour une période de 33 mois au total. S’en suivra la phase “d’exécution” de ce chantier, pendant 51 mois.

“Si l’on fait les comptes, cela renvoie la mise en place du rideau de fer à 2030-2034, ce n’est pas acceptable”, s’agace Saïd Omar Oili. “J’y vois le signe que le gouvernement veut sous-traiter au privé la réflexion globale de la lutte contre l’immigration à Mayotte, un sujet de souveraineté, fustige Estelle Youssouffa. Lancer un tel chantier maintenant, c’est aussi un constat d’échec sur ce qui a été fait ces dernières années”.

Les radars actuels moins performants que les précédents

Dans l’appel d’offres, le ministère reconnaît lui-même que la “couverture des radars installés au début des années 2000 est significativement incomplète”. Celle-ci s’est retrouvée d’autant plus fragilisée par la tempête Chido qui a détruit une large partie des moyens de surveillance et d’interception.

“Des mesures de rattrapage ont été déployées : quatre radars légers et des caméras longue portée ont été achetés”, affirme le ministère de l’Intérieur, sollicité par POLITICO. Mais “ces radars ne disposent toutefois pas d’une portée de détection équivalente à celle des anciens radars”, pointe un rapport sénatorial publié en avril 2026 sur Mayotte et la Réunion. Le programme “rideau de fer […] n’a pas tenu ses promesses”, conclut ce document.

Selon les projections inscrites dans le marché public, le rideau de fer devait rendre “atteignable” l’interpellation de 20 000 étrangers en situation irrégulière en mer par an, contre 4 584 en 2025, d’après le bilan de la préfecture de Mayotte. Cette année-là, un total de 23 421 personnes ont fait l’objet d’un éloignement du territoire.

World.title: Belgium awards scholarships to Palestinian students — but gives them no way to leave Gaza
World.content:
The obstacles facing them are partly procedural, mostly political. POLITICO spoke to four of the scholarship recipients, who were told visas could only be obtained in person at a Belgian diplomatic post, such as the one in Jerusalem. Two of them have been able to successfully obtain visas with the help of lawyers in Belgium, suggesting solutions can be found even in Belgium’s rigid immigration system.

But visas on their own are of little help. None of the students and researchers offered funded places in Belgium currently have any way to actually get there.

In a written statement, Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories said it facilitates and encourages the evacuation of students and researchers from Gaza at the request of a third country.

Anneleen Van Bossuyt speaks during a plenary session at the Belgian Federal Parliament in Brussels on June 5, 2025. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images

But a spokesperson for Belgium’s foreign ministry, led by Prévot of the centrist Les Engagés party, said there was currently no decision in the coalition government to organize any more evacuations. The department said it was “actively investigating” what could be done to help the students but that any decision on new evacuations would be the “responsibility of the government as a whole.”

Two Belgian government officials, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that the coalition was divided on just about everything related to Palestine. While Prévot’s foreign ministry says it is looking for solutions, the French-speaking centrist Reformist Movement party (MR), whose leader Georges-Louis Bouchez is known for his pro-Israeli positions , and De Wever’s New Flemish Alliance (N-VA) are said to be against further evacuations.

“It’s common knowledge that if something gets stuck [on this issue], it’s going to be those two parties that are against it,” one of the officials said. MR and De Wever’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

World.title: Andy Burnham has to shape the UK’s social media ban. Australia and France could show him how.
World.content:
MPs return to Parliament next week after the summer break, and Burnham’s government will need to decide how the ban — which is supposed to come into effect in spring — will work.

Australia

Australia was the first country in the world to introduce a social media ban for kids in December last year. Last month, the Australian government published its first wave of findings on the experiences of more than 4,000 children and families since the ban took effect.

The numbers do not show a huge drop in kids accessing social media. The proportion of under-16s holding at least one social media account fell from 52.4 percent to 42.3 percent at the three-month follow-up. Meanwhile, the proportion who reported using a social media platform (with or without an account) fell even less, from 85.9 percent to 81.5 percent.

Australia only requires age-restricted platforms to take “reasonable steps” to prevent under-16s from creating or keeping accounts. Access via logged-out experiences, for example, is permissible.

The rationale is that account-based access — and the data harvesting that comes with it — increases the likelihood of exposure to potentially harmful design features, such as algorithmic suggestions or infinite scroll.

But the U.K. could go further than Australia by casting a wider net to cover both account ownership and access. That could implicate not just the social media platforms, but internet service providers too. The previous Starmer government has already laid the groundwork by handing itself powers, via the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act, to force ISPs to keep kids out.

World.title: Europe's obsession with return hubs may not live up to the hype
World.content:
The EU's migration policy has increasingly centred on the controversial notion of using "return hubs" to externalise irregular migrants to third countries, as enshrined in the recently adopted Return Regulation.

 

"We need to set up repatriation centres in third countries, as well as other innovative solutions outside Europe. We are working hard on this," Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen wrote in a joint statement earlier this month.

Nineteen EU countries are convinced this is an "innovative solution" to pursue for migration management, as made clear in a joint letter sent to EU leaders last June, suggesting the centres would become a reality sooner rather than later.

A crucial debate on migration will take place at the next European Council summit, with return hubs set to be one of the main points of discussion.

Yet fundamental questions about how the policy would be implemented remain unanswered. How would return hubs work? Where would they be located? And which problems have they run into so far? Here, Euronews breaks down the main issues around the new migration mantra – and why the reality might not match the political narrative.

What are return hubs?

Return hubs are facilities in a "third country" – a non-EU country with which an EU member state has reached an agreement to transfer people even when they have no connection to that country. The people to be transferred will be those with no legal right to remain on European territory who are subject to a return decision.

Hubs can be either places of transit, where a person is placed waiting to be returned to their country of origin, or locations where a person is expected to stay with no guarantee of onward returns.

While the term “return hubs” is not specifically used in the text of the regulation, the law reframes an original proposal from the European Commission, outlining the conditions to set up centres outside the EU. Each hub requires “an agreement or arrangement” to be concluded by the EU, or one or more of its member states, with a non-EU country.

Italy has spearheaded this approach with Albania, where centres opened in October 2024 are used to house migrants rescued or intercepted at sea by Italian authorities. Rome is now pitching this as the model for the rest of the EU to follow.

Ironically, the Albanian facility is not technically a return hub. For one thing, it was meant to host only asylum seekers, externalising the asylum procedure, which was run by Italian authorities on Albanian soil.

After being confronted with legal challenges, in March 2025, the Meloni government turned the centre into a deportation hub for irregular migrants who had already received a return decision. This change made the Albanian facility an early precursor to a return hub, but it is still the Italian authorities who manage the centre and who are responsible for the migrants’ final repatriation.

The European model could yet go further and externalise the entire management and responsibility for the asylum and deportation process to a non-EU country.

Italy's processing and detention centres in Albania would need to be reconsidered once the country joins the EU. Albania is the second-closest candidate to accession after Montenegro.

Which countries are being considered?

The Return Regulation has been politically agreed, but the EU institutions still have to complete its formal adoption: the law has yet to enter into force, as it still has to be published in the bloc's Official Journal.

According to an EU official, the language of the regulation is undergoing legal review and the final adoption is likely to take place in the autumn.

Meanwhile, European governments have reportedly already been working to set up return hubs in third countries, negotiating either bilaterally or as a group.

Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands have confirmed they are negotiating the establishment of such facilities. Their goal is to have the first partnership agreed by the end of the year, to be signed in early 2027, a diplomat told Euronews. The European Commission is informed, but not involved.

According to Greek daily Kathimerini, the five EU countries are in advanced discussions with Uganda, aiming to make a facility operational by next year. The countries involved have declined to confirm this, citing the risk that media disclosures could harm the negotiations.

Rwanda is another African country under discussion with the group of five, according to Germany's Der Spiegel. Rwanda was also at the centre of a highly controversial and now abandoned UK scheme to relocate asylum seekers while their applications were processed.

Immigration ministers from the five countries are due to take stock of progress at a meeting in Copenhagen on 4 September.

In April, meanwhile, the Austrian government announced a migration and readmission agreement with Uzbekistan, which does not include a return hub. Media reports and national MPs have named the country as a potential location, but Uzbekistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs denied it in a statement to Euronews, saying "there are currently no negotiations taking place on this matter".

What are the legal and practical problems?

In a letter published last month, the Council of Europe's Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, asked the five EU countries to ensure that "any relevant initiative be preceded by a comprehensive ex ante assessment of potential direct or indirect human rights risks associated with the proposed co-operation".

The Return Regulation does not explicitly require a human rights impact assessment, but it does state that "such an agreement or arrangement may only be concluded with a third country where international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law, including the principle of non-refoulement, are respected".

In 2024, the EU Ombudsman criticised the Commission for signing a Memorandum of Understanding with Tunisia on border control and migration management without conducting a human rights impact assessment.

Even though the UK is no longer an EU member, the reasoning behind its Supreme Court ruling against the Rwanda asylum-transfer scheme in November 2023 is instructive: the court found Rwanda was not sufficiently safe given the risk of persecution or ill-treatment. The incoming Labour government abandoned the scheme as a result.

Meloni's own relocation scheme in Albania has run into similar judicial trouble, with Italian judges questioning the designation of countries such as Bangladesh and Egypt as "safe" – a designation Italian authorities had relied on to examine asylum applications through an accelerated procedure.

Crucially, the court cases stemming from the Albanian centres have now reached the EU Court of Justice, which has yet to rule on a central question: whether Italy can transfer someone subject to a detention order outside the EU.

Will the hubs work?

"A human rights assessment - that should be carried out for all this kind of agreements - takes time, whilst EU countries are rushing to sign agreements with third countries even when the rules are not yet in place," Sara Prestianni, advocacy director at the NGO Euromed Rights, told Euronews.

Prestianni described the countries being floated to host return hubs as "characterised by human rights violations" and questioned what methodology is being used to carry out the required human rights impact assessments.

Even so, transferring irregular migrants outside the EU's borders is likely to require lengthy negotiations with host countries, and past cases show legal challenges can easily sink the project if human rights safeguards are not in place.

"I definitely see questions as to what the third country might ask in return for hosting people who are not nationals of that country," Davide Colombi, researcher on migration at Brussels-based think tank CEPS, told Euronews.

In the meantime, relocating irregular migrants within the Union has proved far more straightforward, though this piles more pressure on frontline countries like Italy to uphold the country-of-first-arrival principle.

Advocates of the return-hub approach counter that the legal and practical obstacles are not insurmountable, and that European capitals simply need time to build a functioning system capable of removing irregular migrants once the hubs are operational.

But past cases raise doubts over whether reality will match ambition.

"The previous experiences of externalisation or offshoring of migration management have been extremely costly, legally contested, and operationally very limited," Colombi said.

Despite years of preparation and massive financial investment, a total of four people were voluntarily relocated from the UK to Rwanda before that scheme was scrapped. Italy initially projected housing around 3,000 migrants a month in its Albanian centres; the actual figure has reportedly been a mere 500 in total since the conversion into a deportation centre in March 2025.

The entire bill amounts to over €670 million, and according to a recent study from an Italian University, detaining migrants in these centres has proven much more expensive for Italy than hosting them on its own territory.

World.title: Syria's main Kurdish force SDF ceases to exist after army merger
World.content:
The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) dissolved on Tuesday after their commander announced the completion of their integration into the Syrian army, ending the existence of the Kurdish-led force that served as Washington's main partner against the so-called Islamic State group in Syria and once controlled a vast autonomous zone in the country's northeast.

 

"We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and declare, with full responsibility, their dissolution as an independent military force," Mazloum Abdi said in a televised speech at the presidential palace in Damascus, following meetings with President Ahmad al-Sharaa.

The SDF was formed in 2015 at US instigation to fight the IS group, drawing primarily on the People's Protection Units, known by its Kurdish initials YPG, the main armed force of Syria's Kurdish community.

At its peak, the SDF controlled a de facto autonomous zone across much of northeastern Syria, including significant oil and agricultural land.

Turkey regards the YPG as the Syrian branch of the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK — designated a terrorist organisation by Turkey, the US, the EU, the UK and France — and has conducted multiple military operations against it inside Syria.

The integration is part of an agreement reached on 29 January, which stipulated a ceasefire and a gradual transfer of SDF-affiliated military and civilian institutions to Syrian state control, including border crossings, oil and gas fields, prisons and camps housing IS detainees.

The SDF lost most of the territory it controlled in northeastern Syria to a Syrian government offensive in January before signing the deal. After clashes in Aleppo in December 2025, it had already withdrawn from west of the Euphrates.

On 16 January, al-Sharaa signed a decree guaranteeing Kurds' national rights, recognising Kurdish as a national language, declaring Nowruz an official public holiday, and granting citizenship to Kurds previously denied legal status.

The US described the broader integration deal as "historic".

Abdi said the dissolution marked the beginning of "a genuine transition from battlefields to the fields of construction, and from an era of weapons to an era of peace." He added that political efforts would intensify to ensure Kurdish rights were enshrined in the Syrian constitution.

Another win for al-Sharaa

The dissolution is a significant achievement for al-Sharaa, who has been working since taking power after Bashar al-Assad's fall in December 2024 to consolidate state authority across all Syrian territory and integrate previously autonomous or rival armed factions under the Defence Ministry.

Following Abdi's announcement, the Syrian authorities announced an agreement with "all armed factions" to dissolve them and integrate them under the ministry.

The new Syrian army includes factions previously backed by Turkey that fought Kurdish forces for years, making the integration politically delicate.

Turkey, which shares borders with Syria and has long sought to prevent the establishment of a Kurdish autonomous zone on its southern flank, has been closely watching the process.

PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan, who has been held in Imrali Island prison in Turkey since 1999 and communicates only through heavily restricted channels, said the SDF-Damascus integration agreement would "ease and accelerate" what he called the "Turkey without terror" process.

He described the situation in Syria as "a clear reflection of the need for democratisation" and called on Turkey to play a "facilitating, constructive and open to dialogue" role in the process.

World.title: Thessaloniki counters visual vandalism with colourful graffiti in Ano Poli
World.content:
In Thessaloniki's Upper Town, some residents seem to have found a different way to respond to scribbles and haphazard graffiti. Instead of repainting the facades of their houses again and again, they hand them over to artists who turn them into open-air canvases.

 

Colours, flowers and images inspired by Japanese art have begun to appear on homes in the historic neighbourhood, changing the look of the streets and attracting the interest of residents and visitors alike.

In recent days, a particular stir has been caused by an artistic intervention on the outer wall of a house in the traditional settlement. The work draws on the aesthetics and iconography of Katsushika Hokusai's emblematic "Great Wave", complete with blossoming cherry trees, traditional architecture and the characteristic red sun. The result has already turned the spot into a small photo destination.

Behind the creation is artist Souzy Kamaliani, who took on the mural at the owners' request. Their special love for Japan set the direction for the theme, while the design was developed in collaboration with the artist.

Photo of a house in Thessaloniki ΑΠΕ-ΜΠΕ/ Σούζυ Καμαλιάνι

The choice, however, was not only about aesthetics. The owners were looking for a way to curb the repeated spray-paint attacks on the exterior walls of their home.

The idea had already been tested on another house in the Upper Town, where Souzy Kamaliani created a colourful composition with plant pots, flowers and bougainvilleas in February. According to her, the surface did not suffer any further vandalism after the work was completed.

Kamaliani has been consistently involved in painting since 2009 and, beyond the canvas, has also been exploring the large scale of murals in recent years. As she explains, the key difference with a mural lies precisely in its dimensions: a large wall offers a different field of expression and greater freedom of composition than a conventional canvas.

A persistent problem for the city

Uncontrolled slogans and scribbles are a concern not only for property owners but also for the Municipality of Thessaloniki, as clean-up operations often prove short-lived.

Deputy Mayor for Technical Works and Sustainable Mobility Prodromos Nikiforidis has pointed out that the Upper Town is among the areas where the phenomenon is most pronounced. Its particular urban layout, with many low-rise and ground-floor houses, leaves a large number of surfaces exposed to unauthorised markings. It is, as he notes, a problem that has been plaguing the city for many years.

To tackle visual pollution more effectively, the municipal administration believes that clean-ups alone are not enough. Broader awareness-raising and mobilisation of citizens is needed, as well as partnerships with businesses that could contribute materials and equipment for restoring surfaces.

The same logic of "protection through art" has already reached Thessaloniki's commercial centre. Many shopkeepers have commissioned artists to paint the metal shutters of their businesses, especially in spots where facades are often covered with slogans after marches and demonstrations.

In this way, the painted surfaces serve both as an aesthetic choice and as an informal shield against vandalism.

Entrance to a house in Thessaloniki ΑΠΕ-ΜΠΕ / Σούζυ Καμαλιάνι

An artists' register for new murals

At the same time, the Municipality of Thessaloniki is seeking to give a more structured character to public art interventions. As part of this effort, it is creating an open database and networking platform for artists active in mural painting, inviting creators to express their interest.

The initiative provides for the creation of a register of artists with a documented track record and representative portfolios. The aim is for this database to be used for future murals and artistic interventions in public space, strengthening the presence of art in Thessaloniki's everyday urban landscape.

In the Upper Town, however, change has already begun with the homes themselves. Where until recently a bare wall could easily become a target for a tag or scribble, today a Hokusai wave, a blossoming sakura or a bougainvillea are trying to write a different story for the neighbourhood.

World.title: Authorities in Greece issue code red wildfire alert for Ionian islands
World.content:
The Ionian Islands region was placed under a Code Red alert on Wednesday, as a very high risk of wildfires (Category 4) is forecast. The decision was taken by the Ministry of Climate Crisis and Civil Protection.

 

Under the alert, the National Civil Protection Mechanism is fully activated, deploying the necessary personnel, equipment and resources required to prepare for imminent threat, respond to emergencies and manage the consequences of any destructive event.

Short-term recovery, relief and support measures are also activated to help mitigate the impact of the disaster.

A high wildfire risk (Category 3) is forecast for Attica, several mainland areas and all of the country's islands.

The alert comes as Greece is at the height of the summer holiday season, with beaches packed with both domestic and international tourists.

Other wildfires under control

Meanwhile, the situation has improved at the site of a fire that broke out on Tuesday in a quarry containing rubbish and low vegetation in the Elliniko area of Salamina.

file photo AP Photo/Michael Varaklas

According to the Fire Service, the blaze has been contained and there is no risk of further spread.

Another wildfire that broke out in the Agios Vlasios area of Viotia was also largely brought under control, with firefighters still tackling some hot spots.

Residents of the Tsoukalades area had been informed by authorities on Tuesday to evacuate and move towards Livadeia.

Also a wildfire that broke out in a forest area in Stefani in Viotia no longer has an active front. During the night, firefighters fought several flare-ups and are now mainly focusing on several hotspots.

World.title: 'Mini jungle': Alaska is getting greener as the climate warms – with cascading effects
World.content:
With no tall trees reaching to the sky, Alaska's North Slope tundra can look desolate.

 

But up close, “the tundra's kind of like the jungle”, says Adam Bloom, a Florida Atlantic University plant biology student. Except this lush Arctic jungle tops out at about 25 centimetres.

The spongy soil was frozen solid a few weeks earlier. Now, knee-high dwarf birch trees and short but showy rhododendrons sprout from the North Slope, a vast and sparsely populated treeless area stretching from the Brooks mountain range to the Arctic Ocean.

For centuries, Arctic cold has kept plant life small, a sort of dollhouse of Earth's miniatures. The extreme environment has long given researchers a unique perspective on what makes plants grow, insight that would be hard to obtain elsewhere.

Now it offers them one of the world’s most useful windows on how climate change affects plant life, with the Arctic warming four times faster than the rest of Earth, especially in the winter.

For example, researchers at the Toolik Field Station, 320 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle, are studying whether plants facing these harsh conditions evolve to compete or cooperate with one another.

Studies show that the colder and further north in the Arctic, the smaller the plant life. There are several reasons, but the main one is that life is rough in the winter. Anything that protrudes above the shallow, insulating snow cover is more prone to being damaged by the cold and wind or eaten by wildlife, says plant ecologist Anne Bjorkman of the University of Gothenburg in Sweden.

Plus the frozen permafrost doesn't allow roots to grow too deep, she says.

FILE - Jørgen Kristensen rides with his sled dogs in Ilulissat, Greenland, Jan. 27, 2026. AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka, File

Alaska is getting greener as climate warms

But the cold is weakening and the miniatures are stretching. This part of Alaska is about 2.7 degrees Celsius warmer than it was 40 years ago mostly because of the burning of coal, oil and gas.

“Plants that are already there are growing taller,” Bjorkman says, adding that they're likely to grow even taller in the future.

And they are getting greener. Some of the long-term studies here are “trying to understand what controls how much plants grow, what controls how green it is,” and how all that is changing, says Columbia University ecologist Duncan Menge.

Meanwhile, taller plants that previously couldn't survive the cold are moving in, Bjorkman says.

This process, called shrubification, can accelerate warming because of how the plants trap heat, says University of Colorado plant ecologist Sarah Elmendorf. Canopies of the taller, darker shrubs stick out of the snow and absorb more energy from the sun than the blanket of white snow, which reflects heat back.

“It's certainly a major fingerprint of change that we can see,” she says.

FILE - Snow covers the mountains of the Brooks Range in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, Oct. 14, 2024, near Kaktovik, Alaska. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson, File

Darker tundra absorbing more radiation is “one of the main reasons for what we call arctic amplification, which causes climate change to accelerate” especially in the Arctic, Menge says.

The shrubs also trap more snow. That snow warms the ground below and allows microbes during the winter to release more of the heat-trapping gas methane, Elmendorf says. The added greenery from the taller plants and shrubs could compensate somewhat by absorbing more carbon dioxide, she says.

Expanding stands of willows seem to be providing more shade to streams and changing the ecology of fish, insects and birds, according to Chris Neill and Linda Deegan of the Woodwell Climate Research Center. They are conducting a multiyear study to see if an ecosystem adapts and even genetically evolves to handle the stress of climate change. If that is happening, it offers hope for the survival of some of the most fragile Arctic ecosystems, Deegan says.

FILE - The Kaktovik Lagoon and the Brooks Range mountains of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge are visible in the distance, Tuesday, Oct. 15, 2024, in Kaktovik, Alaska. AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson, File

Using a magnifying lens to appreciate tiny plants

“Tiny changes in a tiny jungle make a big difference,” says Jake Francis, a professor at Florida Atlantic University, as he examines the tiny flora at his feet on his first foray into the Arctic.

Big trees in Francis' home base of Florida are showy and amaze people because they're so easy to see, he says. But here on Toolik Lake's spongy tussocks – clumps of plants that jut upward, making walking an ankle-turning adventure – Francis says, “we have three or four different species of flowering plants growing. We have mosses. We have liverworts and it's the same thing. Layers growing on top of plants on top of plants on top of plants. But it's not yelling at us.”

“You have to get down there and stop and look,” Francis says. “You could walk right past it and not even see it. And so this is what to me is cool.”

FILE - The northern lights, or the aurora borealis, appear in the sky over Rat Lake in Yellowknife, Northwest Territories on Aug.8, 2024. Bill Braden/The Canadian Press via AP, File

What helps plants' survival, competition or cooperation?

These plants are competing for sun, nutrients, water and especially pollination in this harsh environment of limited but intense sunlight. Francis and his students are examining if it's more cooperative than the long assumed life-or-death competition. Francis' team focuses on a specific parasitic plant – the Arctic lousewort – that they think is getting a bad rap. The Arctic lousewort taps into the roots of nearby plants to suck out nutrients.

Sure, it's a vampire, siphoning resources from its neighbours. But doctoral student Jonathan Carcache theorises that the lousewort is helping its neighbours as much as stealing from them. That's because its dramatic shaft of purple flowers catches the attention of the not-so-plentiful bumblebees here “like a billboard that advertises pollination”, he says. And once that sought-after bee arrives, everyone gets pollinated.

To test their theory, Carcache and Bloom play bee. It's a painstaking, difficult task that they split between them. Bloom uses tweezers to remove a plant's male parts, and back at the lab he uses a mechanical device to shake out the pollen. It takes several hours each night to produce less than a teaspoon full of microscopic pollen grains.

Then Carcache finishes the job, belly-first on the ground and trying not to crush any of the plants they have come to study. Wearing a net over his head and nitrile gloves to protect him from swarming mosquitoes, he takes a paintbrush to dip grains of pollen on just the right female parts of neighbouring heather blossoms.

By doing the bees' job, Carcache and Bloom hope to figure out whether the plants around the parasite are pollinated more than those further away. If so, there's a fair trade taking place, rather than one plant simply taking advantage of others.

Amid the stresses of the Arctic, scientists are rethinking the idea that all life is a cutthroat competition with winners and losers. It might be more about mutualism, with plant species cooperating so that everybody survives, like the lousewort and its neighbours, Francis says.

“It would be wonderful if humans were the same way,” Francis says.

World.title: Putin signs decree allowing state seizure of businesses hit by drone strikes
World.content:
Vladimir Putin has signed a decree that could place privately owned businesses under state management if the government judges they have failed to protect themselves against Ukrainian drone attacks — a move legal experts described on Wednesday as a potential tool for seizing assets from Russian companies under the pretext of security failures.

 

The edict, which took effect immediately, covers facilities in the fuel and energy sector, industry, communications, energy — including nuclear — utilities, transport and logistics, and any other facility deemed of "particular importance for the security, economic stability and the livelihood of the population of the Russian Federation."

It allows temporary state management to be imposed without a court decision, based on a presidential instruction alone — which lawyers noted could be given orally.

State management can now be triggered by a company's failure to adopt security measures against drone attacks, violations of security requirements, or steps judged ineffective.

Crucially, the Russian president's decree does not define who decides whether the threshold has been met or on what criteria.

A tool for redistribution?

A source within a major Russian energy company, speaking to Euronews on condition of anonymity, said they feared the decree would be used in internal corporate disputes — that employees could use it to denounce management during conflicts, with devastating consequences.

Legal and business experts reacted sharply. Political analyst Abbas Gallyamov called it "hybrid nationalisation". "After they have bombed you, the state will come to you and, accusing you of failing to protect yourself from the attack, will seize it from you," he said.

Plumes of smoke from the Wildberries online retailer's warehouse in St Petersburg rise into the sky after a Ukrainian drone attack, with St Isaac's Cathedral in the foreground, 24 July 2026. AP Photo

Lawyer Andrei Grivtsov said the extremely broad definition of "critical infrastructure" left unanswered the fundamental question of who would assess compliance and on what basis.

A representative of one of Russia's largest agribusiness holdings, speaking anonymously to Forbes Russia, was more direct, calling the decree "a tool that will allow large assets to be taken away from business under the pretext of non-compliance with security measures."

Lawyer Sergei Uchitel warned against taking the word "temporary" at face value. In practice, external management means a company loses control over its operations, cannot set its own strategy, and is eventually forced to sell "on terms that can hardly be described as voluntary," Uchitel said.

Representatives of oil refineries and e-commerce platforms Wildberries and Ozon struck by Ukrainian drones have yet to comment on Putin's decision.

Drone strikes and fuel shortages

The decree was issued against the backdrop of an intensifying Ukrainian drone campaign against Russian economic infrastructure, as Moscow's all-out war against Ukraine continues well into its fifth year.

In the first six months of 2026, Ukrainian drones successfully struck Russian refineries at least 194 times — 11 times more often than in the same period of 2025, according to Financial Times calculations. Wildberries warehouses have been hit 21 times across 16 regions since mid-July, and since Saturday, Ukrainian drones have struck six Ozon logistics facilities in three days.

Kyiv has recently stepped up strikes on Russian logistics and energy infrastructure in a bid to cut the source of funding for Moscow's war machine amid sustained Russian bombardment of Ukrainian cities and villages.

According to the UN, at least 437 civilians were killed in Ukraine in July, the highest monthly figure since May 2022, 30% higher than in June and 70% higher than in July 2025.

Kyiv has repeatedly warned Russian forces are deliberately continuing to target residential areas and civilian infrastructure.

Three days before signing the decree, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak instructed oil companies to revise their refinery maintenance schedules to avoid worsening existing fuel shortages. Under the new decree, any delays in restoring damaged facilities could now have direct legal consequences for their owners.

First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov sought to reassure businesses on the day of publication, telling RBC that the decree "will be applied selectively; this is not about nationalisation."

He said decisions would be taken "at the very highest level" and that there was no mechanism for mass introduction of temporary management.

"Today, the owners of enterprises treat the threats we face with varying degrees of responsibility," he said.

"In a number of cases, ensuring the security of facilities and staff, unfortunately, is not their priority. It is precisely in such cases that the state will assume responsibility."

World.title: Deadly flash flood wipes away villages in Nepal, Tibet
World.content:
Rescue helicopters have been unable to land in affected areas due to high floodwaters. The leaders of Nepal and China ordered major rescue operations.

Several people were confirmed dead and many more a missing after a flash flood swept through remote valleys in Nepal and Tibet on Wedensday.

The floodwaters washed away villages, damaged bridges and destroyed electrical infrastructure.

"There is devastation everywhere we look," ‌Tula ​Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa district, told Reuters.

"The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing."

At 8 people were killed in Nepal while Chinese authorities also reported that a mudslide caused "major casualties" on the other side of the border in Tibet.

Villages in Rasuwa district were swept away by the deluge of water and mud Image: Sunil Sharma/ZUMA/IMAGO

A Nepali police spokesperson told Germany's DPA news agency that dozens of personnel were missing.

"So far, we only have confirmation of 26 police personnel who remain missing in the flood," they said.

"We also have missing information of government revenue officials, hydropower workers among others. But we are still collecting the data.

The burst river also inundated villages in Dhading district Image: REUTERS

Major rescue operations underway

Nepal dispatched more than a dozen rescue helicopters to the mountainous Rasuwa region, but floodwaters were too high for the helicopters to land.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the military and police were assisting with rescues.

"Instructions have been given ... to move ​the people living in the lower areas ⁠to safer places," he said. "People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert."

Rescue helocopters were initually unable to land due to the high floodwaters Image: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP

Chinese President Xi Jinping also ordered an "all out" rescue effort.

He said "the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people... quickly treat injured people and minimize casualties to the greatest extent possible", according to Chinese state media.

More to follow...

World.title: Germany: Carnivalgoers rescued after being trapped on ride
World.content:
Passengers became stranded high up in the air after a swing carousel malfunctioned in Hamburg.

Nearly two dozen carnivalgoers were rescued after a 90 minute ordeal in central Hamburg late on Tuesday, having been stuck 25 meters (82 feet) in the air on a swing carousel ride.

The Hamburger Dom carnival is held in the St.Pauli area of the city three times a year, and is one of Germany's longest-running and most well-visited fun fairs, attracting some 10 million guests annually.

On Tuesday evening, 23 passengers become stuck partly up the 70-meter (230-foot) ride when it malfunctioned and stopped moving.

The 23 passengers were stuck for over an hour Image: Bodo Marks/dpa/picture alliance

Firefighters arrived at the scene, erecting ladders to bring down each guest individually.

Authorities said that no one needed medical attention, but that the ride would remain closed through Sunday when the carnival concludes.

Basic first aid was administered, but no one needed to go to the hospital, authorities said. Image: Bodo Marks/dpa/picture alliance

08/26/2026 August 26, 2026 German exporters most optimistic since 2022

German exporters have become more optimistic about their prospects than at any point in more than four years, according to a survey by the Ifo economic institute.

Ifo's export expectations index jumped to 9.6 points in August, up from -2.8 in July. The institute said it was the highest reading since February 2022 and the sharpest monthly increase since June 2020.

"The export economy is gaining momentum," Ifo survey chief Klaus Wohlrabe said.

He said exports to the European Union were particularly strong, while business with China remained weak.

Companies producing electrical equipment, computers, electronics and optical products were among the most optimistic.

Ifo linked the improvement partly to increasing digitalization and heavy investment in artificial intelligence.

Even Germany's struggling automotive sector reported much stronger confidence about future exports.

The brighter export outlook follows stronger-than-expected economic data.

Germany's gross domestic product grew by 0.3% in the second quarter compared with the previous three months, the Federal Statistical Office said Tuesday, slightly above its initial estimate.

World.title: NYC: Mamdani opposes rally with Hindu nationalist leader
World.content:
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced opposition to an upcoming event featuring RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, calling the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" while acknowledging the city can't block a private event.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it.

Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK.

What did Mamdani say?

When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event."

Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from."

His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India."

"It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision."

Who is organizing the event?

The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity.

Bhagwat is visiting several countries in a bid to reform the RSS's global perception [FILE: August 6, 2026] Image: Rafiq Maqbool/AP Photo/picture alliance

However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled.

"Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity."

What is the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and how is it related to PM Modi?

The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance.

The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization.

In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.

100 years of the Hindu nationalist RSS movement To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rights organizations decry rise in abuses against religious minorities

However, days earlier, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom urged sanctions against the RSS and asked the American government not to extend diplomatic courtesies to RSS members. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims."

United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more.

India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities.

The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

World.title: Pakistan: Islamabad hospital fire kills at least 14 infants
World.content:
A fire broke out in the third floor of a maternity ward in Islamabad. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has called for an immediate investigation into the tragedy.

A least 14 infants were killed after a fire broke out at the maternity ward of a hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, on Wednesday.

"A fire broke out on the third floor of the MCH Ward at PIMS Hospital," the district office of Islamabad said, referring to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences.

The blaze broke out at around 6:45 a.m. (0145 UTC) when an air conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery, rescuers said.

Distraught parents gathered outside the hospital Image: Aamir Qureshi/AFP

Officials said 16 newborns were in the ward at the time, adding that one was rescued.

Outside the hospital, a nurse read out the names of babies who had perished as their families gathered around.

"I lost my daughter. She was only three days old," one father told the AFP news agency.

"My wife was in the ward. They took everyone out. We were sitting on the road waiting for help."

Investigation underway

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident.

"A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss," he said in a statement.

"Those ​responsible should be identified, and ​the strictest action should be taken."

The incident is one of the deadliest hospital fires in recent memory in Pakistan, where healthcare is subsidized but public hospitals are often are under-resourced and overburdened.

World.title: Despite international bans, landmines are back in force
World.content:
It was considered a major achievement when most countries in the world agreed to ban anti-personnel mines in the 1990s. But given the Russia-Ukraine war, the situation in Europe is changing.

Raheela Bibi was outside playing with her siblings when a landmine exploded. It was August 2020 and she was 12, living in Pakistan. Both her hands were amputated after the incident. Her sister suffered a serious leg injury, while her brother's eye was hurt. Bibi told DW in 2023 that though it was extremely difficult for her to do her homework, she was determined to continue with her education.

In 2025, more than 5,000 people, mainly civilians, were killed or injured by landmines or unexploded ordnance according to a preliminary analysis by the NGO Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor. In South Sudan, 90% of the victims last year were children.

Landmines are actually designed to injure adults not kill them. This is because an injured soldier is more of a strain on an enemy country's resources than a dead soldier. But in peacetime, landmines continue to pose a deadly threat not only to soldiers but to civilians and particularly children, who often die.

Decades after the brutal conflicts from 1991 to 2001 that were Yugoslav wars, people continue to be killed and injured by landmines in former Yugoslavia, particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Landmines are not designed to kill adults but to maim them Image: Mast Irham/dpa/picture alliance

Ottawa Treaty in force since 1999

In 1999, there were approximately 25,000 landmine casualties per year. This prompted pressure to ban the use of anti-personnel landmines. In 1997, representatives from more than 120 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty, which became legally binding in 1999. In total, 166 countries ratified the treaty, but not China, India, Russia or the US.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty. Ukraine has also withdrawn though this will not take legal effect until the war ends.

"This is a dangerous precedent that European states, of all countries, have set," Simone Wisotzki from the Frankfurt-based Leibniz Peace Research Institute (PRIF) told DW. "Other parties to the Ottawa Treaty, which could also face equally extreme situations in times of conflict, could take the same step. We would then have to deal with more withdrawals, which would, of course, undermine the legitimacy of the entire treaty."

Last year, Ukraine withdrew from the treaty and justified the move citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines in Ukrainian territory. "We cannot remain bound under conditions when the enemy has no restrictions," said Roman Kostenko, the secretary of the Ukrainian parliament's committee on national security, defense and intelligence.

If a country isn't at war, its withdrawal from the Ottawa Treaty is supposed to take effect six months after its announcement. If it is at war, however, withdrawal should take effect only after a peace treaty has been signed. Despite the legal uncertainty, Ukraine is reportedly already using mines, albeit on a much smaller scale than Russia.

A quarter of Ukraine affected by landmines

According the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS), as of mid-2025 approximately 25% of Ukraine was affected by landmines and explosive ordnance. This applied not only to Ukrainian-controlled territories but also to Russian-occupied areas in the east and southeast of the country.

"Since February 2022, over 1,150 civilians have been killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW)," UNMAS writes on its website, pointing out that the cost of full demining is estimated at just under $35 billion (approx. €30 billion) over 10 years.

Poland, Finland (which joined NATO after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine), Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, which have all suffered from Russian aggression and occupation in the past, also decided to withdraw from the Ottawa Treaty last year.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has stated on several occasions that his country wants to be able to mine its eastern borders with Russia very quickly if need be. The state-owned Polish defense company Belma has been contracted to produce anti-personnel mines in large quantities. Lithuania has also announced that it will resume the manufacture and purchase of landmines.

The Finnish military has said that if mines are necessary, they should be laid responsibly, accurate maps of their position must be created and there should be precise plans for demining.

Wisotzki from PRIF said that this is progress compared to the past but that modern anti-personnel mines often have integrated sensors and smart technologies that make it difficult to remove and destroy the mines.

"That's why I'm very critical of this and say that even new technologies present problems that, in turn, make mine clearance more difficult. In practice, mines are always laid in areas that are also used by civilians. They then remain in those territories and then injure civilians disproportionately."

In its reports, the Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor has pointed out that while mines that were laid during past conflicts continued to be cleared, mines continue to be laid in Ukraine or in other countries such as Myanmar.

Decades after conflicts people continue to demine territories, such as here in Cambodia Image: Tang Chhin Sothy/AFP

Less arms control in the world

This comes at a time when there is increasingly less arms control. In the past few years, three major agreements between the United States and Russia have expired or been terminated: the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty that banned all nuclear and conventional ground-launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and missile launchers with intermediate range; the New Start Treaty which is a nuclear arms reduction treaty; and the Treaty on Open Skies, which set out the framework for a regime of observation flights over the territory of participating states.

In 2023, Russia's withdrawal also effectively put an end to the CFE treaty that aimed to create a secure and stable balance of conventional armed forces in Europe and to remove the capability to launch surprise attacks or large-scale offensives

"Humanitarian arms control — which includes the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention — was in effect the only area that could still be said to be working," Wisotzki said. "And that is no longer the case."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: US military kills 4 in Caribbean boat strike
World.content:
The US military killed four people in a strike on a suspected drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean, the latest in a campaign that has killed more than 200 people and drawn condemnation from rights groups.

The US military struck a boat in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, US Southern Command said.

It's the latest action in a nearly yearlong controversial campaign by President Donald Trump's administration targeting alleged drug traffickers in Latin America.

What do we know about the latest US strike in the Caribbean?

"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southern Command said in a post on X, accompanied by a video showing what appeared to be a boat in motion, followed by a flash.

The command did not identify those killed or give a precise location, saying only that the boat was operating along established smuggling routes in the Caribbean.

No evidence was released showing the vessel carried drugs.

Fishers in Colombia worry as US strikes alleged drug boats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to a count by AP news agency, the strike brings the death toll to at least 227 people across 68 strikes since the campaign began about a year ago. Reuters news agency, tracking Caribbean and Eastern Pacific strikes together, put the total above 210.

Tuesday's strike followed another one in the Eastern Pacific over the weekend that killed two people. The weekend strike was the first by the US military in more than two months.

Rights organizations, including Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and independent United Nations investigators, say the strikes violate international law and amount to extrajudicial killings.

Why is the US conducting these strikes?

Trump says the United States is engaged in an "armed conflict" with drug cartels operating in the region and has framed the strikes as necessary to clamp down on the drug trade and its toll on American lives. But his administration has not made public the evidence behind its claims that those killed were trafficking narcotics.

The campaign is also expanding, with Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth saying this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow joint US military operations against criminal groups within their borders. Guatemala has disputed that any such agreement was reached.

Ecuador began similar joint operations with the US in March.

World.title: China: Dissident artist jailed for satirical Mao sculptures
World.content:
Sculptor Gao Zhen was charged under China's "Law on the Protection ⁠of Heroes ​and Martyrs." His supporters have called for his immediate release.

A court in China has reportedly sentenced a dissident artist to three years in jail for sculptures which satirized former Chinese revolutionary leader Mao Zedong.

Sculptor Gao Zhen, 70, became famous in the 2000s for addressing sensitive topics in China such as the 1966-1976 Cultural Revolution or the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre through artworks he produced with his younger brother Gao Qiang.

Zhen, who is based in New York, was arrested during a visit to Beijing in August 2024. He was tried this year ⁠in a ⁠one-day behind-closed-doors trial and found guilty of "infringing upon the reputation of heroes."

"We feel outraged," Gao's wife Zhao Yaliang told the Reuters news agency. "Ever since I learned of the ​verdict, I haven't been able to recover from it. It's devastating."

Zhao also said she and her son, who is a US citizen, had been barred from leaving China since Zhen's detention two years ago.

Which Mao sculptures were deemed illegal?

Zhen was charged under China's "Law on the Protection ⁠of Heroes ​and Martyrs," legislation which came into effect in 2018 and was strengthened in ​2021.

The artworks found to have broken the law, however, date to 2005 and 2009, according to Shane Yi, a researcher at Chinese Human Rights Defenders who has been advocating for Gao's case.

"The court has now sentenced him to three years ... for artwork he made as far back as 2005, some 16 years before the law he was charged under even existed," Yi told Reuters, calling the punishment "a very clear case of a violation of a person's freedom of expression."

The artworks in question are reported to be "Mao's Guilt," a 2009 bronze statue of the former leader kneeling remorsefully, and the "Miss Mao" series of caricatures which depict Mao with breasts and a Pinocchio-like nose.

Calls for Zhen to be released

"No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history," Amnesty's China Director Sarah Brooks told the Associated Press.

"The lengthy pre-trial detention and, ultimately, decision to convict Gao Zhen and sentence him to the maximum three-year prison term under this offense illustrate the authorities' determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression."

Researcher Yi said: "The only outcome that respects Gao Zhen's rights is his immediate, unconditional release."

There has as yet been no official statement from the court.

Edited by: Kieran Burke
