World.title: Kazakhstan's KazdorNII, China TransInfo agree on technology transfer
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Kazakh Road Research Institute (KazDorNII) and China's China TransInfo Technology Co. have signed a memorandum of cooperation to develop advanced solutions for Kazakhstan's road sector.

This is announced by the press service of the Ministry of Transport of Kazakhstan.

"The parties plan to jointly develop advanced solutions for Kazakhstan's road sector, including technology transfer, equipment localization and retraining of local specialists", the ministry said.

The agreement was signed during a working visit by a KazdorNII delegation to China. One of the key areas of cooperation will be exploring the establishment of a joint competency center at the institute. The proposed center will facilitate the exchange of technological expertise, training of Kazakh specialists, adaptation of foreign technologies to local conditions and the subsequent introduction of advanced solutions in the road sector.

Potential areas of cooperation include intelligent transport systems, dynamic weigh-in-motion control, video analytics and technologies required for the further development of autonomous transport.

The parties also plan to focus on technology transfer and the localization of advanced equipment in Kazakhstan. This approach is expected to enable the country not only to use ready-made foreign solutions but also to develop its own expertise for their implementation, operation and further development.

During the visit, the Kazakh delegation also reviewed projects implemented by China TransInfo Technology and its technical capabilities in the field of intelligent transport infrastructure.

China TransInfo Technology specializes in the development of intelligent transport systems, video analytics technologies, weigh-in-motion control and digital transport infrastructure solutions.

The memorandum is expected to serve as a basis for further developing specific joint projects and applying international technological expertise while taking into account the specific characteristics of Kazakhstan's road infrastructure.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, U.S. discuss expanding trade, economic, and investment ties
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Kyrgyzstan and the United States discussed prospects for expanding trade, economic, and investment cooperation, with a focus on joint projects in key sectors.

This was announced in a statement by the press service of the Kyrgyz MFA, following the meeting between Ambassador to the United States Edil Baisalov and Assistant Secretary of Commerce and Director General of the United States and Foreign Commercial Service for the International Trade Administration (ITA) at the U.S. Department of Commerce, David L. Fogel.

"During the meeting, the sides discussed prospects for expanding trade, economic and investment cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and the United States," the statement said.

According to the Ministry, in the course of the meeting, particular attention was paid to opportunities for implementing joint projects in mining, banking and information technology.

Edil Baisalov briefed the US official on economic reforms being carried out in Kyrgyzstan and measures aimed at improving the country's investment climate. He emphasized the importance of diversifying the Kyrgyz economy, introducing modern technologies and attracting US investment and expertise.

The sides noted significant untapped potential for strengthening direct ties between the business communities of the two countries and expressed interest in further expanding the presence of US companies in the Kyrgyz market.

Following the meeting, the sides outlined further practical steps to promote mutually beneficial projects and continue substantive dialogue between the Kyrgyz side and the US Department of Commerce.

World.title: Tokayev calls for action against aggressive fast-food advertising
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev instructed the government to thoroughly examine the issue of aggressive fast-food advertising, particularly its impact on children's health.

This was announced by the press service of the Kazakh President, citing Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's remarks at the plenary session of the Republican August Conference.

"Another issue is aggressive fast-food advertising that has flooded public spaces. It creates persistent unhealthy habits, increases pressure on the healthcare system and negatively affects the country's workforce potential," Tokayev said.

He noted that around 7,000 children with diabetes are currently under medical supervision in Kazakhstan, adding that the number is not declining and is even increasing.

"Many countries prohibit or restrict advertising of foods high in fat, sugar and salt aimed at younger generations," the president said.

Tokayev acknowledged that the issue is complex and involves a range of sensitive aspects, including medical and political considerations.

"However, the government still needs to thoroughly examine this issue, bearing in mind, above all, the health of our children," he said.

Tokayev also stressed the importance of protecting the psychological well-being of the younger generation. According to the president, psychological well-being, emotional resilience and the moral development of the younger generation have already become important factors of national security and sustainable development.

World.title: Tajikistan holds international conference marking 35 years of independence
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tajikistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Tajikistan held an international conference on the country's experience in peacebuilding, foreign policy, and sustainable development over 35 years of independence.

This was announced by the press service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Tajikistan.

According to the Ministry, the conference, titled "Tajikistan and 35 Years of Independence: Experience of Peacebuilding, Multivector Policy, and Sustainable Development," was held on August 25.

"On August 25, 2026, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Tajikistan hosted the International Conference "Tajikistan and 35 Years of Independence: Experience of Peacebuilding, Multivector Policy, and Sustainable Development" in honor of the 35th anniversary of the Republic of Tajikistan's State Independence. High-ranking representatives of the Government and Parliament of the Republic, heads of ministries and government agencies, the diplomatic corps, as well as political figures, veterans of the diplomatic service, and the country's missions abroad participated in the conference (in a virtual format)," the Ministry said.

The event brought together senior representatives of the Tajik government and parliament, heads of ministries and state agencies, members of the diplomatic corps, political figures, veterans of the diplomatic service and representatives of Tajikistan abroad, including those participating virtually.

The opening session featured remarks by First Deputy Prime Minister of Tajikistan Khokim Kholikzoda, Minister of Foreign Affairs Sirojiddin Muhriddin, the Presidential Assistant for Foreign Relations, as well as heads of several ministries and government agencies.

The thematic sessions focused on cooperation between government bodies, the academic community and the diplomatic corps in implementing the country's foreign policy, as well as the role of women in advancing the country's domestic and foreign policy.

Participants reviewed Tajikistan's achievements over 35 years of independence and discussed prospects for the country's further development.

Concluding the conference, Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin declared that the conclusions and proposals put forward during the event would contribute to further measures aimed at ensuring sustainable development and advancing Tajikistan's foreign policy.

Meanwhile, more than 200 people took part in the conference, while its proceedings were covered by 50 domestic and international media outlets.

World.title: Ford's factory 'helped make Australia'. Can a data centre have the same legacy?
World.content:
For more than half a century, Ford's Broadmeadows manufacturing plant was known as the home of the iconic Falcon.

"That was the manufacturing heartland of Australia," said Basem Abdo, the federal member for Calwell in Melbourne.

" I always say that we didn't just make Australian-made products — that site helped make Australia. "

Now, 10 years after the plant shut its doors, there are plans to turn the former Ford site into the engine room of Australia's AI boom.

Zoe and John live across the road from the former Ford factory in Broadmeadow and are worried about a data centre potentially moving into the site. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)

The $1.1 billion proposal for a massive data centre by Singaporean digital infrastructure firm Zerra DC — dubbed "Project Dune" — is predicted to draw 336MW of power across six buildings and will take 12 years to build.

Zoe, who lives across the road from the site and is a former employee at the Ford plant, is concerned about having the data centre on her doorstep.

"I had to ask my children what it is," she told 7.30.

"They said something to do with batteries, and they will be working 24 hours a day.

"I don't think it's a good idea. I don't know how long we're going to live but it's still not a good idea for us to live in this area [during the construction] and having all those things in and out every day.

"It's terrible."

Fears of a 'pathway to nowhere'

The final car rolls off the production line at Ford in Broadmeadows in 2016. (Supplied: Ford Australia)

At its height, the Broadmeadows factory — which covered the size of 10 MCGs — employed more than 5,000 local workers who were producing generations of Ford vehicles.

In contrast, Zerra DC said 407 jobs would be created annually during the construction phase and 670 jobs created annually once the data centre was fully operational, boosting the Victorian economy by $158 million.

But Mr Abdo said many residents in his diverse community were concerned about the long-term job prospects from the data centre.

"People need to see that it offers a pathway to employment, a pathway to good, secure, well-paying jobs that offer them a career, which was what this site was about and which is what this site should be about," he told 7.30.

Basem Abdo says people in his community are concerned the data centre will not offer many long-term jobs. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

"I will only support a project that is in line with our national standards that we've put forth clearly on a national level.

" At this stage, I'm not satisfied that that proposal meets those standards. "

Mr Abdo said the project was yet to make the case for the same kind of long-term employment pathways that the region's manufacturing industry provided.

"Are they good, secure jobs that provide long-term careers for people in our area?" he asked.

"This must not lead to a pathway to nowhere in terms of jobs and skills."

'Why is it being fast-tracked?'

An artist's impression of part of the proposed Zerra DC data centre. (Supplied)

State governments in Australia, particularly New South Wales and Victoria, are competing to capture billions of dollars in data centre investment.

An Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) report released this week shows the number of Australian data centres in development has more than doubled since 2025, from 97 to 225 this year.

AEMO's report also predicted data centres would account for 13 per cent of the nation's energy consumption by 2035.

But communities are asking whether the speed of approval for these projects is coming at the expense of scrutiny.

Campbellfield resident Anastasia Drapaniotis has taken a leading role in opposing the Project Dune proposal.

Anastasia Drapaniotis is critical of the planning process for the data centre. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)

"I think a lot of the residents feel like they can't do anything about it and I think that's really horrible," she told 7.30.

" It's really awful to feel like you don't have a say in what comes to your area. "

She told 7.30 she was not against data centre developments but was critical of the planning process.

"I would have to say … OK, bring these in, sure, but have stricter regulations," she said.

"Why is it being fast-tracked? Why are they being approved so quickly when something like this would ordinarily take a very long time to get approved?"

Community members protest against the proposed data centre in Broadmeadows. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Zerra DC lodged the development application for the Campbellfield project in April directly with the state government under special planning provisions for big projects and expects the "fast-tracked" decision within four months.

Victoria's Environment Protection Authority lodged a formal objection to the proposal with the Department of Transport and Planning, citing "concerns over potential noise risks and the cumulative impacts associated with the overall site layout and development".

Zoe and her husband John received the letter informing them of the proposal four days before the date on which Victoria's planning minister was permitted to decide on the project.

At the bottom of the letter, it said: "The responsible authority will not decide on the application before: 28 July 2026."

The planning minister is yet to announce a decision on the proposal.

"I think we could fight against it, but as far as it stopping, I don't think so," Zoe said.

"Not when you get a big overseas company coming in with billions of dollars."

Company says it engaged with community

A map showing the proposed Zerra DC project in Broadmeadows. (Supplied)

Zerra DC declined an interview with 7.30 but said in a statement: "We understand that a proposal of this scale can raise genuine questions and concerns for nearby residents and businesses, and we recognise that some people feel they have not had enough opportunity to be heard."

The company said it began its community engagement program in late May and distributed information "to approximately 1,080 nearby households and 470 industrial businesses, supported by translated information, a dedicated project website, community survey, telephone and email channels, and direct visits to neighbouring businesses".

Zerra DC said the redevelopment of the former Ford site represented "a highly-productive long-term use of industrial land", adding that it had "carefully reviewed the issues raised through community feedback and lodged a detailed response to submissions with the Department of Transport and Planning on 7 August".

"No amendments to the proposal have been made at this stage," it said.

Victoria's Minister for Planning Sonya Kilkenny. (ABC News: Maddison Cutajar)

Victoria's Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny also declined an interview with 7.30, but a Victorian government spokesperson said in a statement: "Every proposal is considered on its merits — as this proposal is under consideration it would be inappropriate to comment further.

"Submissions from the community and nearby businesses can be provided up until a decision is made."

The proposal bypassed local government and prompted Hume City Council, which includes the suburb of Broadmeadows, to pass a motion calling for a moratorium on data centre approvals in Victoria.

A further three councils, Melton, Brimbank and Maribyrnong, have since joined Hume in calling for a temporary halt on these types of projects.

Attracting data centres to Australia

Anthony Albanese says Australia wants to attract data centres but "maintaining social licence will be essential". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

While state governments court data centre investment, the federal government increasingly has its own expectations for what large data centres will deliver for Australia and the communities they are built in.

In a speech to business leaders yesterday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said "Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential".

"That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained, and locations are appropriate," he said.

Today, the prime minister took his plan to implement national mandatory standards for the industry to National Cabinet.

Under these legislated rules, the biggest facilities will be required to fund and use renewable energy, pay their share of grid and water infrastructure and meet community expectations.

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Notes allegedly written by woman accused of killing parents released
World.content:
A woman standing trial accused of murdering her elderly parents allegedly scrawled notes — which a court has released — including a reference to police waiting to see if she would "get cocky and slip up".

Raelene Polymiadis, 65, of Craigmore is standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court, after pleading not guilty to murdering her parents, Brenda and Lynton Anderson, by injecting them with her own insulin in 2022 and 2023.

Prosecutors previously told the jury a set of notes were allegedly found during a search of Ms Polymiadis's house and car and detailed what she should be saying to police when she spoke to them.

Brenda and Lynton Anderson, both aged 94, died a year apart. (Supplied: Nine News)

Supreme Court Justice Sandi McDonald, who is presiding over the trial, approved the release of handwritten notes, which prosecutors alleged were penned by Ms Polymiadis.

One note written on the top corner of a piece of paper said: "What they will do is wait for a few weeks months year to see if I think I got away with it and I get cocky and slip up. Hang on buddy, it could be a long ride."

A handwritten note tendered in the Raelene Polymiadis murder trial. (Supplied: Courts SA)

In another note, the author posed questions to authorities.

"Who are you sorry?" the note read.

"What's this about?

"Are you from the Coroner's office?

"Why only now are you speaking with me and it's only a few days after the funeral!!"

One of the handwritten notes released by the Supreme Court lists questions. (Supplied: Courts SA)

Prosecutors previously told the court Ms Polymiadis wrote to herself to "sob here", saying that matched a point in the police interview where she started sobbing.

One of the notes released by the court discussed events occurring in hospital.

"We went to see dad, they were keeping him warm," part of the note said.

"He was out to it — unconscious I guess but breathing with help of oxygen I 'think' — I'm sorry this is really hard relieving all this — is it absolutely necessary."

Another handwritten note prosecutors allege Raelene Polymiadis wrote. (Supplied: Courts SA)

The note went on to say, "… just holding his hand, talking to him, but I got no response (sob)".

The trial previously heard police listening devices captured Ms Polymiadis in her car praying to God, confessing to the crimes.

Ms Polymiadis's lawyer, Marie Shaw KC, previously told the jury the context of the alleged confession would arise during the trial.

"The issue about the alleged confession is: was my client admitting she was responsible for the deaths or was she telling her god she felt responsible for their deaths because if they died of insulin administration, they must have accessed her insulin?" Ms Shaw said.

Another of the handwritten notes tendered in the Raelene Polymiadis murder trial. (Supplied: Courts SA)

Another note made references to Ms Polymiadis's father.

"Then I burst into tears, thinking my God he got into my stuff, it's my fault."

The trial continues.

World.title: Canberra childcare centre ordered to close as provider enters administration
World.content:
The childcare regulator has ordered Edge Early Learning in Charnwood in Canberra's Belconnen area to close for three months.

The notice of suspension, issued by Children's Education and Care Assurance (CECA), comes about a month after an Edge Early Learning centre in nearby Higgins was forced to shut immediately over its response to a serious medical incident involving a child.

The reasons behind the Charnwood centre's notice of suspension remain unknown, with its closure due to begin on September 3.

In a statement, CECA said:

"Edge has the right to appeal the decision and is legally required to communicate the suspension to families. "Under administration, the administrator can also exercise the right to appeal."

The ABC has spoken to parents who said they were unaware that CECA had ordered the Charnwood centre to close for three months from next Thursday.

Edge Early Learning also has a centre operating in Ngunnawal in the Gungahlin area.

The Edge Early Learning centre in the ACT that was forced to close suddenly in July. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

'Business-as-usual'

It comes as the childcare provider, which runs dozens of childcare centres across South Australia, Queensland and the ACT, went into voluntary administration.

In a statement from Edge Early Learning, it said administrators had been appointed to "review the business and work with key stakeholders to determine the best path forward", and that the process would allow the company "to assess its financial position and consider options for its future".

" We understand that this may be a confusing and stressful development for families who rely upon Edge Early Learning to provide care for their children. "

Canberra childcare centre ordered to close A Canberra mother had concerns for her daughter's safety at Edge Early Learning in Higgins long before the ACT regulator ordered the centre to close.

Edge Early Learning said it was continuing to operate all centres "on a business-as-usual basis".

"There will be no change to your care arrangements, centre opening hours or staffing. Families should continue to attend their centre as normal," it told parents.

"Our immediate focus is to maintain the safe and ongoing operation of each centre while this urgent review is undertaken."

World.title: Body found as police investigate shooting of Melbourne father
World.content:
Homicide detectives have found a body in their search for a Melbourne father who went missing after allegedly being shot.

A desperate search has been underway for Khaled Malas, 37, who has not been seen since he was allegedly attacked at a home in Wildwood, north-west of the city, on August 19.

Police allege he was shot after a dispute, which is understood to involve a significant debt, and there were grave fears for his welfare.

Police last week searched near a waste facility at Sunbury for missing man Khaled Malas. (ABC News)

Mohammed Aboueid, 56, has been charged with intentionally causing serious injury.

On Wednesday afternoon, investigators found human remains covered in grass on Havelock Road in Clarkefield, about 15 kilometres from Wildwood.

The coroner has been notified, and an autopsy is expected to take place.

Victoria Police said it would consider alternative charges upon receiving the results of the autopsy.

Mr Malas has been remembered as a loving father.

World.title: Queensland allowed to use coal, gas for data centres despite renewable push
World.content:
Queensland will be allowed to go its own way using gas or coal to power data centres, despite Prime Minister Anthony Albanese previously demanding states use renewables.

State and territory leaders met on Wednesday to settle national standards for data centre construction, but instead agreed to undertake further work.

Queensland Premier Crisafulli had pushed for an energy-agnostic approach and told the ABC the carve out was a "good win" for his state, which owns much of its own electricity infrastructure.

Data centre fight heats up Premiers are heading into national cabinet divided over how Australia should meet the rapidly growing energy demands of AI data centres.

"It shows because we own our assets, both our distribution and our generation, we are able to control a different mixture of energy right across the board, and that enables us to bring on new energy opportunities," he said.

Premiers and chief ministers met with Mr Albanese in Sydney to discuss issues including AI, domestic violence, bird flu, fuel security and the embattled national gun buyback.

Ahead of the meeting, federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen had insisted the Commonwealth would legislate over the top of states and territories that refused to adopt the renewables standard.

Queensland argued the state-owned nature of its energy infrastructure put it in a position to maintain a technology-agnostic approach, meaning gas or coal could be used to power its data centres.

The Northern Territory also opposed the renewables focus and has indicated it would use gas to power data centre projects.

Following the meeting, Mr Albanese said both jurisdictions were in a "different position" to other states, as he justified the apparent backdown on renewables.

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli had argued for a technology-neutral approach. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas rejected suggestions the prime minister had been rolled on the issue.

"What you see emerging from national cabinet is a genuine desire to make sure we work through the issues associated with a rollout of data centres in Australia in a way that has a degree of uniformity," Mr Malinauskas told 7.30.

"And I think today's discussion was very much an example of us all being aligned on the best way to do that."

Mr Malinauskas said there was unity about the principle that data centres should add to the electricity grid without negatively impacting the national energy market.

"What we agreed upon is that renewables will principally be the form of energy that will power data centres in the future in Australia," he said.

A communique released after national cabinet said the standards would "ensure consistency and clarity for investors, while protecting Australia's economy, strengthening our sovereignty and securing benefits in line with our national interests".

The meeting of national cabinet also agreed to make Australian citizenship a condition of holding a firearm licence. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

The prime minister said the new standards, which would also include rules on water usage and community consultation, would be legislated early next year.

"We have buy-in on Australia's first national AI laws," he said.

Ongoing discussions are expected to include ensuring data centres do not raise power prices for households and other businesses.

Mr Bowen has consistently argued renewables were the cheapest form of energy to ensure this did not happen.

But Mr Crisafulli has rejected this and insisted his state would be able to keep power prices low even where other energy sources were used.

"We believe that we can control our data sovereignty, protect the rights of local communities, and enable that energy mix even with those data centres on," he said.

Citizenship a condition of holding gun licence

The meeting of national cabinet also agreed to make Australian citizenship a condition of holding a firearm licence, though the prime minister indicated there would be some exceptions.

Albanese to override Queensland on data centres Queensland's rejection of rules tying data centre construction to new renewables projects means the federal government will be forced to legislate to override the state.

There was little movement on a national gun buyback scheme, which the federal government tried to roll out following the Bondi terrorist attack in December last year.

Queensland had refused to take part, while others including Victoria and South Australia are yet to sign up.

Mr Albanese said the offer was "still there", though jurisdictions were "responsible for their own decisions".

He said the new firearm agreement would allow the sharing of Commonwealth criminal intelligence with the states and territories.

"This is about improving our laws following the horrific antisemitic attack in Bondi last year," Mr Albanese said.

GST distribution was largely off the agenda after Mr Albanese declared on Tuesday he would not meddle with Western Australia's portion of the carve-up while he was prime minister, despite opposition from other jurisdictions.

Cabinet also heard a report from Australia's head vet as the federal government prepares to tip an additional $125 million to protect the nation from bird flu, which has now been detected in all six states.

World.title: Wife of key figure in ICAC probe paid $254k for three months of work
World.content:
The NSW corruption watchdog has heard that the wife of a key figure in an inquiry was paid $254,666 for three months of consulting.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is examining allegations that prohibited political donations were funnelled through third parties to support the Liberal-aligned, right-wing faction known as the NSW Reformers and advance the interests of fugitive property developer Jean Nassif.

Anita Perrottet is the wife of Charles Perrottet, a Reformers member and the brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet.

Charles is a brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet. (Supplied: Facebook)

ICAC is investigating payments made to Ms Perrottet's company, Macquarie Consulting, by lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood's businesses Beckington and JPG Advisory, and whether those payments were for genuine consulting work or used to disguise money allegedly intended for Charles Perrottet.

The commission heard Ms Perrottet was paid $254,666 for three months of consulting work in 2022, despite telling the inquiry she mainly provided verbal marketing and strategic advice and could recall little documentation of the work.

Counsel assisting the commission, Peggy Dwyer SC, challenged the scale of the payments, which were made through Mr Greenwood's businesses.

"That's based on a salary of $1 million, Mrs Perrottet … let's get serious," Dr Dwyer said. "You are giving evidence under oath … Do you seriously suggest that the commission should accept that as truthful evidence that you were entitled to charge $254,666 for work that you actually did … providing an oral sounding board or advice to Jeremy Greenwood for that quarter?"

Ms Perrottet insisted the evidence was truthful.

$10,000 monthly retainer

The ICAC is investigating allegations of prohibited political donations. (ABC News)

Ms Perrottet also told the commission she received a $10,000 monthly retainer from Beckington, without a written or signed agreement.

She said her work was primarily delivered through conversations with Mr Greenwood, either in person or by phone.

Dr Dwyer said the commission had found no evidence of phone calls between Ms Perrottet and Mr Greenwood during the relevant periods.

The commission heard Ms Perrottet could remember only one Beckington client, Greyhound Racing NSW, and that she gave Mr Greenwood advice about the client during face-to-face meetings but could not recall when or where those meetings occurred.

"Are you struggling to remember because it actually didn't happen?" Dr Dwyer asked.

The commission was also shown an invoice from Macquarie Consulting for $150,000, covering 12 months of work for Beckington, which was sent by Charles Perrottet.

Ms Perrottet could not remember why the invoice had been issued, why Charles Perrottet sent it or why three lump-sum payments subsequently received from Beckington did not reconcile with the $150,000 invoice.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

Ms Perrottet said she could not recall the details of the fee arrangement but maintained she probably discussed it with Mr Greenwood.

The commission also heard evidence that lobbyist Christian Ellis, also a key figure in the inquiry, sent Charles Perrottet instructions about how invoices from Macquarie Consulting should be structured, including the amounts and periods to be billed.

The commission has also ordered Ms Perrottet to provide phone records and messages involving Mr Greenwood and Mr Ellis as it tests her account of the consulting work.

Ms Perrottet will continue giving evidence on Friday before her husband takes the stand.

Dominic Perrottet is not accused of any wrongdoing.

World.title: Hobart council advances ban on full-home short stays
World.content:
A plan to block Hobart property owners from converting their entire homes into short-stay accommodation has passed another milestone, with the local council voting to send the proposal off for final approval.

Council revives bid to curb whole-home short-stays A fresh proposal from the Hobart City Council would block about 90 per cent of the city's homes from being wholly converted into short-stay accommodation.

The proposal, which aims to restrict the creation of new short-stay accommodation in the city, was considered by the Hobart City Council (HCC) at its planning committee meeting on Wednesday.

The tweak to planning rules would block about 20,000 homes from being wholly converted into visitor accommodation, such as Airbnb or Stayz.

"The draft amendment delivers a clear net community benefit through improved housing outcomes while still allowing the visitor economy to be accommodated," council officers wrote.

"The primary purpose of the proposed amendment is to limit the impact of new visitor accommodation use on the availability and affordability of housing for long-term residents in the city.

"It was informed by extensive background analysis, including data on housing and rental markets, tourism trends, existing visitor accommodation supply and planning approvals."

Council officers said the plan delivers a "clear net community benefit" by improving housing outcomes, while still accommodating the visitor economy. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

More than 50 submissions were made while the plan was out for public consultation across June and July, with 15 supporting the amendment while 41 were in opposition.

The representations in support of the amendment focused largely on the impact that whole-home short stays have on the rental market, housing affordability, neighbourhood cohesion and the function of residential zoning.

Those against the amendment highlighted the benefits short stays have on the city's economy and tourism, their role in providing accommodation for workers and families, private property rights, investment certainty and the impact on small business owners.

The planning amendment will now be sent to the Tasmanian Planning Commission (TPC) for final approval, with the council anticipating a public hearing will be held.

Short stay rental host says 'hosting is an economic lifeline'

Merrydith Callegari, who has been a short-stay rental host in Hobart for more than 10 years, addressed the planning committee ahead of the vote.

She was opposed to the amendment and called for an opportunity to work constructively with the council to develop a framework where short-term rental owners and the council could work together.

"Short-term rentals are a vital part of Tasmania's accommodation requirements, hosting is an economic lifeline for many hosts and related industries, they fill gaps that hotels can't, they give visitors a home," Ms Callegari said.

"I believe banning does not give the result you seek … we need to make building easier, to support landlords, not tear them down — after all, if renting is too hard, landlords will stop renting.

" Every host should have the right to host … it allows people to earn an income they never could before. "

Councillors divided on if move will help rental crisis

Lord Mayor Anna Reynolds said cities all over the world were dealing with an increase in short-term rentals, while housing stock continued to fall short of demand.

"It's got to the stage where it's having a very significant impact on our rental market," she said.

"We are losing young people to other parts of Hobart because they can't get a rental here.

"This is rental stock that's been basically turned into small hotels in our suburbs."

Anna Reynolds says short-stay accommodation is having a "significant impact" on the city's rental market. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Cr Reynolds said the amendment was a "good compromise" and still allowed for permits in the CBD, while also not removing any existing permits.

Council locks in 1,050 per cent short-stay conversion fee hike A Tasmanian council has pushed through a 1,050 per cent increase in fees for applications to turn a property into short-stay accommodation.

"We have a higher penetration of short stays as a percentage of our rental market than I think any other capital city," she said.

Councillor Ben Lohberger supported the amendment and said whole-home short-stay rentals have filled some streets with "mini hotels".

"It's quite obvious to me that we do need some way to have discretion on whether we approve these and that's what this is about," he said.

"It's not about banning anything that exist, its not about banning every single future application; it's about giving the council the power to decide.

" We are simply trying to respond to a growing issue. "

Ben Lohberger says whole-home short-stays have filled some residential streets with "mini hotels". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Alderman Marti Zucco said property owners should be able to do whatever they wanted with their homes.

"We should be listening to those representations we got and maybe instead sit down and see if we can find another way forward," Cr Zucco said.

" This is not going to solve the rental crisis in Hobart … we've missed that boat. "

Marti Zucco says property owners should be able to do what they like with their homes. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Deputy Lord Mayor Zelinda Sherlock stressed that the amendment was not "about banning anything" and only applied to residential areas.

The restriction would apply to properties zoned as general residential, inner residential or low-density residential, which account for about 90 per cent of dwellings in Hobart.

The historic suburb of Battery Point, which is very popular for tourists, and Hobart's inner CBD would not be affected.

The councillors who voted in support of the proposal included Anna Reynolds, Ryan Posselt, Gemma Kitsos, Bill Harvey, Ben Lohberger, Mike Dutta and Zelinda Sherlock.

Those who voted against were Marti Zucco, Will Coats and Louise Bloomfield, while councillors Louise Elliot and John Kelly were not present.

World.title: Breaking: Macquarie Group dumps KPMG from audit contract
World.content:
Macquarie Group has announced it is parting ways with KPMG, the accounting firm currently the subject of a parliamentary inquiry over mishandled client data.

Macquarie released a statement today citing the ongoing scrutiny of KPMG and said the board held concerns over the firm's auditing practices.

"The decision follows continued scrutiny of KPMG Australia’s audit practice, including information exposed by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services," the statement said.

"It also follows Macquarie’s formal enquiries of KPMG to consider its capacity to deliver the audit, as well as the nature and impact of ongoing issues at KPMG Australia."

At Macquarie's 2027 Annual General Meeting, the board said they will recommend retaining PwC as the incumbent auditor.

KPMG also released a statement acknowledging the decision.

"While disappointed by the outcome, KPMG respects the decision taken by Macquarie," the statement read.

KPMG CEO John Sams said Macquarie's announcement was "a clear reminder that the consequences of our past failings are real".

"Rebuilding trust will require sustained action, transparency and time. I am committed to leading this change with honesty, transparency and urgency," he said.

World.title: Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex Jack Gramenz Updated August 26, 2026 — 8:55pm ,first published 3:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old girl on Sydney’s northern beaches after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital two days after emergency services responded to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights on Sunday night. They found the girl unresponsive. Loading She was flown in a critical condition to Royal North Shore Hospital, where she died on Tuesday night. Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex.



Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young people’s understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Consent education advocate Chanel Contos said she was devastated by news of the teen’s death: “This just feels insanely preventable.” “There is no safe way to engage in strangulation during sex, and unfortunately, mainly because of pornography, where young people are learning and mimicking scripts from that, this act that was traditionally on the fringes of kink culture has made its way into the mainstream,” the Teach Us Consent founder said. “We need to seriously investigate the impact that pornography is having on shaping the sexual scripts and behaviours of young people.” Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in 2024 that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely.



“And there’s really no reason to think that the effects of strangulation would be any different if the strangulation was consensual or otherwise,” the study’s lead author, University of Melbourne Professor Heather Douglas, said. “Even lower levels of strangulation, it can result in brain injuries like problem-solving difficulties, memory issues, and so on, and that’s without even being made unconscious, so it’s a really serious thing to do.” “There’s such a range of injuries associated with strangulation. Some are permanent, some are fleeting … it doesn’t take much pressure, and it doesn’t take very long, to have really terrible consequences.” Douglas said there were no safe ways to undertake strangulation, and she questioned aspects of consent surrounding it. Among the almost 5000 people aged between 18 and 35 surveyed in the research were reports of consent having been assumed from previous instances of strangulation, consent without an understanding of the risks, and consent influenced by pressure or power differentials, Douglas said.



“A lot of people just want to be normal … and doing normal things in their sex life. “And I think there is a bit of a normalisation of strangulation in many young people’s sex lives,” Douglas said. The 16-year-old died at Royal North Shore Hospital on Tuesday night. Renee Nowytarger Collective Shout co-founder Melinda Tankard Reist said she’s spoken to thousands of girls who have reported feeling pressured into engaging in strangulation during sex, which has been normalised by pornography and social media. “It’s put forward as something desirable and it can heighten sexual experience, but they’re not learning that, well, actually you could die.



“Young people have a right to know the injuries and the potential life-threatening risk. “This is again, just another fruit of a pornographic education,” she said. The NSW government’s own submission to a recent parliamentary inquiry said depictions of sexual aggression including strangulation in pornography has been linked to increased intimate partner violence, citing research from 2017 by the federal government’s Australian Institute of Family Studies. Federal independent MP Zali Steggall, from the neighbouring electorate of Warringah, said the teenager’s death underscored the need for a national education campaign to tackle misogyny and teach respectful relationships. “My thoughts are with her family, friends and community at this incredibly difficult time,” she said.



“Police are investigating the circumstances of the girl’s death and no charges have been laid. We must allow the legal process to take place. “Regardless of the circumstances of this particular case, the Albanese government itself has confirmed that rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are rising. “The Albanese government must urgently roll out a national campaign ensuring young people receive ongoing sexual health and relationship education.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Hundreds of people were reported missing after an avalanche of ice and rock triggered massive flash floods that swept through parts of Nepal on Wednesday, killing at least eight people and causing widespread damage to villages and infrastructure.

Officials said 384 tourists, including 291 from countries including India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Malaysia, were reported missing as a result of the flash flood.

Damaged houses stand precariously near the swollen, debris-choked banks of the Trishuli River after flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha

The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9am on Wednesday, destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. They issued warnings to residents of several of Nepal’s districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.

“We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts,” said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government.

World.title: Brisbane’s schools are bursting at the seams. It’s only going to get worse
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Brisbane’s schools are bursting at the seams. It’s only going to get worse Dominique Tassell August 26, 2026 — 8:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“It’s just really reactive planning, as opposed to proactive planning.” That’s how a parent at one of Brisbane’s biggest schools describes the government’s approach to our bursting-at-the-seams education system, where large school cohorts are managed by split start times and staggered lunch breaks. Suburban Futures director Ross Elliott agrees the city’s social infrastructure has not been keeping pace with population growth. Pallara State School is the fourth-largest state primary school in Brisbane. John-Paul Langbroek “I think in the last 10 to 20 years, we’ve spent too much time patting ourselves on the back saying how wonderful population growth is for the economy,” Elliott said. “At the same time, [the government] wasn’t looking at the demands on schools, on hospitals – on all infrastructure.”



Pallara State School in Brisbane’s south is the city’s fourth-biggest state primary school and an example of an institution juggling surging demand and limited space. Related Article Schools ‘Space for growth’: $55m cash splash to boost Brisbane primary schools’ capacity The split-campus school, which caters to more than 1300 students, was built in 1956 but has had multiple expansions since, most recently a new junior campus for prep and year 1. The school’s senior campus – for years 2 to 6 – is located 2.5 kilometres down the road. Before the new campus opened in January, P&C treasurer Chad Redgwell said the school used demountables for years.



He said it was forced to cancel its athletics carnival in 2024 due to limited space caused by demountables on the oval. When the new junior campus opened, there was no oval, hall, or library for the first term. Pallara State School opened a new junior campus 2.5 kilometres away from the rest of the primary school in January. John-Paul Langbroek “They didn’t want to delay the kids from entering that site because they would have then had to go to the senior school site, spend one term down there, then move the kids down,” Redgwell said. The large student body was previously managed by splitting start and finish times, as well as lunch breaks.



“So you can imagine you had kids in the classroom trying to learn while the other half of the school’s playing outside,” Redgwell said. “Because there wasn’t enough play space for the kids at lunchtime, they were running into each other, they were fighting over the space – there were a lot of fights.” Redgwell said it was his impression that the government was consistently caught off guard by the number of students at the school, and was therefore unprepared for future demand. He said most in the school community were still anticipating the installation of demountables at the junior school in 2028. Brisbane’s population boom is taking a toll, Elliott said.



Almost three-quarters of the city’s state primary schools have an enrolment management plan – meaning they are at or over 80 per cent of their capacity. Enrolments at just under 90 per cent of the state’s high schools are also managed. Seven schools have opened in Brisbane proper this century. Two are private, and only one was opened in the past decade – two if you count the resurrection of Fortitude Valley State School. Just over 20 schools have been built in the past decade, WHERE? while the population almost doubled from 737,000 residents to approximately 1.38 million residents.



During the same period, 11 schools closed in Brisbane proper. The only new school on the horizon for the city is a primary school in Brisbane’s inner west, which is under consideration and unconfirmed.WHERE? Related Article NAPLAN Why private schools are asking for your kids’ NAPLAN results Building new schools is especially difficult because of the scarcity of appropriate sites, Elliott said. Another option is repurposing buildings, such as large stores like Bunnings, or office buildings that are largely unsuitable for housing because of the plumbing. “It’s always the plumbing,” Elliott said. “In a school, you could have the boys’ and girls’ toilets in the central services core, as they are for an office building.



“Then you can have each different level at school, and then you have the tuck shop and the indoor gym. “The question then becomes, ‘well, where do they go for exercise?’ And, like a lot of schools around the world, they get in a bus and go to a shared sporting field. “That’s the model we’re going to have to look at.” Such schools could also have the benefit of being central, and therefore close to public transport, Elliott said. Schools are a big part of Brisbane’s infrastructure challenge, he said.



“It’s certainly not easy, and you can understand why not everyone would be happy with the way it’s going,” he said. “It’s a symptom of the growth, and it’s probably symptomatic of the fact we should have been doing a lot more planning for it many years ago.” Elliott believes we need to get creative with solutions and look at spaces including office buildings, old shopping buildings, and industrial sheds. “It requires a different way of thinking about it because in terms of infill, no one’s spoilt for choice,” he said. “There are no 5-hectare blocks of vacant land. There are no big blocks of land floating around with no one interested in developing them.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Retired psychologist loses $180k to deepfake romance scam
World.content:
NationalQueenslandScams Retired psychologist loses $180k to deepfake romance scam Davina Smith August 26, 2026 — 8:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Watching the video call between Michael and Melanie, it’s hard to believe one person isn’t real. The conversation flows back and forth, full of emotion and feelings. Michael, a retired psychologist in his 70s living in far north Queensland, believed he was speaking with Melanie, a softly spoken nurse in South Africa. The pair met over a dating app and courted the old-fashioned way – through words and correspondence, sharing their deepest thoughts, passions and fears. The deepfake image of a woman used to scam retired psychologist Michael out of $180,000. A Current Affair “She said she was only about 50 years of age, and getting somebody interested [in me], it was obviously flattering,” Michael told A Current Affair.



“My head said, this can’t be true, but my heart said I don’t want to abandon her.” It was a whirlwind 12-month long-distance romance, until Michael exposed Melanie as a deepfake: an online persona created through identity theft and artificial intelligence. Michael suspected he was being scammed early in the relationship, but his doubts were put to rest when “Melanie” shared her identity documents. A Current Affair Scammers stole images from the social media profile of an American doctor, who had no knowledge of the scheme, combining them with YouTube videos she had created. Together with voice-cloning technology and the latest face-swapping applications, the fraudsters created a digital mask that they put on every time Michael dialled in to make a video call.



Dr Priyanka Singh, a specialist in digital forensics at the University of Queensland, analysed the final 10-minute break-up video call between the pair. She pointed out slight distortions in the woman’s earrings, and stray hairs as subtle clues that Melanie was not real, as the face-swapping software struggled to keep up with the actual fraudster’s movements. The scammers blamed these visual discrepancies on a poor internet connection. The gotcha moment was when Melanie brushed her face with her hand, which had an extra finger. A Current Affair Singh identified other major red flags, with Melanie’s chair changing shape and position during the call. At one point, it even disappears. For Singh, the gotcha moment was when Melanie brushed her face with her hand. For a fleeting moment, it appeared she had six fingers.



Michael suspected he was being scammed early in the relationship, but his doubts were put to rest when Melanie shared her passport, South African identity card, and nurse registration certificate. He also received an influx of photos, some stolen from the American doctor’s website, and others photoshopped. And when Melanie needed financial help, Michael obliged. “I didn’t question that, and I was just really, probably, falling in love very quickly,” he said. “Being an empath, it’s very hard to look away.” Michael admitted he sent $180,000 to the scammers, despite warnings from his bank and its repeated attempts to block the transactions. “I was aware that I would take a big risk, but I thought, ‘meet the love of my life and my soulmate’,” he said while shedding tears. “It feels like I’ve been so stupid.”



Related Article Scams The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise Singh said rather than scrutinising increasingly sophisticated technology, the best test when meeting someone online was to seek the opinion of loved ones. In Michael’s case, his family, including his daughter, voiced concerns about Melanie very early in the relationship. “He’s lost a lot of dignity, self-respect and self-confidence,” she told A Current Affair. “Even if he wants to get out there again and find a partner, he’s now wary of this online dating world.”



Ultimately for Michael, revenge came when he confronted the scammers while recording a video call with Melanie. She had set up the meeting hoping to get a further $7000 out of the retiree. The 10-minute call is at times agonising to watch, as the fraudster tries to put doubt in Michael’s head, questioning his commitment to the relationship, his love for her, and even questioning if he is a fraud. Singh said it was a masterclass in how these romance scams play on emotions. When Michael accused Melanie of being a scammer and demanded she admit the fraud, the scammer hung up. Michael reported the case to New South Wales police, who conducted an investigation but concluded the scam was based overseas and it was unlikely he would recover the lost money.



As for his future finding love? “I stopped all my internet accounts ... the best way is to meet somebody in person, isn’t it?” he said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Scientists make giant cyborg cockroaches that can fire drug-filled syringes
World.content:
Exclusive NationalInsects Scientists make giant cyborg cockroaches that can fire drug-filled syringes Angus Dalton August 26, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Australian scientists have created insect-robot hybrids for search-and-rescue missions.

The cockroach cyborgs are designed to find people trapped in areas human rescuers can’t reach.

The cyborgs can fire syringes from their backs for emergency treatment.

Other teams have made diving suits for cockroaches so they can operate during floods.

The concept has been trialled in the aftermath of a deadly earthquake in Myanmar.

If you ever find yourself buried beneath the rubble of an earthquake’s aftermath or expiring in a remote cave, salvation may not arrive in the form of a dashing rescuer or detection dog, but of a hulking, hissing, spiky-legged cockroach. Scientists are developing cyborg paramedic cockroaches designed to find people trapped in places human rescuers can’t reach, with the latest recruits capable of delivering medicine by firing syringes from a harpoon system on their backs. A cyborg cockroach armed with a syringe-firing backpack. The University of Queensland The “paraborg” (a portmanteau of paramedic and cyborg) insects are made from giant burrowing cockroaches, which are the world’s heaviest cockroach species and native to north Queensland. “It’s not for everyone,” biorobotics specialist and cyborg creator Dr T. Thang Vo-Doan, from the University of Queensland, said of working with the cockroaches. “But we have very good relationship with them in the lab.”



The glossy arthropods are fashioned into cyborgs by the insertion of electrodes into their antennae, so the cockroaches can be remote-controlled with a joystick. Antennae detect obstacles, so when the left one is stimulated, the cockroaches bear right, and vice versa. Other electrodes in the “cerci” – sensory appendages at the back of the insect – allow researchers to accelerate or stop the cyborg roaches. Scientists eventually want to make fully robotic, insect-inspired rescue devices but Vo-Doan said robots aren’t small, agile or efficient enough yet to operate in disaster zones. Cockroaches, however, are ready to rumble.



“The insect can climb and run, even carry heavy loads in different orientations in a complex environment,” Vo-Doan said. “You already have everything from nature. It simplifies our system a lot in terms of design and engineering.” PhD student Hai Nhan Le remotely controls “paraborg” cockroaches. The University of Queensland He believes more lives can be saved now by harnessing the insects, with agility and efficiency honed by evolution, to carry devices including cameras and sensors into collapsed buildings. While small robots are restricted by limited battery life, cockroaches can go for days, powered simply by gum leaves and apple slices. There’s no requirement for scientists to obtain ethical approval for research with insects. But the cockroaches are anaesthetised for the insertion of electrodes, and electronic systems are carefully removed after experiments.



Vo-Doan said the cyborg recruits seem to live as long and well as their civilian counterparts. The latest study, published in Advanced Science, focused on the “rescue” part of search and rescue. If a swarm of cyborg cockroaches discovered a victim buried beneath rubble who was suffering from sepsis, what happens next? Cyborg cockroaches can traverse complex, rubble-strewn environments better than robots. The University of Queensland Enter the medic class. The researchers created and tested needle-firing cyborgs and showed they could successfully navigate to a target and deliver a jab in 72 per cent of proof-of-concept trials. When cockroaches came within 15 centimetres of a mock target, the hit rate was 95 per cent.



“A lot of people might not like the sight of a giant cockroach scurrying towards them,” said PhD candidate and first author of the research Hai Nhan Le. “But if you’re trapped in rubble or stuck in a cave and need help, it could make a real difference between life and death.” The idea, eventually, is to create a “fully autonomous paramedic team composed of terrestrial cyborg insects” that can independently search for victims, relay information and deliver medication, the researchers write. The concept might seem far-fetched but other international teams are taking the same approach and have been trialling it in the field.



Ten cyborg Madagascan hissing cockroaches fitted with infrared cameras and sensors were deployed alongside Singapore’s Operation Lionheart rescue team in the aftermath of a 2025 earthquake in Myanmar that killed at least 3600 people. (The cockroach squad didn’t detect any survivors but researchers said the mission yielded valuable lessons to improve the cyborgs.) Other researchers have made 3D-printed diving suits for cyborg cockroaches that could help in flood rescues. NTU Singapore Meanwhile, in June, another team of researchers introduced the aquatic class. They designed flexible cockroach diving suits 3D-printed from resin. Cockroaches wearing the suits could operate underwater for three hours despite being a terrestrial species, the researchers reported in Nature. The amphibious cyborgs could one day carry out missions in flooded areas or help explore the deep ocean – or other planets. “The ultimate goal is to [take this technology to] space,” lead author Professor Hirotaka Sato told New Scientist. “Exploration over the Mars surface, for example.”



Related Article Analysis

China relations Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics So when might we see cyborg cockroaches rolled out to disaster zones? Perhaps five years, perhaps 20, depending on the level of support the idea gains, Vo-Doan said. Experts such as Superintendent Tim Hassiotis, from Fire & Rescue NSW, are open to the concept if the cyborgs prove effective in real emergencies. “If cyborg insects can safely enter spaces we can’t, locate casualties and ultimately help deliver emergency care, they could become another valuable tool in the future of urban search and rescue,” Hassiotis said. World.title: Police probe link between Fadi Haddara shooting and Tassie tobacco operation
World.content:
Police are investigating if the near-fatal shooting of crime figure Fadi Haddara is linked to his crime network’s alleged involvement in a multimillion-dollar tobacco and money laundering operation in Tasmania. Haddara’s targeting by a hit team was the first of three shootings targeting associates, the latest on Wednesday when a 37-year-old man was shot on a property in broad daylight in Heidelberg West. Fadi Haddara is recovering after being shot in his driveway. Jason South Haddara himself was nearly killed after being gunned down in the driveway of his family home in Altona North on August 16. He was released from hospital this week, but doctors are waiting to attempt to remove one bullet still lodged near his jawline.



“He’s up walking around, speaking properly. Friends couldn’t believe it,” an associate said. A week after the failed hit, a known Haddara associate was shot in the arm while sitting in a cafe in Altona North’s Borrack Square commonly frequented by figures linked to the clan. On Wednesday afternoon, Victoria Police said a victim had been left suffering from serious injuries after being shot outside a property on Malacca Street in Heidelberg West. A spokesperson said the unknown offenders fled in a car, and the incident is being treated as targeted. Two sources, who have knowledge of the incident but spoke anonymously for their safety, identified the 37-year-old as an associate of the Haddara patriarch.



Organised crime gang The Commission is the prime suspect behind the attacks, which signals a renewal of the hostilities that first ignited Melbourne’s tobacco wars. Related Article Organised crime He lived like a man with nothing to fear. His shooting has left even the underworld shocked The Commission, also known as the 313, is the transnational crime gang established by exiled gangland boss Kazem “Kaz” Hamad in early 2023 that has created a nationwide illicit tobacco cartel after waging a campaign of firebombings and shootings. They had reached an uneasy truce with Haddara who had stepped back from active involvement in the family’s activities after he “surrendered” to Hamad in early 2024 in exchange for an end to a campaign of fire bombings targeting family businesses and a $1 million hit contract put on his head. However, there have been a number of branches of the extended Haddara family that have allegedly continued to operate in the illicit tobacco market. Some even switched sides and were absorbed into The Commission.



The shootings started just days after the federal and state Joint Organised Crime Taskforce took down a money-laundering syndicate operating between Tasmania and Victoria. “It is alleged they facilitated the movement of criminal proceeds in cash from Tasmania and Victoria using hire cars and a commercial passenger and freight vessel,” the Australian Federal Police, Australian Border Force and Tasmanian and Victorian police announced. Loading The operation on August 12 uncovered more than $2.5 million worth of tobacco, over $1 million in cash and $34,000 in silver and gold in raids in Melbourne and near Hobart and Devonport. A 33-year-old from Hoppers Crossing and a 22-year-old Tasmanian, arrested in Melbourne, have been charged with knowingly dealing with the proceeds of crime and recklessly dealing with proceeds of crime.

World.title: Other people’s dreams bore me rigid. So why are films and TV shows full of them?
World.content:
CultureMoviesThe Verdict Other people’s dreams bore me rigid. So why are films and TV shows full of them? Dream sequences are a lazy storytelling device. The only place they belong is the cutting room floor. John Bailey August 26, 2026 — 7:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

How good is that bit in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey where Matt Damon skydives naked with the sexy chimp who talks just like his Grade 6 English teacher? No, wait, that’s a dream I had, and I won’t bore anyone further with the grubby details. Nobody likes to hear another person’s dream, especially my partner and children. Jeff Bridges dreaming of flying (among other things) in The Big Lebowski. YouTube Christopher Nolan knows that dream sequences are the worst, which is why the director famous for his flashbacks and flash-forwards and all sorts of timey-wimey shenanigans generally steers clear of sleepytime nonsense. He even directed an entire film set within dreams that strenuously avoided surrealist imagery or flights of fancy. The “dreams” in Inception were closer to your daily commute than a nude plummet with a primate playmate. This is the storytelling equivalent of waving your palms and pleading, “No, no, I take it all back!” There’s a piece of writing advice sometimes attributed to the novelist Henry James: tell a dream, lose a reader. The irony here is that James himself could really knock out a killer dream story. He wrote in an autobiography of “the most appalling yet most admirable nightmare of my life,” in which he was chased through The Louvre by a terrible creature, the whole affair lit only by lightning. But James would agree with Nolan, who recently argued that audiences “devalue” dream sequences.



How many times does a film or TV show just start to become interesting before our protagonist bolts upright amid a snarl of bedsheets, panting with relief that none of what they’ve just experienced really happened? This is the storytelling equivalent of waving your palms and pleading, “No, no, I take it all back!” It’s like ending a chapter of your book with the line “haha not really, lol”. It’s a failure of commitment, undoing the very thing that is likely the dramatic highlight of your tale. Rather than escalating tension and ratcheting up the stakes, it deflates whatever energy the dream sequence was supposed to generate. There’s also the sorry tendency to treat dreams as perfectly legible pieces of code. Thanks to Freud and Jung, storytellers feel justified in treating our complex and jumbled inner worlds as if they were simple ciphers describing our fears and desires. Yawn. Not everything that appears in our dreams represents something at the core of our psyche. Freud was forced to remind us that sometimes a cigar is just a cigar, just as I’ve been forced to remind my partner and children that sometimes a naked skydive with your Grade 6 English teacher is perfectly innocent.



I can already hear the cinephiles unsheathing their poison pens, so let me issue a caveat: I’m not against stories that are dream-like. In fact, they’re some of the best. Think of Picnic at Hanging Rock, a gossamer dream of the Australian landscape as shared by young white women under an oppressive colonial regime. The films of directors as diverse as Yasujiro Ozu, Ingmar Bergman, Sofia Coppola and Lynne Ramsay all possess a dreamlike weightlessness, even though they’re grounded in the waking world. Henry James himself pulled off the same trick with his classic The Turn of the Screw, in which the boundary between the real and the imagined is never resolved. Related Article Opinion

The Verdict Enough with the boring alpha men – I can’t get enough of this TV trend Paul Kalina Contributor Then there’s David Lynch, whose art was almost entirely defined by dream logic but who rarely stooped to anything as low as an actual dream sequence. From Twin Peaks to Mulholland Drive, dreams and reality overlap to the point that there’s little difference. Lynch often said that our partial, fragmented perception of existence means that we all essentially live inside our own private dream. His films, then, were dreams within a dream, and that’s a phrase that a whole bunch of his characters would repeat across his work. If a film is already a fantasy, then why not go the whole hog and commit? How much more compelling is it to happen upon the moment in a story that has you thinking, “This can’t be happening, not really”, only to gradually realise that yes, we’re going there, and you won’t believe what happens next, too. Take this alluring primate by the hand and leap out into that wide blue sky. No need to tell us it was just a dream all along.

World.title: Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex Jack Gramenz Updated August 26, 2026 — 8:55pm ,first published 3:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old girl on Sydney’s northern beaches after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital two days after emergency services responded to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights on Sunday night. They found the girl unresponsive. Loading She was flown in a critical condition to Royal North Shore Hospital, where she died on Tuesday night. Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex.



Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young people’s understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Consent education advocate Chanel Contos said she was devastated by news of the teen’s death: “This just feels insanely preventable.” “There is no safe way to engage in strangulation during sex, and unfortunately, mainly because of pornography, where young people are learning and mimicking scripts from that, this act that was traditionally on the fringes of kink culture has made its way into the mainstream,” the Teach Us Consent founder said. “We need to seriously investigate the impact that pornography is having on shaping the sexual scripts and behaviours of young people.” Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in 2024 that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely.



“And there’s really no reason to think that the effects of strangulation would be any different if the strangulation was consensual or otherwise,” the study’s lead author, University of Melbourne Professor Heather Douglas, said. “Even lower levels of strangulation, it can result in brain injuries like problem-solving difficulties, memory issues, and so on, and that’s without even being made unconscious, so it’s a really serious thing to do.” “There’s such a range of injuries associated with strangulation. Some are permanent, some are fleeting … it doesn’t take much pressure, and it doesn’t take very long, to have really terrible consequences.” Douglas said there were no safe ways to undertake strangulation, and she questioned aspects of consent surrounding it. Among the almost 5000 people aged between 18 and 35 surveyed in the research were reports of consent having been assumed from previous instances of strangulation, consent without an understanding of the risks, and consent influenced by pressure or power differentials, Douglas said.



“A lot of people just want to be normal … and doing normal things in their sex life. “And I think there is a bit of a normalisation of strangulation in many young people’s sex lives,” Douglas said. The 16-year-old died at Royal North Shore Hospital on Tuesday night. Renee Nowytarger Collective Shout co-founder Melinda Tankard Reist said she’s spoken to thousands of girls who have reported feeling pressured into engaging in strangulation during sex, which has been normalised by pornography and social media. “It’s put forward as something desirable and it can heighten sexual experience, but they’re not learning that, well, actually you could die.



“Young people have a right to know the injuries and the potential life-threatening risk. “This is again, just another fruit of a pornographic education,” she said. The NSW government’s own submission to a recent parliamentary inquiry said depictions of sexual aggression including strangulation in pornography has been linked to increased intimate partner violence, citing research from 2017 by the federal government’s Australian Institute of Family Studies. Federal independent MP Zali Steggall, from the neighbouring electorate of Warringah, said the teenager’s death underscored the need for a national education campaign to tackle misogyny and teach respectful relationships. “My thoughts are with her family, friends and community at this incredibly difficult time,” she said.



“Police are investigating the circumstances of the girl’s death and no charges have been laid. We must allow the legal process to take place. “Regardless of the circumstances of this particular case, the Albanese government itself has confirmed that rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are rising. “The Albanese government must urgently roll out a national campaign ensuring young people receive ongoing sexual health and relationship education.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Hundreds of people were reported missing after an avalanche of ice and rock triggered massive flash floods that swept through parts of Nepal on Wednesday, killing at least eight people and causing widespread damage to villages and infrastructure.

Officials said 384 tourists, including 291 from countries including India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Malaysia, were reported missing as a result of the flash flood.

Damaged houses stand precariously near the swollen, debris-choked banks of the Trishuli River after flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha

The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9am on Wednesday, destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. They issued warnings to residents of several of Nepal’s districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.

“We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts,” said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government.
